A Theory of Generalization in Deep Learning

Elon Litman Thanks: Corresponding author: elonlit@stanford.edu    Gabe Guo
Abstract

We present a non-asymptotic theory of generalization in deep learning where the empirical neural tangent kernel partitions the output space. In directions corresponding to signal, error dissipates rapidly; in the vast orthogonal dimensions corresponding to noise, the kernel’s near-zero eigenvalues trap residual error in a test-invisible reservoir. Within the signal channel, minibatch SGD ensures that coherent population signal accumulates via fast linear drift, while idiosyncratic memorization is suppressed into a slow, diffusive random walk. We prove generalization survives even when the kernel evolves 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) in operator norm, the full feature-learning regime. This theory naturally explains disparate phenomena in deep learning theory, such as benign overfitting, double descent, implicit bias, and grokking. Lastly, we derive an exact population-risk objective from a single training run with no validation data, for any architecture, loss, or optimizer, and prove that it measures precisely the noise in the signal channel. This objective reduces in practice to an SNR preconditioner on top of Adam, adding one state vector at no extra cost; it accelerates grokking by 5×5\times, suppresses memorization in PINNs and implicit neural representations, and improves DPO fine-tuning under noisy preferences while staying 3×3\times closer to the reference policy.

Stanford University

1 Introduction

A neural network with more parameters than training examples can memorize arbitrary labels, including pure noise (31), yet the same training procedure usually generalizes on real data. Classical capacity bounds are vacuous at practical scale, and frozen-kernel theory (17) describes the lazy regime, whereas modern architectures train in the full feature-learning regime. We develop a theory of generalization that handles full feature learning, and we derive a practical method that trains directly on population risk.

We work in output space along the realized trajectory. The empirical tangent kernel 𝑲S​S=𝑱S​𝑱S⊤\bm{K}_{\!SS}=\bm{J}_{S}\bm{J}_{S}^{\top} selects which output directions training can move, and integrating its evolution gives the cumulative dissipation 𝒲S\mathcal{W}_{S}, whose range is the signal channel and whose kernel is the reservoir. The test-train kernel 𝑲Q​S=𝑱Q​𝑱S⊤\bm{K}_{\!QS}=\bm{J}_{Q}\bm{J}_{S}^{\top} shares the factor 𝑱S⊤\bm{J}_{S}^{\top}, so every reservoir direction is invisible to every test set; SGD attenuates surviving label noise because its centered minibatch fluctuation diffuses while drift accumulates; and on the signal-channel side the training and test displacements both factor through 𝒲S1/2\mathcal{W}_{S}^{1/2}, so under squared loss test motion is determined exactly by training motion along the realized path, even when the kernel drifts by 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) in operator norm. Figure 1 summarizes the resulting decomposition of test error and locates the classical phenomena: grokking, double descent, implicit bias, and benign overfitting, within it.

Exchangeability turns the same operators into population risk. The test transfer 𝖦\mathsf{G} instantiated with each training point as a one-point test set against the remaining batch is an unbiased rate of population-risk decrease, and on a one-step window it pulls back through the per-example Jacobians to tr⁡(M​𝑨B)\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{A}_{B}) with 𝑨B=𝒈¯B​𝒈¯B⊤−1b−1​𝚺B\bm{A}_{B}=\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}^{\top}-\tfrac{1}{b-1}\bm{\Sigma}_{B}. Maximizing this through the optimizer’s metric updates parameter kk only when μk2\mu_{k}^{2} exceeds σk2/(b−1)\sigma_{k}^{2}/(b-1), a one-line change to Adam with one extra state vector.

2 Related Work

The question of why overparameterized neural networks generalize has attracted sustained attention from both the statistical and optimization communities.

Worst-case bounds and algorithmic stability.

Uniform-convergence bounds, whether expressed in terms of VC dimension (28), covering numbers (10), Rademacher complexity (4), weight norms (5; 24), or spectral complexity (2), are vacuous at practical scale (31), and 21 argued that uniform convergence is insufficient for deep learning. Algorithmic stability (7; 13) bounds the sensitivity to single-point perturbations and requires global Lipschitz constants, which are unavailable for nonconvex losses. PAC-Bayes bounds (20; 11) incorporate a data-dependent posterior; the KL penalty becomes meaningful at practical scale once the prior is optimized along the training trajectory, reintroducing path dependence. Our theory provides the appropriate localization: global Lipschitz constants are replaced by path-dependent output-space quantities that capture the actual landscape encountered during training.

Kernel theories and benign overfitting.

The neural tangent kernel (NTK) (17; 9) shows that sufficiently wide networks evolve as kernel methods with a frozen tangent kernel, and generalization follows from classical kernel bounds (1; 19). The benign-overfitting literature (6; 22; 3; 27; 14) established that interpolation can be statistically harmless under appropriate spectral decay, primarily for linear or kernel models. Our theory unifies both regimes: the frozen-kernel limit is a special case, full feature learning is handled with an evolving kernel, and benign overfitting is explained mechanistically as noise trapped in test-invisible directions.

Influence functions and leave-one-out.

Classical influence functions (8) approximate the effect of removing a training point via a single Newton step at the empirical risk minimizer. 18 brought the tool to deep learning for data attribution, retaining the single-step linearization at the trained weights. The population-risk objective of Section 6 reads the leave-one-out displacement directly off the test-transfer operator 𝖦\mathsf{G} at the current step, with each training point treated as a one-point test set against the remaining batch. Where classical influence linearizes at the trained weights and folds the trajectory into a Hessian, the operator form gives a one-step kernel-block expression that the optimizer can compute from the gradients it already sees, and the same operator at the full window TT recovers the expected generalization gap as an average of self-influences (Theorem F.6).

3 Output Space Dynamics: Signal Channel and Reservoir

We work in output space, since that is where train and test predictions actually live. Let 𝒵\mathcal{Z} be a measurable instance space, let S=(z1,…,zn)∈𝒵nS=(z_{1},\dots,z_{n})\in\mathcal{Z}^{n} be the training set, and let F:ℝd×𝒵→ℝpF\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}^{p} be C2C^{2} in the parameters 𝒘\bm{w} for every instance zz, supporting residual networks (15) and Transformers (29). ∂t𝒈⁡(t)\displaystyle\partial_{t}\bm{g}(t) =−𝑩⁡(t)​𝑲S​S​(t)​𝒈​(t),\displaystyle=-\bm{B}(t)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(t)\bm{g}(t), (5)
dd​t​ΦS​(𝒖⁡(t))\displaystyle\tfrac{d}{dt}\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(t)) =−𝒈​(t)⊤​𝑲S​S​(t)​𝒈​(t)=−‖𝑱S⊤​𝒈‖22.\displaystyle=-\bm{g}(t)^{\top}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(t)\bm{g}(t)=-\|\bm{J}_{S}^{\top}\bm{g}\|_{2}^{2}. (6)

The output gradient therefore propagates as 𝒈⁡(t)=𝒫g​(t,0)​𝒈​(0)\bm{g}(t)=\mathcal{P}_{g}(t,0)\bm{g}(0), where the propagator 𝒫g​(⋅,s)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\cdot,s) solves the linear ODE

∂t𝒫g​(t,s)=−𝑩⁡(t)​𝑲S​S​(t)​𝒫g​(t,s),𝒫g​(s,s)=𝑰.\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathcal{P}_{g}(t,s)=-\bm{B}(t)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(t)\mathcal{P}_{g}(t,s),\hskip 20.00003pt\mathcal{P}_{g}(s,s)=\bm{I}. (7)

Definition 3.1 (Cumulative Dissipation, Signal Channel, and Reservoir).

Fix 0≤s≤T0\leq s\leq T. The cumulative dissipation Gramian and its spectral projectors (derivation from output dynamics in Section C.1) are

𝒲S​(s,T)\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,T) ≜∫sT𝒫g​(τ,s)⊤​𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝑑τ,\displaystyle\triangleq\int_{s}^{T}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)^{\top}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)d\tau, (8)

For a test set QQ and 𝑾≜𝒲S​(s,T)\bm{W}\triangleq\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,T), the test transfer operator is

𝖦Q​(T,s)\displaystyle\mathsf{G}_{Q}(T,s) ≜∫sT𝑲Q​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\triangleq\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)d\tau. (11)

The chain rule gives 𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)=−𝖦Q​(T,s)​𝒈​(s)\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)=-\mathsf{G}_{Q}(T,s)\bm{g}(s), so 𝖦Q\mathsf{G}_{Q} propagates the output gradient to test displacement.

Proposition 3.2 (Reservoir test-invisibility).

The test transfer operator vanishes on the reservoir,

ker⁡𝑾⊆ker⁡𝖦Q,\displaystyle\ker\bm{W}\subseteq\ker\mathsf{G}_{Q}, (12)

so spectral projectors of 𝐖\bm{W} onto small or zero eigenvalues annihilate 𝖦Q\mathsf{G}_{Q}. The corresponding inequality 𝐆⊤​𝐆⪯‖ΓQ​(s,T)‖op​𝐖\bm{G}^{\top}\bm{G}\preceq\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}\bm{W} on bounded functions of 𝐖\bm{W} is recorded in Appendix C.

Reservoir directions cannot affect any test prediction: residual error sitting in ker⁡𝒲S\ker\mathcal{W}_{S} shows up on training outputs while contributing nothing at test. The same conclusion holds after any positive-semidefinite preconditioning of the parameter updates: substituting 𝑱S↦𝑱S​M1/2\bm{J}_{S}\mapsto\bm{J}_{S}M^{1/2} in the proof yields ker⁡𝒲SM⊆ker⁡𝖦QM\ker\mathcal{W}_{S}^{M}\subseteq\ker\mathsf{G}_{Q}^{M} for the preconditioned operators (Section C.1), so the optimizer’s choice of MtM_{t} at each step determines which parameter directions enter the signal channel; Section 6 picks the MtM_{t} that maximizes a population-safe rate. The frozen-kernel limit reduces 𝒲S\mathcal{W}_{S} to a closed-form spectral filter that recovers benign overfitting, double descent, implicit bias, grokking, and ridge regression as different choices of one preconditioner (Theorem H.1); we record this in Appendix H, with the linear-model worked example in Section H.2.

Two questions remain about the signal channel. Inside it, what happens to the residual label noise the optimizer fitted? Section 4 shows that minibatch SGD’s drift accumulates linearly along population-gradient directions while its centered fluctuation diffuses, so noise channels die at rate 1/n+η​T/b1/\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{\eta T/b} against the Θ⁡(T)\Theta(T) accumulation on signal channels. And what predicts test motion from training motion when the kernel evolves over a typical run? Section 5 shows that 𝑫\bm{D} and 𝖦Q\mathsf{G}_{Q} both factor through 𝒲S1/2\mathcal{W}_{S}^{1/2}, and that under squared loss the test displacement is determined exactly by the training displacement on the realized window.

4 Minibatch Drift Versus Diffusion

The reservoir cannot affect any test prediction. Inside the signal channel, the residual label noise the optimizer fitted is suppressed by minibatch SGD itself: the centered fluctuation 𝝃k=𝒈^k−𝝁k\bm{\xi}_{k}=\hat{\bm{g}}_{k}-\bm{\mu}_{k} has 𝔼⁡[𝝃k∣ℱk]=0\mathbb{E}[\bm{\xi}_{k}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}]=0, so it contributes only diffusion, and on a noise direction the population gradient at fresh draws also vanishes, so the drift dies as 1/n1/\sqrt{n}. A genuine signal direction has Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) drift and accumulates linearly.

To make this precise, decompose each minibatch gradient into its conditional mean and a centered fluctuation, and write the test prediction under preconditioner 𝑴k\bm{M}_{k},

𝒈^k\displaystyle\hat{\bm{g}}_{k} =𝝁k+𝝃k,\displaystyle=\bm{\mu}_{k}+\bm{\xi}_{k}, 𝝁k\displaystyle\bm{\mu}_{k} ≜𝔼⁡[𝒈^k∣ℱk],\displaystyle\triangleq\mathbb{E}[\hat{\bm{g}}_{k}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}], 𝑳Q,k\displaystyle\bm{L}_{Q,k} ≜𝑱Q​(𝒘k)​𝑴k.\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{J}_{Q}(\bm{w}_{k})\bm{M}_{k}. (13)

Taylor-expanding the test prediction along NN SGD steps with step size η\eta and horizon T=N​ηT=N\eta gives the decomposition together with a step-size bound on the second-order remainder, valid whenever 𝑱Q\bm{J}_{Q} is βQ\beta_{Q}-Lipschitz along the trajectory:

𝑼Q​(𝒘N)−𝑼Q​(𝒘0)\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}_{N})-\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}_{0}) =−η∑k=0N−1𝑳Q,k𝝁k⏟𝚫Qdrift−η​∑k=0N−1𝑳Q,k​𝝃k⏟𝚫Qdiff+𝓡Q,\displaystyle=\underbrace{-\eta\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bm{L}_{Q,k}\bm{\mu}_{k}}_{\bm{\Delta}_{Q}^{\mathrm{drift}}}-\underbrace{\eta\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bm{L}_{Q,k}\bm{\xi}_{k}}_{\bm{\Delta}_{Q}^{\mathrm{diff}}}+\bm{\mathcal{R}}_{Q}, (14)
‖𝓡Q‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{\mathcal{R}}_{Q}\|_{2} ≤βQ2​∑k=0N−1‖𝒘k+1−𝒘k‖22.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\beta_{Q}}{2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\|\bm{w}_{k+1}-\bm{w}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}. (15)

The fluctuations η​𝑳Q,k​𝝃k\eta\bm{L}_{Q,k}\bm{\xi}_{k} are martingale differences with respect to {ℱk}\{\mathcal{F}_{k}\}.

Theorem 4.1 (Drift–diffusion separation).

If the test-projected fluctuation covariance is uniformly bounded by Vk/bV_{k}/b, the drift and diffusion terms accumulate at separated rates,

‖𝚫Qdrift‖2\displaystyle\bigl\|\bm{\Delta}_{Q}^{\mathrm{drift}}\bigr\|_{2} =O⁡(T),\displaystyle=O(T), ‖𝚫Qdiff‖L2\displaystyle\bigl\|\bm{\Delta}_{Q}^{\mathrm{diff}}\bigr\|_{L^{2}} =O⁡(η​T/b),\displaystyle=O\!\left(\sqrt{\eta T/b}\right), 𝔼​‖𝚷​𝝁k‖22\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\bm{\Pi}\bm{\mu}_{k}\|_{2}^{2} =O⁡(1/n),\displaystyle=O(1/n), (16)

where the last bound holds on a noise channel with vanishing population gradient at fresh draws under a replace-two stability hypothesis on the projected gradient (Appendix D), and is exact when the minibatch is independent of ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k}. The channel’s test displacement is therefore O⁡(T/n+η​T/b)O(T/\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{\eta T/b}), asymptotically smaller than the Θ⁡(T)\Theta(T) accumulation of a genuine signal channel.

A genuine signal channel has 𝔼Z∼𝒟​[𝚷​∇𝒘ℓ∣ℱk]≠0\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}[\bm{\Pi}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}]\neq 0, so ‖𝚷​𝝁k‖2=Θ⁡(1)\|\bm{\Pi}\bm{\mu}_{k}\|_{2}=\Theta(1) and the drift accumulates linearly (Appendix D). The squared-mean-versus-trace comparison driving the off-diagonal agreement ΩB\Omega_{B} reappears here as the separation between Θ⁡(T)\Theta(T) drift and O⁡(η​T/b)O(\sqrt{\eta T/b}) diffusion (Theorem 6.2). The next section restricts this trajectory-level statement to a per-parameter update at a single optimizer step.

5 Train-Test Coupling under Feature Learning

The reservoir is invisible at test, and Section 4 showed that residual label noise inside the signal channel decays under SGD. The remaining piece is the signal in the signal channel: when does training motion determine test motion in the feature-learning regime? Abbreviating 𝑾≜𝒲S​(s,T)\bm{W}\triangleq\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,T), the training-side analogue of 𝖦Q\mathsf{G}_{Q} and its dissipation-normalized counterpart are

𝑫\displaystyle\bm{D} ≜∫sT𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝑑τ=𝖢S​𝑾1/2,\displaystyle\triangleq\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)d\tau=\mathsf{C}_{S}\bm{W}^{1/2}, 𝖢S\displaystyle\mathsf{C}_{S} ≜𝑫𝑾†/2,\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{D}\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}, (17)
𝑮\displaystyle\bm{G} ≜∫sT𝑲Q​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝑑τ=𝖢Q​𝑾1/2,\displaystyle\triangleq\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)d\tau=\mathsf{C}_{Q}\bm{W}^{1/2}, 𝖢Q\displaystyle\mathsf{C}_{Q} ≜𝑮𝑾†/2,\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{G}\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}, (18)

both well-defined since 𝑫\bm{D} and 𝑮\bm{G} vanish on ker⁡𝑾\ker\bm{W} (Section 3); the chain rule gives the train-side companion 𝑼S​(T)−𝑼S​(s)=−𝑫​𝒈​(s)\bm{U}_{S}(T)-\bm{U}_{S}(s)=-\bm{D}\bm{g}(s) to the test relation 𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)=−𝑮​𝒈​(s)\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)=-\bm{G}\bm{g}(s). Orthogonally projecting 𝖢Q\mathsf{C}_{Q} onto range⁡(𝖢S⊤)\operatorname{range}(\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\top}) produces the optimal linear predictor 𝑨∘\bm{A}_{\circ} and an irreducible remainder 𝑹⟂\bm{R}_{\perp},

𝑨∘≜𝖢Q​𝖢S†,𝑹⟂≜𝖢Q​(𝑰−𝖢S†​𝖢S),\displaystyle\bm{A}_{\circ}\triangleq\mathsf{C}_{Q}\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\dagger},\hskip 20.00003pt\bm{R}_{\perp}\triangleq\mathsf{C}_{Q}\bigl(\bm{I}-\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\dagger}\mathsf{C}_{S}\bigr), (19)

in the operator analogue of regressing one Gaussian variable on another. For an arbitrary linear predictor 𝑨\bm{A}, the error operator (𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)​𝑾†​(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)⊤(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger}(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})^{\top} splits orthogonally into the irreducible piece 𝑹⟂​𝑹⟂⊤\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{R}_{\perp}^{\top} and a quadratic penalty in 𝑨−𝑨∘\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ} (Theorem E.3), so 𝑨∘\bm{A}_{\circ} is the unique minimizer in the positive-semidefinite order. The frozen-kernel limit recovers classical kernel regression, 𝑨∘=𝑲Q​S​𝑲S​S†\bm{A}_{\circ}=\bm{K}_{\!QS}\bm{K}_{\!SS}^{\dagger} and 𝑹⟂=𝟎\bm{R}_{\perp}=\bm{0} (Appendix H, Section H.2).

Theorem 5.1 (Train-test coupling).

Suppose ΦS​(𝐮)=12​(𝐮−𝐲)⊤​𝐁​(𝐮−𝐲)\Phi_{S}(\bm{u})=\tfrac{1}{2}(\bm{u}-\bm{y})^{\top}\bm{B}(\bm{u}-\bm{y}) for some 𝐁≻0\bm{B}\succ 0 (squared loss has 𝐁=1n​𝐈\bm{B}=\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{I}). 𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)=𝑨∘​(𝑼S​(T)−𝑼S​(s)),𝑨∘=𝑮​𝑫†,\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)=\bm{A}_{\circ}\bigl(\bm{U}_{S}(T)-\bm{U}_{S}(s)\bigr),\hskip 20.00003pt\bm{A}_{\circ}=\bm{G}\bm{D}^{\dagger}, (20)

with no kernel-stability or asymptotic hypothesis.

Sketch.

With constant 𝑩\bm{B}, integrating (7) gives explicitly

𝑫=𝑩−1​(𝑰−𝒫g​(T,s)),𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉=12​(‖𝒉‖𝑩−12−‖𝒫g​(T,s)​𝒉‖𝑩−12),\displaystyle\bm{D}=\bm{B}^{-1}\bigl(\bm{I}-\mathcal{P}_{g}(T,s)\bigr),\hskip 20.00003pt\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\|\bm{h}\|_{\bm{B}^{-1}}^{2}-\|\mathcal{P}_{g}(T,s)\bm{h}\|_{\bm{B}^{-1}}^{2}\bigr), (21)

so 𝑫​𝒉=𝟎\bm{D}\bm{h}=\bm{0} forces 𝒫g​(T,s)​𝒉=𝒉\mathcal{P}_{g}(T,s)\bm{h}=\bm{h} and then 𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉=0\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}=0, giving ker⁡𝑫=ker⁡𝑾\ker\bm{D}=\ker\bm{W}. Reservoir test-invisibility yields ker⁡𝑫⊆ker⁡𝑮\ker\bm{D}\subseteq\ker\bm{G}, equivalent to 𝑹⟂=𝟎\bm{R}_{\perp}=\bm{0}. Full proof in Appendix E. ∎

Test error decomposes into bias plus signal-channel variance.

Write the labels as 𝒚=f⋆​(S)+𝜺\bm{y}=f^{\star}(S)+\bm{\varepsilon} and split the noise along the signal channel range⁡(𝑾)\operatorname{range}(\bm{W}) and the reservoir ker⁡𝑾\ker\bm{W} via projectors 𝑷sig,𝑷res\bm{P}_{\mathrm{sig}},\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}}. Under squared loss the initial gradient is 𝒈⁡(0)=1n​(𝑼S​(0)−𝒚)\bm{g}(0)=\tfrac{1}{n}(\bm{U}_{S}(0)-\bm{y}), so the exact test displacement 𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(0)=−𝑮​𝒈​(0)=1n​𝑮​(𝒚−𝑼S​(0))\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(0)=-\bm{G}\bm{g}(0)=\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{G}(\bm{y}-\bm{U}_{S}(0)) separates as

𝑼Q​(T)−f⋆​(Q)=𝑼Q​(0)+1n​𝑨∘​𝑫​(f⋆​(S)−𝑼S​(0))−f⋆​(Q)⏟bias, controlled by ​𝑹⟂+1n​𝑮​𝑷res​𝜺⏟=𝟎+1n​𝑮​𝑷sig​𝜺⏟signal-channel variance.\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-f^{\star}(Q)=\underbrace{\bm{U}_{Q}(0)+\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D}\bigl(f^{\star}(S)-\bm{U}_{S}(0)\bigr)-f^{\star}(Q)}_{\text{bias, controlled by }\bm{R}_{\perp}}+\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{G}\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}}\bm{\varepsilon}}_{=\bm{0}}+\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{G}\bm{P}_{\mathrm{sig}}\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\text{signal-channel variance}}. (22)

The bias is the optimal train-to-test predictor 𝑨∘\bm{A}_{\circ} applied to the clean training displacement 1n​𝑫​(f⋆​(S)−𝑼S​(0))\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{D}(f^{\star}(S)-\bm{U}_{S}(0)), exact under squared loss (𝑮=𝑨∘​𝑫\bm{G}=\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D}, 𝑹⟂=𝟎\bm{R}_{\perp}=\bm{0}); the Sobolev refinement ‖𝑹⟂‖op≤C​hSm−dℳ/2\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}\leq Ch_{S}^{m-d_{\mathcal{M}}/2} in Theorem E.9 extends this to smooth networks on dense samples (tight without smoothness, Section E.3). The reservoir term vanishes unconditionally by reservoir invisibility: ker⁡𝑾⊆ker⁡𝑮\ker\bm{W}\subseteq\ker\bm{G} (Section 3) and range⁡(𝑷res)=ker⁡𝑾\operatorname{range}(\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}})=\ker\bm{W}, so 𝑮​𝑷res=𝟎\bm{G}\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}}=\bm{0} as an algebraic identity, with no appeal to a pseudoinverse. The signal-channel term is the only remaining failure mode; Section 4 shows SGD’s drift along it accumulates as O⁡(T)O(T) against O⁡(T)O(\sqrt{T}) noise diffusion, and Section 6 derives the population-risk gate that targets it directly. Full statement and proof in Section E.5; the operators are computable on the realized path (Section E.8).

Inside the signal channel, both stable structure and idiosyncratic memorization reduce training loss, so a complexity measure R≻0R\succ 0 on output space turns the ranking into an eigenvalue problem for R−1/2𝒲SR−1/2R^{-1/2}\mathcal{W}_{S}R^{-1/2}; the natural RR is the self-influence metric (Appendix G), which at a single optimizer step collapses to the gradient covariance 𝚺B\bm{\Sigma}_{B} used in Section 6.

6 Population Risk Training

The previous sections describe how training motion shapes test motion. The same operators turn the training data into an unbiased rate of population-risk decrease, and localizing to a single optimizer step yields a per-parameter rule the optimizer can compute from the gradients it already sees.

We use i.i.d. sampling only through exchangeability of the training nn-tuple: (S−i,Zi)=d(Sn−1,Z)(S_{-i},Z_{i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(S_{n-1},Z). A held-out point’s loss is then an unbiased sample of population risk for the model trained on the remaining data.

Lemma 6.1 (Exchangeability).

For a held-out subset I⊂[n]I\subset[n] and the model 𝐰T​(S−I)\bm{w}_{T}(S_{-I}) trained without SIS_{I},

𝔼⁡[1|I|​∑i∈Iℓ⁡(𝒘T​(S−I),Zi)]=𝔼⁡[ℒ𝒟​(𝒘T​(Sn−|I|))].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{i\in I}\ell\bigl(\bm{w}_{T}(S_{-I}),Z_{i}\bigr)\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}\bigl(\bm{w}_{T}(S_{n-|I|})\bigr)\right]. (23)

For |I|=1|I|=1 this is leave-one-out; for |I|=n/K|I|=n/K it is KK-fold cross-validation; for |I|=b|I|=b on a fresh online minibatch it is the case the algorithm uses.

Population risk through the test transfer.

Fix a window [s,T][s,T] and an exchangeable batch B=(z1,…,zb)B=(z_{1},\dots,z_{b}). For each aa, set Qa≜{za}Q_{a}\triangleq\{z_{a}\} and S−a≜B∖{za}S_{-a}\triangleq B\setminus\{z_{a}\}, and read off the test transfer of Equation 11 for this pair under preconditioner MM. The new ingredient is the choice of zaz_{a} as a one-point test set against the remainder of the batch; the operator itself is the same one that governed train-test coupling in Section 5.

Theorem 6.2 (Population-risk rate).

On a one-step window [t,t+η][t,t+\eta] from 𝐰t\bm{w}_{t} the propagator is the identity to first order, so

𝖦Qa,S−aM​(t+η,t)=η​𝑲Qa,S−aM​(t)+O⁡(η2),\displaystyle\mathsf{G}_{Q_{a},S_{-a}}^{M}(t+\eta,t)=\eta\,\bm{K}^{M}_{Q_{a},S_{-a}}(t)+O(\eta^{2}), (24)

the row block of 𝐊S​SM\bm{K}_{\!SS}^{M} pairing point aa with the rest of the batch (the self-block Ka​aMK_{aa}^{M} is absent because a∉S−aa\notin S_{-a}). Averaging the leave-one-out improvement over aa,

1b​∑a=1b(ℓa​(𝒘t)−ℓa​(𝒘−a+))\displaystyle\frac{1}{b}\sum_{a=1}^{b}\bigl(\ell_{a}(\bm{w}_{t})-\ell_{a}(\bm{w}_{-a}^{+})\bigr) =η​ΩB​(M)+O⁡(η2),\displaystyle=\eta\Omega_{B}(M)+O(\eta^{2}), ΩB​(M)\displaystyle\Omega_{B}(M) ≜1b⁡(b−1)​∑a≠c𝒓a⊤​Ka​cM​𝒓c,\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{1}{b(b-1)}\sum_{a\neq c}\bm{r}_{a}^{\top}K_{ac}^{M}\bm{r}_{c}, (25)

and by Section 6 the conditional expectation of the left side given ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} is the population risk of the one-step learner trained on an independent (b−1)(b-1)-sample.

The off-diagonal agreement ΩB​(M)\Omega_{B}(M) is the kernel-block expression of the only failure mode left after Section 3 and Theorem E.13: the signal-channel noise 1n​𝑮​𝑷sig​𝜺\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{G}\bm{P}_{\mathrm{sig}}\bm{\varepsilon} in (22). The reservoir is invisible to both sides at once: ker⁡𝒲S⊆ker⁡𝖦\ker\mathcal{W}_{S}\subseteq\ker\mathsf{G} kills the directions the run did not dissipate for every test prediction and for the population-safe rate. The training transfer 𝑫\bm{D} rides the full quadratic form 𝒈⊤​𝑲S​SM​𝒈\bm{g}^{\top}\bm{K}_{\!SS}^{M}\bm{g} including the self-blocks Ka​aMK_{aa}^{M} that empirical-risk minimization sees, while 𝖦Qa,S−a\mathsf{G}_{Q_{a},S_{-a}} excludes them. Population-risk training is therefore the test-side analogue of empirical-risk descent. Specializing to a one-step window and lifting through 𝒈a=𝑱a⊤​𝒓a\bm{g}_{a}=\bm{J}_{a}^{\top}\bm{r}_{a} collapses ΩB​(M)\Omega_{B}(M) to a parameter-space objective tr⁡(M​𝑨B)\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{A}_{B}) with 𝑨B=𝒈¯B​𝒈¯B⊤−1b−1​𝚺B\bm{A}_{B}=\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}^{\top}-\tfrac{1}{b-1}\bm{\Sigma}_{B} (Section F.2, Theorem F.1, Theorem F.5).

Corollary 6.3 (Population-Risk Descent).

For diagonal 𝐏t=diag⁡(pk)\bm{P}_{t}=\operatorname{diag}(p_{k}), the unique binary mask maximizing tr⁡(M​𝐀B)\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{A}_{B}) over 0⪯M⪯𝐏t0\preceq M\preceq\bm{P}_{t} updates parameter kk exactly when μk2>σk2/(b−1)\mu_{k}^{2}>\sigma_{k}^{2}/(b-1), where μk=g¯B,k\mu_{k}=\bar{g}_{B,k} and σk2=(𝚺B)k​k\sigma_{k}^{2}=(\bm{\Sigma}_{B})_{kk}. The cutoff is tight in both directions: a parameter that fails it admits an adversarial loss curvature forcing a strict first-order increase in population risk (Section F.2).

Influence functions on the realized path.

Evaluated at the full window TT rather than a single step, the same operator 𝖦Qi,S​(T)\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i},S}(T) becomes the leave-one-out displacement that controls each training point’s contribution to the generalization gap, and averaging over ii recovers the gap exactly (Theorem F.6, subsubsection G.3.1). This generalizes classical influence functions (8; 18): where those linearize a Hessian and lose the path, the operator form integrates 𝖦\mathsf{G} along the realized trajectory and so remains exact under 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) kernel drift.

From the rate to the algorithm.

Each one-step kernel increment η​𝑲S​SMt\eta\bm{K}_{\!SS}^{M_{t}} integrates into 𝒲SM\mathcal{W}_{S}^{M}, so a sequence of one-step rate-maximizers is the greedy policy whose integral is the signal-channel content of the trajectory through 𝖦\mathsf{G}, exactly as plain SGD is the greedy step whose integral is empirical-risk descent through 𝑫\bm{D}. The diagonal cutoff μk2>σk2/(b−1)\mu_{k}^{2}>\sigma_{k}^{2}/(b-1) is the optimal first-order preconditioner for population risk on any diagonal base, and a streaming variance EMA 𝒔^t\hat{\bm{s}}_{t} of squared gradient deviations realizes it as a one-line change to AdamW: one extra parameter-sized state vector and a per-parameter gate that multiplies the standard moment update (Equation 241, Algorithm 1). The leave-one-out coefficient is α=1\alpha=1 on the fresh-batch boundary and α=b/(n−b)\alpha=b/(n-b) on the finite-dataset boundary (Theorem F.5); soft and SNR forms of the gate and multi-epoch corrections are in Section F.4.

Results.

We test the resulting rule across three regimes where empirical-risk training is known to overfit structured noise or to memorize before generalizing; architecture, data split, and optimizer hyperparameters are held fixed and only the population-risk update changes. On a PINN solving ut+β​ux=0u_{t}+\beta u_{x}=0 at β=5\beta=5 from a Gaussian-noisy initial condition, the rule reaches relative ℓ2≤0.40\ell_{2}\leq 0.40 in 2.4×2.4\times fewer iterations than the best learning-rate-tuned AdamW (Figure 3, Table 3). On modular division a⋅b−1mod97a\cdot b^{-1}\bmod 97 at 25%25\% training fraction, where empirical-risk training is known to grok (25), the same update reaches 95%95\% held-out accuracy at step 5,9505{,}950 versus 29,45029{,}450 for AdamW (Figure 4). Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (30) with DPO under 30%30\% swapped UltraFeedback preferences (Figure 5, Table 4) improves final reward accuracy from 0.5660.566 to 0.6410.641 while staying 3.05×3.05\times closer to the reference policy in mean absolute reward drift.

7 Conclusion

As a deep network trains, its empirical NTK rotates label noise into a test-invisible reservoir, and SGD’s centered fluctuation suppresses what survives in the signal channel; on the signal side, training motion determines test motion, even when the kernel drifts by 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1). The same operators turn a single batch into an unbiased rate of population-risk decrease, maximized through the optimizer’s metric by a per-parameter gate. The frozen-kernel limit of our theory reproduces benign overfitting, double descent, implicit bias, and grokking from one spectral filter.

Appendix C Output-Space Dynamics: Proofs

Intuition.

Under gradient flow the loss gradient decays at rates set by a tangent kernel weighted by loss curvature, and every quantity of interest (training displacement, test displacement, dissipation) is the integral of how that vector flows. The proofs below extend the neural tangent kernel framework of 17, 9 to the feature-learning regime where the kernel itself evolves with the parameters, and isolate the operators used in the train-test coupling and population-risk arguments later.

C.1 Deriving the Operators from Output Dynamics

Intuition.

The operators 𝑫S\bm{D}_{S}, 𝑮Q\bm{G}_{Q}, and 𝒲S\mathcal{W}_{S} used throughout Section 3 and Section 5 derive from integrating the output dynamics of Section 3 over time. Here, we write that integration explicitly so the dissipation Gramian’s spectrum has a direct reading: the eigenvalue along 𝝍j\bm{\psi}_{j} is the total integrated squared reachability of 𝝍j\bm{\psi}_{j} across the window.

Train and test displacement integrals.

The output dynamics give ∂τ𝒖⁡(τ)=−𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒈​(τ)\partial_{\tau}\bm{u}(\tau)=-\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\bm{g}(\tau), and the propagator gives 𝒈⁡(τ)=𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒈​(s)\bm{g}(\tau)=\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{g}(s). Substituting and integrating over [s,T][s,T], with 𝒈⁡(s)\bm{g}(s) constant in τ\tau,

𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s)\displaystyle\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s) =−∫sT𝑲S​S(τ)𝒫g(τ,s)𝒈(s)dτ=−𝑫S(T,s)𝒈(s),\displaystyle=-\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{g}(s)d\tau=-\bm{D}_{S}(T,s)\bm{g}(s), (26)
𝑫S​(T,s)\displaystyle\bm{D}_{S}(T,s) ≜∫sT𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\triangleq\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)d\tau. (27)

The same derivation with the test-side dynamics ∂τ𝑼Q=−𝑲Q​S​𝒈\partial_{\tau}\bm{U}_{Q}=-\bm{K}_{\!QS}\bm{g} and 𝑲Q​S​(τ)=𝑱Q​(τ)​𝑱S​(τ)⊤\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)=\bm{J}_{Q}(\tau)\bm{J}_{S}(\tau)^{\top} in place of 𝑲S​S​(τ)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau) yields

𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s) =−𝑮Q​(T,s)​𝒈​(s),\displaystyle=-\bm{G}_{Q}(T,s)\bm{g}(s), (28)
𝑮Q​(T,s)\displaystyle\bm{G}_{Q}(T,s) ≜∫sT𝑲Q​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\triangleq\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)d\tau. (29)

Same integral, same propagator, different kernel: 𝑫S\bm{D}_{S} records how training outputs moved, 𝑮Q\bm{G}_{Q} how test outputs moved.

Cumulative dissipation as a quadratic form.

Substituting 𝒈⁡(τ)=𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒈​(s)\bm{g}(\tau)=\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{g}(s) into the instantaneous dissipation rate from Section 3, integrating over [s,T][s,T], and pulling out 𝒈⁡(s)\bm{g}(s),

ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T))\displaystyle\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T)) =∫sT𝒈​(s)⊤​𝒫g​(τ,s)⊤​𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒈​(s)​𝑑τ\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{T}\bm{g}(s)^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)^{\top}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{g}(s)d\tau (30)
=𝒈​(s)⊤​𝒲S​(s,T)​𝒈​(s).\displaystyle=\bm{g}(s)^{\top}\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,T)\bm{g}(s). (31)

Total loss dissipated over [s,T][s,T] is therefore the quadratic form of 𝒲S\mathcal{W}_{S} evaluated at the initial gradient. For an arbitrary direction 𝒉∈ℝn​p\bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{np}, factoring 𝑲S​S​(τ)=𝑱S​(τ)​𝑱S​(τ)⊤\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)=\bm{J}_{S}(\tau)\bm{J}_{S}(\tau)^{\top} rewrites the quadratic form as a squared-norm integrand,

𝒉⊤​𝒲S​(s,T)​𝒉=∫sT‖𝑱S​(τ)⊤​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒉‖22​𝑑τ≥0,\displaystyle\bm{h}^{\top}\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,T)\bm{h}=\int_{s}^{T}\|\bm{J}_{S}(\tau)^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{h}\|_{2}^{2}d\tau\geq 0, (32)

which gives 𝒲S⪰0\mathcal{W}_{S}\succeq 0 from the integrand and reads 𝒉⊤​𝒲S​𝒉\bm{h}^{\top}\mathcal{W}_{S}\bm{h} as the dissipation that direction 𝒉\bm{h} would have experienced.

Reading off the eigenvalues.

The dissipation Gramian is symmetric PSD, so it has orthonormal eigenvectors 𝝍j\bm{\psi}_{j} with eigenvalues λj≥0\lambda_{j}\geq 0, 𝒲S​𝝍j=λj​𝝍j\mathcal{W}_{S}\bm{\psi}_{j}=\lambda_{j}\bm{\psi}_{j}. Left-multiplying by 𝝍j⊤\bm{\psi}_{j}^{\top} and using 𝝍j⊤​𝝍j=1\bm{\psi}_{j}^{\top}\bm{\psi}_{j}=1, then specializing (32) to 𝒉=𝝍j\bm{h}=\bm{\psi}_{j},

λj=𝝍j⊤​𝒲S​(s,T)​𝝍j=∫sT‖𝑱S​(τ)⊤​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝝍j‖22​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\lambda_{j}=\bm{\psi}_{j}^{\top}\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,T)\bm{\psi}_{j}=\int_{s}^{T}\|\bm{J}_{S}(\tau)^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{\psi}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}d\tau. (33)

The eigenvalue along 𝝍j\bm{\psi}_{j} equals the total integrated squared reachability of 𝝍j\bm{\psi}_{j} over the window. A direction 𝒉\bm{h} might align with a large eigenvalue of 𝑲S​S​(τ)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau) at one time and a small eigenvalue at another, so the instantaneous spectrum does not tell the whole story; the cumulative integral 𝒲S\mathcal{W}_{S} records the total integrated effect over the entire training window.

C.2 Scaled Tangent Kernel and Timescales

Intuition.

The decay rate of the loss gradient is set by the kernel weighted by the curvature of the loss. We make this precise by introducing a scaled tangent kernel whose eigenvalues read off as relaxation rates. Directions with the largest eigenvalues are fit quickly; the smallest eigenvalues control the slowest modes, and the gap between them sets training timescales.

Section 3shows that 𝒈\bm{g} decays according to ∂t𝒈=−𝑩​𝑲S​S​𝒈\partial_{t}\bm{g}=-\bm{B}\bm{K}_{\!SS}\bm{g}. To read off timescales, scale the kernel by the loss curvature:

K~B\displaystyle\widetilde{K}_{B} =𝑩1/2​𝑲S​S​𝑩1/2​(general losses),\displaystyle=\bm{B}^{1/2}\bm{K}_{\!SS}\bm{B}^{1/2}\hskip 9.24994pt\text{(general losses),} 𝑴⁡(t)\displaystyle\bm{M}(t) ≜𝑲S​S​(𝒘⁡(t))/n​(squared loss),\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\bm{w}(t))/n\hskip 9.24994pt\text{(squared loss),} (34)

with eigenvalues

λ1​(t)≥λ2​(t)≥⋯≥λn​p​(t)≥0\displaystyle\lambda_{1}(t)\geq\lambda_{2}(t)\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{np}(t)\geq 0 (35)

and orthonormal eigenvectors {𝒗i​(t)}\{\bm{v}_{i}(t)\}. For squared loss, 𝒈=𝒓/n\bm{g}=\bm{r}/n and 𝑩=𝑰/n\bm{B}=\bm{I}/n, so the residual obeys ∂t𝒓=−𝑴⁡(t)​𝒓\partial_{t}\bm{r}=-\bm{M}(t)\bm{r} and its component along 𝒗i​(t)\bm{v}_{i}(t) decays at rate λi​(t)\lambda_{i}(t). In practice the spectrum has extreme separation: the condition number among nonzero eigenvalues is typically enormous, creating a sharp split between fast- and slow-decaying directions.

Proof of Section 3 and Section C.3.

The chain rule applied to LS=ΦS∘𝑼SL_{S}=\Phi_{S}\circ\bm{U}_{S} gives

∂t𝒖\displaystyle\partial_{t}\bm{u} =𝑱S​(𝒘)​∂t𝒘=−𝑱S​𝑱S⊤​𝒈=−𝑲S​S​𝒈,\displaystyle=\bm{J}_{S}(\bm{w})\partial_{t}\bm{w}=-\bm{J}_{S}\bm{J}_{S}^{\top}\bm{g}=-\bm{K}_{\!SS}\bm{g}, (36)
∂t𝒈\displaystyle\partial_{t}\bm{g} =∇2ΦS​(𝒖⁡(t))​∂t𝒖=−𝑩⁡(t)​𝑲S​S​(t)​𝒈​(t),\displaystyle=\nabla^{2}\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(t))\partial_{t}\bm{u}=-\bm{B}(t)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(t)\bm{g}(t), (37)
∂t𝒘\displaystyle\partial_{t}\bm{w} =−𝑱S​(𝒘)⊤​𝒈,\displaystyle=-\bm{J}_{S}(\bm{w})^{\top}\bm{g}, (38)
proving (3). Dissipation follows by the same substitution:
dd​t​ΦS​(𝒖⁡(t))\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(t)) =⟨𝒈⁡(t),∂t𝒖⁡(t)⟩=−𝒈​(t)⊤​𝑲S​S​(t)​𝒈​(t)=−‖𝑱S⊤​𝒈‖22=−‖∂t𝒘‖22,\displaystyle=\langle\bm{g}(t),\partial_{t}\bm{u}(t)\rangle=-\bm{g}(t)^{\top}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(t)\bm{g}(t)=-\|\bm{J}_{S}^{\top}\bm{g}\|_{2}^{2}=-\|\partial_{t}\bm{w}\|_{2}^{2}, (39)

∂t𝑼Q\displaystyle\partial_{t}\bm{U}_{Q} =𝑱Q​(𝒘)​∂t𝒘=−𝑲Q​S​𝒈,\displaystyle=\bm{J}_{Q}(\bm{w})\partial_{t}\bm{w}=-\bm{K}_{\!QS}\bm{g}, (40)
