C.3 Deferred Corollaries from Section 3

Intuition.

This subsection records two consequences of the output-dynamics theorem that we reuse later. The first writes the test trajectory through the loss-gradient propagator and pairs it with a complementary relation that splits the cumulative training operator into two pieces. The second translates a small-dissipation direction into a quantitative bound on test displacement.

For a convex differentiable ψ\psi, the Bregman divergence is

Dψ​(a,b)≜ψ⁡(a)−ψ⁡(b)−⟨∇ψ​(b),a−b⟩.\displaystyle D_{\psi}(a,b)\triangleq\psi(a)-\psi(b)-\langle\nabla\psi(b),a-b\rangle. (52)

The first corollary expresses the test trajectory through the propagator and yields the complementary relation 𝖥S​S+𝒫g=𝑰\mathsf{F}_{SS}+\mathcal{P}_{g}=\bm{I} used throughout the proofs.

Corollary C.1 (Test Trajectory and Propagator Complement).

For any test set QQ,

𝑼Q​(t)=𝑼Q​(0)−∫0t𝑲Q​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,0)​𝒈​(0)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(t)=\bm{U}_{Q}(0)-\int_{0}^{t}\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,0)\bm{g}(0)d\tau. (53)

Define the train-on-train cumulative output operator

𝖥S​S​(T)≜∫0T𝑩⁡(τ)​𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,0)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\mathsf{F}_{SS}(T)\triangleq\int_{0}^{T}\bm{B}(\tau)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,0)d\tau. (54)

Then the complement holds:

𝖥S​S​(T)+𝒫g​(T,0)=𝑰.\displaystyle\mathsf{F}_{SS}(T)+\mathcal{P}_{g}(T,0)=\bm{I}. (55)

If ΦS∗\Phi_{S}^{*} is differentiable at 𝐠⁡(t)\bm{g}(t) and 𝐮¯\bar{\bm{u}} minimizes ΦS\Phi_{S} with ∇ΦS​(𝐮¯)=0\nabla\Phi_{S}(\bar{\bm{u}})=0, then

ΦS​(𝒖⁡(t))−ΦS​(𝒖¯)=DΦS∗​(0,𝒈⁡(t)).\displaystyle\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(t))-\Phi_{S}(\bar{\bm{u}})=D_{\Phi_{S}^{*}}(0,\bm{g}(t)). (56)

The second corollary makes the small-dissipation principle quantitative: whenever 𝒲S\mathcal{W}_{S} is small along a direction, 𝑮\bm{G} is small there too, with the same constant.

Corollary C.2 (Low-Loss-dissipation Bound).

Under the notation of Equation 11,

𝑮​P{0}​(s,T)\displaystyle\bm{G}P_{\{0\}}(s,T) =0,\displaystyle=0, (57)
‖𝑮​P[0,ε]​(s,T)​𝒉‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{G}P_{[0,\varepsilon]}(s,T)\bm{h}\|_{2} ≤‖ΓQ​(s,T)‖op1/2​ε​‖P[0,ε]​(s,T)​𝒉‖2.\displaystyle\leq\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{1/2}\sqrt{\varepsilon}\|P_{[0,\varepsilon]}(s,T)\bm{h}\|_{2}. (58)

Equivalently, every direction producing terminal test displacement at least τ\tau obeys

‖𝑮​𝒉‖2≥τ⟹𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉≥τ2/‖ΓQ​(s,T)‖op.\displaystyle\|\bm{G}\bm{h}\|_{2}\geq\tau\Longrightarrow\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}\geq\tau^{2}/\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}. (59)

Appendix D Minibatch Drift–Diffusion: Proof

Intuition.

SGD’s effect on the test outputs splits into two pieces of very different sizes. The mean (drift) part of the gradient produces a contribution that, in the worst case, accumulates linearly in TT along directions the optimizer can actually see; the zero-mean fluctuation (diffusion) part is a martingale and, by orthogonality of its increments, only adds up like T\sqrt{T}. Signal directions, where the drift is nonzero, dominate over time, while pure-noise directions are washed out as T/T→0\sqrt{T}/T\to 0. The proof is a Taylor expansion of the test prediction across one optimizer step, plus a martingale variance computation, plus a replace-two argument needed to handle the dependence of the iterates on the training set.

We prove that on a signal direction SGD’s drift accumulates linearly in TT, while on a noise direction it grows only like T\sqrt{T}.

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Taylor-expanding the test prediction over a single SGD step,

𝑼Q​(𝒘k+1)−𝑼Q​(𝒘k)\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}_{k+1})-\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}_{k}) =𝑱Q​(𝒘k)​(𝒘k+1−𝒘k)+𝒓Q,k,\displaystyle=\bm{J}_{Q}(\bm{w}_{k})(\bm{w}_{k+1}-\bm{w}_{k})+\bm{r}_{Q,k}, (60)
‖𝒓Q,k‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{r}_{Q,k}\|_{2} ≤βQ2​‖𝒘k+1−𝒘k‖22.\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{\beta_{Q}}{2}\|\bm{w}_{k+1}-\bm{w}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}. (61)

Substituting 𝒘k+1−𝒘k=−η​𝑴k​(𝝁k+𝝃k)\bm{w}_{k+1}-\bm{w}_{k}=-\eta\bm{M}_{k}(\bm{\mu}_{k}+\bm{\xi}_{k}) and summing yields (14). Since 𝑳Q,k,𝝁k\bm{L}_{Q,k},\bm{\mu}_{k} are ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k}-measurable and 𝔼⁡[𝝃k∣ℱk]=𝟎\mathbb{E}[\bm{\xi}_{k}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}]=\bm{0}, the increments η​𝑳Q,k​𝝃k\eta\bm{L}_{Q,k}\bm{\xi}_{k} are martingale differences, so

𝔼​‖η​∑k=0N−1𝑳Q,k​𝝃k‖22\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigl\|\eta\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bm{L}_{Q,k}\bm{\xi}_{k}\Bigr\|_{2}^{2} =η2​∑k=0N−1𝔼​tr⁡(𝑳Q,k​𝚺k(b)​𝑳Q,k⊤)\displaystyle=\eta^{2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\bm{L}_{Q,k}\bm{\Sigma}_{k}^{(b)}\bm{L}_{Q,k}^{\top}\bigr) (62)
≤η​Tb​V¯T,\displaystyle\leq\frac{\eta T}{b}\bar{V}_{T}, (63)

where the bound uses

tr⁡(𝑳Q,k​𝚺k(b)​𝑳Q,k⊤)≤Vkb,V¯T=1T​∑kη​Vk,\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}(\bm{L}_{Q,k}\bm{\Sigma}_{k}^{(b)}\bm{L}_{Q,k}^{\top})\leq\frac{V_{k}}{b},\hskip 18.49988pt\bar{V}_{T}=\tfrac{1}{T}\sum_{k}\eta V_{k}, (64)

and the drift bound is the deterministic estimate

∑kη​‖𝑳Q,k​𝝁k‖2≤T​supk‖𝑳Q,k​𝝁k‖2.\displaystyle\sum_{k}\eta\|\bm{L}_{Q,k}\bm{\mu}_{k}\|_{2}\leq T\sup_{k}\|\bm{L}_{Q,k}\bm{\mu}_{k}\|_{2}. (65)

For the empirical noise mean, the summands of

𝚷​𝝁k=1n​∑i𝚷​∇𝒘ℓ​(𝒘k​(S),Zi)\displaystyle\bm{\Pi}\bm{\mu}_{k}=\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\bm{\Pi}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell(\bm{w}_{k}(S),Z_{i}) (66)

are not independent because 𝒘k​(S)\bm{w}_{k}(S) depends on every ZiZ_{i}, so the cross terms must be decoupled by replacing the two examples that appear in each one. Let S(i​j)S^{(ij)} be the dataset obtained from SS by replacing Zi,ZjZ_{i},Z_{j} with independent fresh draws from 𝒟\mathcal{D}, write 𝒘k(i​j)≜𝒘k​(S(i​j))\bm{w}_{k}^{(ij)}\triangleq\bm{w}_{k}(S^{(ij)}), and assume the bounded second moment VkV_{k} on the projected gradient together with the replace-two defect

εk,n\displaystyle\varepsilon_{k,n} ≜supi≠j(𝔼∥𝚷∇𝒘ℓ(𝒘k(S),Zi)\displaystyle\triangleq\sup_{i\neq j}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\bigl\|\bm{\Pi}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell(\bm{w}_{k}(S),Z_{i})
−𝚷∇𝒘ℓ(𝒘k(i​j),Zi)∥22)1/2.\displaystyle\hskip 18.49988pt-\bm{\Pi}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell(\bm{w}_{k}^{(ij)},Z_{i})\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2}. (67)

Then 𝒘k(i​j)\bm{w}_{k}^{(ij)} is independent of (Zi,Zj)(Z_{i},Z_{j}), so fresh-sample centering gives

𝔼⁡⟨𝚷​∇𝒘ℓ​(𝒘k(i​j),Zi),𝚷​∇𝒘ℓ​(𝒘k(i​j),Zj)⟩=0.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\langle\bm{\Pi}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell(\bm{w}_{k}^{(ij)},Z_{i}),\bm{\Pi}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell(\bm{w}_{k}^{(ij)},Z_{j})\rangle=0. (68)

Writing

𝚷​∇𝒘ℓ​(𝒘k​(S),Zi)=𝚷​∇𝒘ℓ​(𝒘k(i​j),Zi)+𝒓i(i​j)\displaystyle\bm{\Pi}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell(\bm{w}_{k}(S),Z_{i})=\bm{\Pi}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell(\bm{w}_{k}^{(ij)},Z_{i})+\bm{r}_{i}^{(ij)} (69)

and expanding the cross inner product, Cauchy–Schwarz with (D) bounds the three residual terms by Vk​εk,n\sqrt{V_{k}}\varepsilon_{k,n}, Vk​εk,n\sqrt{V_{k}}\varepsilon_{k,n}, and εk,n2\varepsilon_{k,n}^{2}, so summing diagonal and off-diagonal contributions yields

𝔼​‖𝚷​𝝁k‖22\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\bm{\Pi}\bm{\mu}_{k}\|_{2}^{2} ≤Vkn+2​Vk​εk,n+εk,n2.\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{V_{k}}{n}+2\sqrt{V_{k}}\varepsilon_{k,n}+\varepsilon_{k,n}^{2}. (70)

Under εk,n=O⁡(1/n)\varepsilon_{k,n}=O(1/n) this is O⁡(1/n)O(1/n), and the drift contribution becomes T2​V¯T/nT^{2}\bar{V}_{T}/n.∎

Multi-epoch caveat.

The one-step LOO result in Theorem F.1 requires BB to be independent of the optimizer history ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}. In streaming or online training this holds by construction; in multi-epoch training a replayed batch carries information about 𝒘t\bm{w}_{t} and the equality acquires a residual,

𝔼⁡[ℛ1​e​x,Btη∣ℱt]=ℛfreshη​(𝒘t,𝑷t)+rt,|rt|≤2​M​TV​(PBt|ℱt,𝒟b),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}^{\eta}_{\mathrm{1ex},B_{t}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=\mathcal{R}^{\eta}_{\mathrm{fresh}}(\bm{w}_{t},\bm{P}_{t})+r_{t},\hskip 18.49988pt|r_{t}|\leq 2M\mathrm{TV}(P_{B_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}},\mathcal{D}^{b}), (71)

where ℛfreshη\mathcal{R}^{\eta}_{\mathrm{fresh}} is the fresh-boundary one-step risk, rt=∫φt​(B)​d​(PBt|ℱt−𝒟b)r_{t}=\int\varphi_{t}(B)d(P_{B_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}}-\mathcal{D}^{b}) for a bounded test function |φt|≤M|\varphi_{t}|\leq M, and rtr_{t} vanishes in the first epoch.

Appendix E Train-Test Coupling: Proofs

Intuition.

This appendix proves the train-test coupling results of Section 5. The basic question is when motion on a held-out point can be reconstructed from motion observed on the training set. Classical NTK analysis assumes the kernel is frozen at initialization [17, 9]; here the kernel evolves with the parameters and can move by 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) in operator norm over a typical run. We ask when the test displacement is predictable from the observed training displacement, and what quantity controls the prediction error in the feature-learning regime. The bounds we derive are computable from a single run.

E.1 Feature Learning with Stable Transfer

Intuition.

This subsection sets up the proof of Theorem 5.1. The dissipation Gramian 𝒲S​(s,T)\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,T) and the transfer operator 𝖦Q​(T,s)\mathsf{G}_{Q}(T,s) from Section 3 already absorb kernel motion, so the analysis applies in full feature learning. We work directly with these pathwise objects and show that a stable train-test relationship survives even when each kernel moves by 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1).

The stability condition holds for the relationship between training and test kernels even when the individual kernels move by 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) in operator norm. The next subsection proves the train-test coupling theorem under this condition. Subsequent subsections develop the path-error decomposition and the test-prediction bounds in Section E.7.

E.2 Proof of the Train-Test Coupling Theorem

Intuition.

The proof of Theorem 5.1 rests on a simple observation: once both the training and test displacement operators are normalized by the dissipation Gramian, the test side decomposes orthogonally into a piece predictable from the training side plus an orthogonal remainder. This is the operator analogue of regressing one Gaussian variable on another. Fix 0≤s≤T0\leq s\leq T and a test set QQ, and write 𝑫≜𝖣S​(T,s)\bm{D}\triangleq\mathsf{D}_{S}(T,s), 𝑮≜𝖦Q​(T,s)\bm{G}\triangleq\mathsf{G}_{Q}(T,s), 𝑾≜𝒲S​(s,T)\bm{W}\triangleq\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,T).

Per-eigendirection reading of the normalization.

On each eigenvector 𝒖i\bm{u}_{i} of 𝑾\bm{W} with eigenvalue σi>0\sigma_{i}>0,

𝖢S​𝒖i\displaystyle\mathsf{C}_{S}\bm{u}_{i} =𝑫​𝒖iσi,\displaystyle=\frac{\bm{D}\bm{u}_{i}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{i}}}, 𝖢Q​𝒖i\displaystyle\mathsf{C}_{Q}\bm{u}_{i} =𝑮​𝒖iσi.\displaystyle=\frac{\bm{G}\bm{u}_{i}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{i}}}. (72)

Both channels measure displacement along 𝒖i\bm{u}_{i} divided by the square root of how much training dissipated along 𝒖i\bm{u}_{i}, putting train displacement and test transfer in the same per-root-dissipation units. In these units the optimal linear predictor and irreducible remainder of Section E.2,

𝑨∘=𝖢Q​𝖢S†,𝑹⟂=𝖢Q​(𝑰−Ptr),\displaystyle\bm{A}_{\circ}=\mathsf{C}_{Q}\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\dagger},\hskip 18.49988pt\bm{R}_{\perp}=\mathsf{C}_{Q}(\bm{I}-P_{\mathrm{tr}}), (73)

read as the regression of test-transfer on training-displacement along the eigenbasis of 𝑾\bm{W}, plus the part of test transfer that cannot be predicted from training displacement.

Definition E.1 (Dissipation-normalized channels, optimal linear predictor, and irreducible remainder).

The dissipation-normalized train channel and dissipation-normalized test channel are

𝖢S​(s,T)\displaystyle\mathsf{C}_{S}(s,T) ≜𝑫𝑾†/2,\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{D}\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}, 𝖢Q​(s,T)\displaystyle\mathsf{C}_{Q}(s,T) ≜𝑮𝑾†/2.\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{G}\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}. (74)

The transfer projector Ptr≜𝖢S†​𝖢SP_{\mathrm{tr}}\triangleq\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\dagger}\mathsf{C}_{S} is the orthogonal projector onto the column space of 𝖢S\mathsf{C}_{S}. The optimal linear predictor and irreducible remainder are

𝑨∘\displaystyle\bm{A}_{\circ} ≜𝖢Q​𝖢S†=𝑮​𝑾†​𝑫⊤​(𝑫​𝑾†​𝑫⊤)†,\displaystyle\triangleq\mathsf{C}_{Q}\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\dagger}=\bm{G}\bm{W}^{\dagger}\bm{D}^{\top}\bigl(\bm{D}\bm{W}^{\dagger}\bm{D}^{\top}\bigr)^{\dagger}, (75)
𝑹⟂\displaystyle\bm{R}_{\perp} ≜𝖢Q​(𝑰−Ptr).\displaystyle\triangleq\mathsf{C}_{Q}\bigl(\bm{I}-P_{\mathrm{tr}}\bigr). (76)

For an arbitrary predictor Ψ:range⁡(𝑫)→ℝ|Q|​p\Psi:\operatorname{range}(\bm{D})\to\mathbb{R}^{|Q|p}, the normalized worst-case error is

Err⁡(Ψ)≜sup𝒉∉ker⁡𝑾‖𝑮​𝒉−Ψ⁡(𝑫​𝒉)‖2𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉.\displaystyle\operatorname{Err}(\Psi)\triangleq\sup_{\bm{h}\notin\ker\bm{W}}\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}-\Psi(\bm{D}\bm{h})\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}}. (77)

Both 𝑫\bm{D} and 𝑮\bm{G} pass through 𝑾1/2\bm{W}^{1/2}, and the part of the test channel orthogonal to the train channel becomes 𝑹⟂\bm{R}_{\perp}.

Theorem E.2 (Train-Test Coupling: Factorization).

Adopt the notation of Section E.2. The train and test displacements share the same right-hand dissipation factor, and the dissipation-normalized test channel decomposes orthogonally into a part driven by training and an irreducible remainder:

𝑫\displaystyle\bm{D} =𝖢S​(s,T)​𝑾1/2,\displaystyle=\mathsf{C}_{S}(s,T)\bm{W}^{1/2}, 𝑮\displaystyle\bm{G} =𝖢Q​(s,T)​𝑾1/2,\displaystyle=\mathsf{C}_{Q}(s,T)\bm{W}^{1/2}, (78)
𝖢Q​(s,T)\displaystyle\mathsf{C}_{Q}(s,T) =𝑨∘​𝖢S​(s,T)+𝑹⟂,\displaystyle=\bm{A}_{\circ}\mathsf{C}_{S}(s,T)+\bm{R}_{\perp}, 𝑹⟂​𝖢S​(s,T)⊤\displaystyle\bm{R}_{\perp}\mathsf{C}_{S}(s,T)^{\top} =0.\displaystyle=0. (79)

Every linear predictor’s error splits as 𝑹⟂​𝑹⟂⊤\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{R}_{\perp}^{\top} plus a quadratic penalty in 𝑨−𝑨∘\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ}, so 𝑨∘\bm{A}_{\circ} minimizes the error in the positive-semidefinite order.

Theorem E.3 (Transfer error decomposition).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem E.2, every linear predictor 𝐀\bm{A} satisfies

(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)​𝑾†​(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)⊤=𝑹⟂​𝑹⟂⊤+(𝑨−𝑨∘)​𝑫​𝑾†​𝑫⊤​(𝑨−𝑨∘)⊤⪰𝑹⟂​𝑹⟂⊤,\displaystyle(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger}(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})^{\top}=\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{R}_{\perp}^{\top}+(\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ})\bm{D}\bm{W}^{\dagger}\bm{D}^{\top}(\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ})^{\top}\succeq\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{R}_{\perp}^{\top}, (80)

so 𝐀∘\bm{A}_{\circ} is the unique linear predictor minimizing the path error in the positive-semidefinite order.

Allowing the predictor to be nonlinear yields the same minimum error, achieved by the linear 𝑨∘\bm{A}_{\circ}.

Corollary E.4 (Nonlinear optimality).

The optimal linear predictor matches the best nonlinear post-processing of the training displacement:

infΨErr(Ψ)=∥𝑹⟂∥op=sup𝒉∉ker⁡𝑾𝑫​𝒉=0‖𝑮​𝒉‖2𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉=inf𝑨∥(𝑮−𝑨𝑫)𝑾†/2∥op.\displaystyle\inf_{\Psi}\operatorname{Err}(\Psi)=\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{h}\notin\ker\bm{W}\\ \bm{D}\bm{h}=0\end{subarray}}\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}}=\inf_{\bm{A}}\|(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\|_{\operatorname{op}}. (81)
Remark E.5 (Equivalent formulations).

In terms of the original operators,

𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s)=−𝑫​𝒈​(s),𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)=−𝑮​𝒈​(s),\displaystyle\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s)=-\bm{D}\bm{g}(s),\hskip 18.49988pt\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)=-\bm{G}\bm{g}(s), (82)
𝑮=𝑨∘​𝑫+𝑹⟂​𝑾1/2,(𝑮−𝑨∘​𝑫)​𝑾†​𝑫⊤=0.\displaystyle\bm{G}=\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D}+\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{W}^{1/2},\hskip 18.49988pt(\bm{G}-\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger}\bm{D}^{\top}=0. (83)

On the true trajectory,

𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)=𝑨∘​(𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s))−𝑹⟂​𝑾1/2​𝒈​(s).\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)=\bm{A}_{\circ}\bigl(\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s)\bigr)-\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{W}^{1/2}\bm{g}(s). (84)
Proof of the four results above.

By Section 3, ker⁡𝑾⊆ker⁡𝑫∩ker⁡𝑮\ker\bm{W}\subseteq\ker\bm{D}\cap\ker\bm{G}, and since 𝑾†/2𝑾1/2=PW\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\bm{W}^{1/2}=P_{W} is the orthogonal projector onto range⁡(𝑾)\operatorname{range}(\bm{W}),

𝑫=𝑫PW=𝑫𝑾†/2𝑾1/2=𝖢S(s,T)𝑾1/2,\displaystyle\bm{D}=\bm{D}P_{W}=\bm{D}\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\bm{W}^{1/2}=\mathsf{C}_{S}(s,T)\bm{W}^{1/2}, (85)
𝑮=𝑮PW=𝑮𝑾†/2𝑾1/2=𝖢Q(s,T)𝑾1/2,\displaystyle\bm{G}=\bm{G}P_{W}=\bm{G}\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\bm{W}^{1/2}=\mathsf{C}_{Q}(s,T)\bm{W}^{1/2}, (86)

which is (78); (82) then follows from the definitions of 𝑫\bm{D} and 𝑮\bm{G}.

Since Ptr=𝖢S†​𝖢SP_{\mathrm{tr}}=\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\dagger}\mathsf{C}_{S} is the orthogonal projector onto range⁡(𝖢S⊤)\operatorname{range}(\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\top}),

𝖢Q=𝖢Q​Ptr+𝖢Q​(𝑰−Ptr)=𝑨∘​𝖢S+𝑹⟂.\displaystyle\mathsf{C}_{Q}=\mathsf{C}_{Q}P_{\mathrm{tr}}+\mathsf{C}_{Q}(\bm{I}-P_{\mathrm{tr}})=\bm{A}_{\circ}\mathsf{C}_{S}+\bm{R}_{\perp}. (87)

Also,

𝑹⟂​𝖢S⊤=𝖢Q​(𝑰−Ptr)​𝖢S⊤=0,\displaystyle\bm{R}_{\perp}\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\top}=\mathsf{C}_{Q}(\bm{I}-P_{\mathrm{tr}})\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\top}=0, (88)

because range⁡(𝖢S⊤)⊆range⁡(Ptr)\operatorname{range}(\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\top})\subseteq\operatorname{range}(P_{\mathrm{tr}}). This proves (79). Multiplying by 𝑾1/2\bm{W}^{1/2} gives (83), and then (84) follows from (82). The explicit formula for 𝑨∘\bm{A}_{\circ} is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse 𝑴†=𝑴⊤​(𝑴​𝑴⊤)†\bm{M}^{\dagger}=\bm{M}^{\top}(\bm{M}\bm{M}^{\top})^{\dagger} applied to 𝑴=𝖢S=𝑫𝑾†/2\bm{M}=\mathsf{C}_{S}=\bm{D}\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}.

For any linear 𝑨\bm{A}, expanding the residual and using 𝑹⟂​𝖢S⊤=0\bm{R}_{\perp}\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\top}=0 gives

𝖢Q−𝑨​𝖢S\displaystyle\mathsf{C}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathsf{C}_{S} =𝑹⟂+(𝑨∘−𝑨)​𝖢S,\displaystyle=\bm{R}_{\perp}+(\bm{A}_{\circ}-\bm{A})\mathsf{C}_{S}, (89)
(𝖢Q−𝑨​𝖢S)​(𝖢Q−𝑨​𝖢S)⊤\displaystyle(\mathsf{C}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathsf{C}_{S})(\mathsf{C}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathsf{C}_{S})^{\top} =𝑹⟂​𝑹⟂⊤+(𝑨−𝑨∘)​𝖢S​𝖢S⊤​(𝑨−𝑨∘)⊤.\displaystyle=\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{R}_{\perp}^{\top}+(\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ})\mathsf{C}_{S}\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\top}(\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ})^{\top}. (90)

With 𝖢Q−𝑨𝖢S=(𝑮−𝑨𝑫)𝑾†/2\mathsf{C}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathsf{C}_{S}=(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger/2} and 𝖢S​𝖢S⊤=𝑫​𝑾†​𝑫⊤\mathsf{C}_{S}\mathsf{C}_{S}^{\top}=\bm{D}\bm{W}^{\dagger}\bm{D}^{\top}, this is (80), and the operator and Frobenius minimizers follow.

For (81), let

Err⁡(Ψ)≜sup𝒉∉ker⁡𝑾‖𝑮​𝒉−Ψ⁡(𝑫​𝒉)‖2𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉.\displaystyle\operatorname{Err}(\Psi)\triangleq\sup_{\bm{h}\notin\ker\bm{W}}\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}-\Psi(\bm{D}\bm{h})\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}}. (91)

If 𝑫​𝒉=0\bm{D}\bm{h}=0, then also 𝑫⁡(−𝒉)=0\bm{D}(-\bm{h})=0. Thus for any predictor Ψ\Psi,

Err⁡(Ψ)≥max⁡{‖𝑮​𝒉−Ψ⁡(0)‖2𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉,‖−𝑮​𝒉−Ψ⁡(0)‖2𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉}≥‖𝑮​𝒉‖2𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉.\displaystyle\operatorname{Err}(\Psi)\geq\max\left\{\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}-\Psi(0)\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}},\frac{\|-\bm{G}\bm{h}-\Psi(0)\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}}\right\}\geq\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}}. (92)

Taking the supremum over 𝑫​𝒉=0\bm{D}\bm{h}=0 gives

Err⁡(Ψ)≥sup𝒉∉ker⁡𝑾𝑫​𝒉=0‖𝑮​𝒉‖2𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉.\displaystyle\operatorname{Err}(\Psi)\geq\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{h}\notin\ker\bm{W}\\ \bm{D}\bm{h}=0\end{subarray}}\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}}. (93)

Writing z=𝑾1/2​𝒉z=\bm{W}^{1/2}\bm{h}, we have 𝑫​𝒉=0⇔𝖢S​z=0\bm{D}\bm{h}=0\iff\mathsf{C}_{S}z=0, ‖𝑮​𝒉‖2=‖𝖢Q​z‖2\|\bm{G}\bm{h}\|_{2}=\|\mathsf{C}_{Q}z\|_{2}, and 𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉=‖z‖22\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}=\|z\|_{2}^{2}. Hence

sup𝒉∉ker⁡𝑾𝑫​𝒉=0‖𝑮​𝒉‖2𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉=supz∈ker⁡𝖢S∖{0}‖𝖢Q​z‖2‖z‖2=‖𝖢Q​(𝑰−Ptr)‖op=‖𝑹⟂‖op.\displaystyle\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{h}\notin\ker\bm{W}\\ \bm{D}\bm{h}=0\end{subarray}}\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}}=\sup_{z\in\ker\mathsf{C}_{S}\setminus\{0\}}\frac{\|\mathsf{C}_{Q}z\|_{2}}{\|z\|_{2}}=\|\mathsf{C}_{Q}(\bm{I}-P_{\mathrm{tr}})\|_{\operatorname{op}}=\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}. (94)

On the other hand, the linear predictor x↦𝑨∘​xx\mapsto\bm{A}_{\circ}x satisfies

∥(𝑮−𝑨∘𝑫)𝑾†/2∥op=∥𝑹⟂∥op,\displaystyle\|(\bm{G}-\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\|_{\operatorname{op}}=\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}, (95)

so both infima in (81) equal ‖𝑹⟂‖op\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}. ∎

The fixed-transfer problem becomes an operator regression: 𝑨∘​𝑫\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D} captures every test component determined by the observed training displacement, while 𝑹⟂​𝑾1/2​𝒈​(s)\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{W}^{1/2}\bm{g}(s) is the irreducible remainder. Each anchored predictor 𝑨\bm{A} pays the positive-semidefinite misspecification penalty

(𝑨−𝑨∘)​𝑫​𝑾†​𝑫⊤​(𝑨−𝑨∘)⊤\displaystyle(\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ})\bm{D}\bm{W}^{\dagger}\bm{D}^{\top}(\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ})^{\top} (96)

on top of the irreducible 𝑹⟂​𝑹⟂⊤\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{R}_{\perp}^{\top}.

The next corollary collects equivalent characterizations of 𝑨∘\bm{A}_{\circ} that we use later and gives a trajectory bound on the realized path.

Corollary E.6 (Exact transfer equivalences and trajectory bounds).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem E.2, the following are equivalent:

𝑹⟂=0\displaystyle\bm{R}_{\perp}=0 ⇔ker⁡𝑫⊆ker⁡𝑮⇔range⁡(𝑮⊤)⊆range⁡(𝑫⊤)\displaystyle\iff\ker\bm{D}\subseteq\ker\bm{G}\iff\operatorname{range}(\bm{G}^{\top})\subseteq\operatorname{range}(\bm{D}^{\top}) (97)
⇔𝑮⊤​𝑮⪯λ​𝑫⊤​𝑫​ for some ​λ≥0.\displaystyle\iff\bm{G}^{\top}\bm{G}\preceq\lambda\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{D}\textup{ for some }\lambda\geq 0. (98)

When these hold, the predictor on range⁡(𝐃)\operatorname{range}(\bm{D}) is unique, necessarily linear, and given by Ψ♯​(x)=𝐆​𝐃†​x\Psi_{\sharp}(x)=\bm{G}\bm{D}^{\dagger}x with Lipschitz norm ΣQ​(s,T)=‖𝐆​𝐃†‖op\Sigma_{Q}(s,T)=\|\bm{G}\bm{D}^{\dagger}\|_{\operatorname{op}}.

On the true trajectory,

‖𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)−𝑨∘​(𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s))‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)-\bm{A}_{\circ}\bigl(\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s)\bigr)\|_{2} ≤‖𝑹⟂‖op​ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T)).\displaystyle\leq\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}\sqrt{\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T))}. (99)

More generally, for any linear predictor 𝐀\bm{A},

‖𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)−𝑨⁡(𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s))‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)-\bm{A}\bigl(\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s)\bigr)\|_{2} ≤‖𝖢Q​(s,T)−𝑨​𝖢S​(s,T)‖op\displaystyle\leq\|\mathsf{C}_{Q}(s,T)-\bm{A}\mathsf{C}_{S}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}} (100)
⋅ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T)).\displaystyle\hskip 18.49988pt\cdot\sqrt{\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T))}. (101)
Proof.

Since ker⁡Ptr=ker⁡𝖢S\ker P_{\mathrm{tr}}=\ker\mathsf{C}_{S},

𝑹⟂=0⇔𝖢Q​(𝑰−Ptr)=0⇔ker⁡𝖢S⊆ker⁡𝖢Q.\displaystyle\bm{R}_{\perp}=0\iff\mathsf{C}_{Q}(\bm{I}-P_{\mathrm{tr}})=0\iff\ker\mathsf{C}_{S}\subseteq\ker\mathsf{C}_{Q}. (102)

Using (78) and the fact that both 𝖢S\mathsf{C}_{S} and 𝖢Q\mathsf{C}_{Q} vanish on ker⁡𝑾\ker\bm{W}, this is equivalent to ker⁡𝑫⊆ker⁡𝑮\ker\bm{D}\subseteq\ker\bm{G}. The equivalence with range⁡(𝑮⊤)⊆range⁡(𝑫⊤)\operatorname{range}(\bm{G}^{\top})\subseteq\operatorname{range}(\bm{D}^{\top}) is finite-dimensional duality. For the positive-semidefinite condition, 𝑮=𝑨​𝑫\bm{G}=\bm{A}\bm{D} gives 𝑮⊤​𝑮⪯‖𝑨‖op2​𝑫⊤​𝑫\bm{G}^{\top}\bm{G}\preceq\|\bm{A}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{2}\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{D}, and conversely 𝑮⊤​𝑮⪯λ​𝑫⊤​𝑫\bm{G}^{\top}\bm{G}\preceq\lambda\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{D} implies 𝑫​𝒉=0⇒𝑮​𝒉=0\bm{D}\bm{h}=0\Rightarrow\bm{G}\bm{h}=0. When these hold, the predictor on range⁡(𝑫)\operatorname{range}(\bm{D}) is 𝑮​𝑫†\bm{G}\bm{D}^{\dagger}, unique by well-definedness on the range, and its Lipschitz norm is ‖𝑮​𝑫†‖op\|\bm{G}\bm{D}^{\dagger}\|_{\operatorname{op}}.

(99) follows from (84) and 𝒈​(s)⊤​𝑾​𝒈​(s)=ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T))\bm{g}(s)^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{g}(s)=\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T)). For the general linear predictor bound, use

𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)−𝑨⁡(𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s))\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)-\bm{A}\bigl(\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s)\bigr) =−(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)​𝒈​(s)\displaystyle=-(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{g}(s) (103)
=−(𝖢Q​(s,T)−𝑨​𝖢S​(s,T))​𝑾1/2​𝒈​(s).\displaystyle=-(\mathsf{C}_{Q}(s,T)-\bm{A}\mathsf{C}_{S}(s,T))\bm{W}^{1/2}\bm{g}(s). (104)

Therefore

‖𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)−𝑨⁡(𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s))‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)-\bm{A}\bigl(\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s)\bigr)\|_{2} ≤‖𝖢Q​(s,T)−𝑨​𝖢S​(s,T)‖op​‖𝑾1/2​𝒈​(s)‖2\displaystyle\leq\|\mathsf{C}_{Q}(s,T)-\bm{A}\mathsf{C}_{S}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}\|\bm{W}^{1/2}\bm{g}(s)\|_{2} (105)
=‖𝖢Q​(s,T)−𝑨​𝖢S​(s,T)‖op\displaystyle=\|\mathsf{C}_{Q}(s,T)-\bm{A}\mathsf{C}_{S}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}} (106)
⋅ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T)),\displaystyle\hskip 18.49988pt\cdot\sqrt{\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T))}, (107)

which is (100). ∎

E.3 Smoothness is Required for Test Prediction

Intuition.

Predicting test motion from training data requires a smoothness hypothesis on the network. We exhibit two networks producing identical training trajectories, Jacobian paths, and training losses but different test displacements at a held-out point, so the smoothness assumption used in Section E.4 is necessary.

Theorem E.7 (Smoothness is necessary).

Fix z⋆∉Sz_{\star}\notin S. There exist two C∞C^{\infty} networks FF and F~\widetilde{F} such that for every zi∈Sz_{i}\in S and every t≤Tt\leq T,

F⁡(w⁡(t),zi)\displaystyle F(w(t),z_{i}) =F~​(w​(t),zi),\displaystyle=\widetilde{F}(w(t),z_{i}), Dw​F​(w⁡(t),zi)\displaystyle D_{w}F(w(t),z_{i}) =Dw​F~​(w⁡(t),zi),\displaystyle=D_{w}\widetilde{F}(w(t),z_{i}), (108)

so the entire training trajectory, Jacobian path, kernel path, and training losses are identical, but

F⁡(w⁡(T),z⋆)−F⁡(w⁡(0),z⋆)≠F~​(w⁡(T),z⋆)−F~​(w⁡(0),z⋆).\displaystyle F(w(T),z_{\star})-F(w(0),z_{\star})\neq\widetilde{F}(w(T),z_{\star})-\widetilde{F}(w(0),z_{\star}). (109)
Proof.

Pick a C∞C^{\infty} bump ψ\psi on input space and a C∞C^{\infty} scalar ϕ\phi on weight space with

ψ⁡(zi)=0,∇zψ​(zi)=0​∀zi∈S,ψ⁡(z⋆)≠0,ϕ⁡(w⁡(T))−ϕ⁡(w⁡(0))≠0,\displaystyle\psi(z_{i})=0,\hskip 9.24994pt\nabla_{z}\psi(z_{i})=0\ \ \forall z_{i}\in S,\hskip 18.49988pt\psi(z_{\star})\neq 0,\hskip 18.49988pt\phi(w(T))-\phi(w(0))\neq 0, (110)

and define the perturbed network

F~​(w,z)=F⁡(w,z)+ψ⁡(z)​ϕ​(w).\displaystyle\widetilde{F}(w,z)=F(w,z)+\psi(z)\phi(w). (111)

Then F~\widetilde{F} agrees with FF to first order on SS, so the training dynamics are identical, but the test displacement at z⋆z_{\star} differs by ψ⁡(z⋆)​[ϕ⁡(w⁡(T))−ϕ⁡(w⁡(0))]≠0\psi(z_{\star})\bigl[\phi(w(T))-\phi(w(0))\bigr]\neq 0. ∎

E.4 Sobolev Bound on the Transfer Remainder

Intuition.

When the data lies on a low-dimensional manifold and the network is sufficiently smooth, the irreducible remainder 𝑹⟂\bm{R}_{\perp} shrinks with sample density. The argument routes through a single pathwise displacement field on the manifold: test motion is its value at unseen points, training motion is its value at the observed sample, and a Sobolev sampling inequality controls how much the second determines the first. The bound applies with 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) kernel drift and quantifies the role of fill distance.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a compact dℳd_{\mathcal{M}}-dimensional data manifold and assume F⁡(w,⋅)F(w,\cdot) is CmC^{m} on ℳ\mathcal{M}, with m>dℳ/2m>d_{\mathcal{M}}/2. For z∈ℳz\in\mathcal{M} write

𝑱z​(t)=Dw​F​(w⁡(t),z),𝑲z​S​(t)=𝑱z​(t)​𝑱S​(t)⊤.\displaystyle\bm{J}_{z}(t)=D_{w}F(w(t),z),\hskip 18.49988pt\bm{K}_{zS}(t)=\bm{J}_{z}(t)\bm{J}_{S}(t)^{\top}. (112)

Define the pathwise displacement field

(𝒯s,T​𝒉)​(z)≜∫sT𝑲z​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒉​𝑑τ.\displaystyle(\mathscr{T}_{s,T}\bm{h})(z)\triangleq\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{zS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{h}d\tau. (113)

Then

𝑫=ES​𝒯s,T,𝑮=EQ​𝒯s,T,\displaystyle\bm{D}=E_{S}\mathscr{T}_{s,T},\hskip 18.49988pt\bm{G}=E_{Q}\mathscr{T}_{s,T}, (114)

where EA​f=(f⁡(a1),…,f⁡(a|A|))E_{A}f=(f(a_{1});\ldots;f(a_{|A|})) is evaluation on a finite set.

Define the pathwise Jacobian-Sobolev norm

𝔞m​(τ)\displaystyle\mathfrak{a}_{m}(\tau) ≜sup‖𝒗‖2=1∥z↦𝑱z(τ)𝒗∥Hm​(ℳ,ℝp),\displaystyle\triangleq\sup_{\|\bm{v}\|_{2}=1}\bigl\|z\mapsto\bm{J}_{z}(\tau)\bm{v}\bigr\|_{H^{m}(\mathcal{M};\mathbb{R}^{p})}, Λm​(s,T)\displaystyle\Lambda_{m}(s,T) ≜(∫sT𝔞m​(τ)2​𝑑τ)1/2.\displaystyle\triangleq\left(\int_{s}^{T}\mathfrak{a}_{m}(\tau)^{2}d\tau\right)^{1/2}. (115)

Let 𝑾=𝒲S​(s,T)\bm{W}=\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,T) and let

𝒞s,T≜𝒯s,T𝑾†/2.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{s,T}\triangleq\mathscr{T}_{s,T}\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}. (116)

The first piece is an operator-norm bound on the dissipation-normalized displacement field. Then we combine it with a Sobolev sampling inequality to bound the irreducible remainder in terms of the fill distance.

Lemma E.8 (Operator-norm bound on the dissipation-normalized field).
‖𝒞s,T‖op⁡(ℓ2,Hm)≤Λm​(s,T).\displaystyle\|\mathcal{C}_{s,T}\|_{\operatorname{op}(\ell_{2},H^{m})}\leq\Lambda_{m}(s,T). (117)
Theorem E.9 (Pathwise Sobolev Transfer).

If SS has fill distance

hS=supz∈ℳmini≤n⁡dℳ​(z,zi),\displaystyle h_{S}=\sup_{z\in\mathcal{M}}\min_{i\leq n}d_{\mathcal{M}}(z,z_{i}), (118)

then the irreducible train-test remainder satisfies

‖𝑹⟂‖op\displaystyle\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}} ≤Cℳ,m,p​|Q|1/2​hSm−dℳ/2​Λm​(s,T).\displaystyle\leq C_{\mathcal{M},m,p}|Q|^{1/2}h_{S}^{m-d_{\mathcal{M}}/2}\Lambda_{m}(s,T). (119)

The bound holds with no frozen-kernel or small-kernel-drift condition.

The remainder bound translates directly into a deterministic bound on test displacement along the realized trajectory.

Corollary E.10 (Trajectory form of the Sobolev transfer bound).
‖𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)−𝑨∘​(𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s))‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)-\bm{A}_{\circ}(\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s))\|_{2} ≤Cℳ,m,p​|Q|1/2​hSm−dℳ/2​Λm​(s,T)\displaystyle\leq C_{\mathcal{M},m,p}|Q|^{1/2}h_{S}^{m-d_{\mathcal{M}}/2}\Lambda_{m}(s,T) (120)
⋅ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T)).\displaystyle\hskip 18.49988pt\cdot\sqrt{\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T))}. (121)
Proof of Section E.4, Theorem E.9, and Section E.4.

For 𝒉∈ℝn​p\bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{np} set 𝒗h​(τ)=𝑱S​(τ)⊤​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒉\bm{v}_{h}(\tau)=\bm{J}_{S}(\tau)^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{h}, so

(𝒯s,T​𝒉)​(z)=∫sT𝑱z​(τ)​𝒗h​(τ)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle(\mathscr{T}_{s,T}\bm{h})(z)=\int_{s}^{T}\bm{J}_{z}(\tau)\bm{v}_{h}(\tau)d\tau. (122)

Cauchy–Schwarz then gives

‖𝒯s,T​𝒉‖Hm≤∫sT𝔞m​(τ)​‖𝒗h​(τ)‖2​𝑑τ≤Λm​(s,T)​(∫sT‖𝑱S​(τ)⊤​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒉‖22​𝑑τ)1/2.\displaystyle\|\mathscr{T}_{s,T}\bm{h}\|_{H^{m}}\leq\int_{s}^{T}\mathfrak{a}_{m}(\tau)\|\bm{v}_{h}(\tau)\|_{2}d\tau\leq\Lambda_{m}(s,T)\left(\int_{s}^{T}\|\bm{J}_{S}(\tau)^{\top}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{h}\|_{2}^{2}d\tau\right)^{1/2}. (123)

The final integral equals 𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}, and substituting 𝒉=𝑾†/2𝒂\bm{h}=\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\bm{a} gives

‖𝒯s,T​𝒉‖Hm\displaystyle\|\mathscr{T}_{s,T}\bm{h}\|_{H^{m}} ≤Λm​(s,T)​𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉,\displaystyle\leq\Lambda_{m}(s,T)\sqrt{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}, (124)
‖𝒞s,T​𝒂‖Hm\displaystyle\|\mathcal{C}_{s,T}\bm{a}\|_{H^{m}} ≤Λm​(s,T)​‖𝒂‖2.\displaystyle\leq\Lambda_{m}(s,T)\|\bm{a}\|_{2}. (125)

Set ΠS=(ES​𝒞s,T)†​(ES​𝒞s,T)\Pi_{S}=(E_{S}\mathcal{C}_{s,T})^{\dagger}(E_{S}\mathcal{C}_{s,T}) and, for any unit vector 𝒂\bm{a}, f𝒂=𝒞s,T​(𝑰−ΠS)​𝒂f_{\bm{a}}=\mathcal{C}_{s,T}(\bm{I}-\Pi_{S})\bm{a}. Then ES​f𝒂=0E_{S}f_{\bm{a}}=0 and

‖f𝒂‖Hm≤Λm​(s,T).\displaystyle\|f_{\bm{a}}\|_{H^{m}}\leq\Lambda_{m}(s,T). (126)

The Sobolev sampling inequality [23] for functions vanishing on an hSh_{S}-net then gives

‖EQ​f𝒂‖2\displaystyle\|E_{Q}f_{\bm{a}}\|_{2} ≤Cℳ,m,p​|Q|1/2​hSm−dℳ/2​‖f𝒂‖Hm,\displaystyle\leq C_{\mathcal{M},m,p}|Q|^{1/2}h_{S}^{m-d_{\mathcal{M}}/2}\|f_{\bm{a}}\|_{H^{m}}, (127)
𝒈​(s)⊤​𝑾​𝒈​(s)\displaystyle\bm{g}(s)^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{g}(s) =ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T)).\displaystyle=\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T)). (128)

Taking the supremum over ‖𝒂‖2=1\|\bm{a}\|_{2}=1 in the first display yields the bound for 𝑹⟂\bm{R}_{\perp}, and the second display delivers the trajectory bound. ∎

Remark E.11 (Dimensional limitation).

When dℳd_{\mathcal{M}} is large, the fill distance of nn points on a dℳd_{\mathcal{M}}-dimensional manifold scales as hS∼n−1/dℳh_{S}\sim n^{-1/d_{\mathcal{M}}}, so the bound becomes n−(m/dℳ−1/2)n^{-(m/d_{\mathcal{M}}-1/2)}. This is useful only when m≫dℳm\gg d_{\mathcal{M}}, i.e. when the network map is much smoother than the intrinsic dimension requires. The result is therefore most informative for low-dimensional data manifolds; in high-dimensional settings the operator bound from Theorem 5.1 remains the operative guarantee.

Combining fill distance with Sobolev sampling yields a population-risk bound from finite-sample training error.

Theorem E.12 (Pathwise Sobolev Generalization).

Assume squared loss and let 𝐲:ℳ→ℝp\bm{y}:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{p} be the population target. Let

𝒓T​(z)=F⁡(w⁡(T),z)−𝒚⁡(z).\displaystyle\bm{r}_{T}(z)=F(w(T),z)-\bm{y}(z). (129)

Let ρ\rho be the population law on ℳ\mathcal{M}, and let ViV_{i} be the Voronoi cell of ziz_{i} under the manifold metric, with μi=ρ⁡(Vi)\mu_{i}=\rho(V_{i}) and μmax=maxi⁡μi\mu_{\max}=\max_{i}\mu_{i}. Then

‖𝒓T‖L2​(ρ)\displaystyle\|\bm{r}_{T}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} ≤n​μmax​‖𝒓T‖ℓ2​(S)\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{n\mu_{\max}}\|\bm{r}_{T}\|_{\ell_{2}(S)} (130)
+Cℳ,m,p​hSm​(‖F⁡(w⁡(s),⋅)−𝒚‖Hm+Λm​(s,T)​ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T))).\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt+C_{\mathcal{M},m,p}h_{S}^{m}\left(\|F(w(s),\cdot)-\bm{y}\|_{H^{m}}+\Lambda_{m}(s,T)\sqrt{\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T))}\right). (131)

Thus small training error plus finite pathwise Jacobian-Sobolev norm gives a non-asymptotic population-risk bound under full feature learning.

Proof.

Apply the deterministic sampling inequality [23] to f=𝒓Tf=\bm{r}_{T} and combine with the residual decomposition:

‖f‖L2​(ρ)\displaystyle\|f\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} ≤(∑iμi​‖f⁡(zi)‖22)1/2+Cℳ,m,p​hSm​‖f‖Hm,\displaystyle\leq\left(\sum_{i}\mu_{i}\|f(z_{i})\|_{2}^{2}\right)^{1/2}+C_{\mathcal{M},m,p}h_{S}^{m}\|f\|_{H^{m}}, (132)
(∑iμi​‖𝒓T​(zi)‖22)1/2\displaystyle\left(\sum_{i}\mu_{i}\|\bm{r}_{T}(z_{i})\|_{2}^{2}\right)^{1/2} ≤n​μmax​‖𝒓T‖ℓ2​(S),\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{n\mu_{\max}}\|\bm{r}_{T}\|_{\ell_{2}(S)}, (133)
𝒓T\displaystyle\bm{r}_{T} =F⁡(𝒘⁡(s),⋅)−𝒚−𝒯s,T​𝒈​(s),\displaystyle=F(\bm{w}(s),\cdot)-\bm{y}-\mathscr{T}_{s,T}\bm{g}(s), (134)
‖𝒓T‖Hm\displaystyle\|\bm{r}_{T}\|_{H^{m}} ≤‖F⁡(𝒘⁡(s),⋅)−𝒚‖Hm+‖𝒯s,T​𝒈​(s)‖Hm.\displaystyle\leq\|F(\bm{w}(s),\cdot)-\bm{y}\|_{H^{m}}+\|\mathscr{T}_{s,T}\bm{g}(s)\|_{H^{m}}. (135)

Theorem E.9 bounds the last term by

‖𝒯s,T​𝒈​(s)‖Hm\displaystyle\|\mathscr{T}_{s,T}\bm{g}(s)\|_{H^{m}} ≤Λm​(s,T)​𝒈​(s)⊤​𝑾​𝒈​(s)=Λm​(s,T)​ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T)),\displaystyle\leq\Lambda_{m}(s,T)\sqrt{\bm{g}(s)^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{g}(s)}=\Lambda_{m}(s,T)\sqrt{\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T))}, (136)

which proves the claim. ∎

E.5 Test Error Decomposition: Bias, Reservoir Variance, Signal-Channel Variance

Intuition.

Train-test coupling, reservoir invisibility, and SGD drift-diffusion act on three different parts of the test error. We record the decomposition as a single algebraic identity: under labels 𝒚=f⋆​(S)+𝜺\bm{y}=f^{\star}(S)+\bm{\varepsilon} at interpolation, the test error splits into a bias controlled by the irreducible remainder 𝑹⟂\bm{R}_{\perp}, a reservoir-noise term that vanishes, and a signal-channel noise term that the algorithm of Section 6 suppresses.

Theorem E.13 (Bias and signal-channel variance under train-test coupling).

Assume the hypotheses of Theorem 5.1 on [0,T][0,T], so 𝐆=𝐀∘​𝐃\bm{G}=\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D} and 𝐑⟂=𝟎\bm{R}_{\perp}=\bm{0} on the realized trajectory. Take labels 𝐲=f⋆​(S)+𝛆\bm{y}=f^{\star}(S)+\bm{\varepsilon} with target f⋆:𝒵→ℝpf^{\star}:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}^{p} and noise 𝛆∈ℝn​p\bm{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{np}, and let 𝐏sig,𝐏res\bm{P}_{\mathrm{sig}},\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}} be the orthogonal projectors onto range⁡(𝒲S)\operatorname{range}(\mathcal{W}_{S}) and ker⁡(𝒲S)\ker(\mathcal{W}_{S}). Under squared loss with 𝐁=1n​𝐈\bm{B}=\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{I},

𝑼Q​(T)−f⋆​(Q)=𝑼Q​(0)+1n​𝑮​(𝒚−𝑼S​(0))−f⋆​(Q),\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-f^{\star}(Q)=\bm{U}_{Q}(0)+\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{G}\bigl(\bm{y}-\bm{U}_{S}(0)\bigr)-f^{\star}(Q), (137)

and decomposing the residual along 𝐲=f⋆​(S)+𝛆\bm{y}=f^{\star}(S)+\bm{\varepsilon} and 𝛆=𝐏sig​𝛆+𝐏res​𝛆\bm{\varepsilon}=\bm{P}_{\mathrm{sig}}\bm{\varepsilon}+\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}}\bm{\varepsilon}, then using 𝐆=𝐀∘​𝐃\bm{G}=\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D},

𝑼Q​(T)−f⋆​(Q)=𝑼Q​(0)+1n​𝑨∘​𝑫​(f⋆​(S)−𝑼S​(0))−f⋆​(Q)⏟𝒃⁡(T,S)+1n​𝑮​𝑷res​𝜺⏟=𝟎+1n​𝑮​𝑷sig​𝜺⏟𝒗sig​(T,S,𝜺).\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-f^{\star}(Q)=\underbrace{\bm{U}_{Q}(0)+\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D}\bigl(f^{\star}(S)-\bm{U}_{S}(0)\bigr)-f^{\star}(Q)}_{\bm{b}(T,S)}+\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{G}\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}}\bm{\varepsilon}}_{=\bm{0}}+\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{G}\bm{P}_{\mathrm{sig}}\bm{\varepsilon}}_{\bm{v}_{\mathrm{sig}}(T,S,\bm{\varepsilon})}. (138)

The reservoir term vanishes: 𝐆​𝐏res=𝟎\bm{G}\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}}=\bm{0}.

Proof.

The chain rule gives 𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(0)=−𝑮​𝒈​(0)\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(0)=-\bm{G}\bm{g}(0) exactly (Section C.1). Squared loss with 𝑩=1n​𝑰\bm{B}=\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{I} has 𝒈⁡(0)=1n​(𝑼S​(0)−𝒚)\bm{g}(0)=\tfrac{1}{n}(\bm{U}_{S}(0)-\bm{y}), so −𝑮​𝒈​(0)=1n​𝑮​(𝒚−𝑼S​(0))-\bm{G}\bm{g}(0)=\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{G}(\bm{y}-\bm{U}_{S}(0)), which is (137). Substituting 𝒚=f⋆​(S)+𝜺\bm{y}=f^{\star}(S)+\bm{\varepsilon} and 𝜺=𝑷sig​𝜺+𝑷res​𝜺\bm{\varepsilon}=\bm{P}_{\mathrm{sig}}\bm{\varepsilon}+\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}}\bm{\varepsilon} splits the right side into a clean part 1n​𝑮​(f⋆​(S)−𝑼S​(0))\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{G}(f^{\star}(S)-\bm{U}_{S}(0)) and the two noise pieces. On the clean part, train-test coupling under squared loss gives 𝑮=𝑨∘​𝑫\bm{G}=\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D}, rewriting it as 1n​𝑨∘​𝑫​(f⋆​(S)−𝑼S​(0))\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D}(f^{\star}(S)-\bm{U}_{S}(0)) and yielding (138). Reservoir invisibility (Section 3) is the inclusion ker⁡𝑾⊆ker⁡𝑮\ker\bm{W}\subseteq\ker\bm{G}, so 𝑮\bm{G} kills range⁡(𝑷res)=ker⁡𝑾\operatorname{range}(\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}})=\ker\bm{W}, giving 𝑮​𝑷res=𝟎\bm{G}\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}}=\bm{0} directly, with no appeal to a pseudoinverse. ∎

What controls each term.

The bias 𝒃⁡(T,S)\bm{b}(T,S) is the optimal train-to-test predictor 𝑨∘\bm{A}_{\circ} applied to the clean training displacement 1n​𝑫​(f⋆​(S)−𝑼S​(0))\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{D}(f^{\star}(S)-\bm{U}_{S}(0)): it asks, given the clean signal alone, what test prediction the realized-trajectory operators would produce. Train-test coupling under squared loss gives 𝑮=𝑨∘​𝑫\bm{G}=\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D} exactly, so this is the literal physical translator of clean structure; under a Sobolev or RKHS prior of order m>dℳ/2m>d_{\mathcal{M}}/2 on the data manifold, ‖𝑹⟂‖op≤C​hSm−dℳ/2\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}\leq Ch_{S}^{m-d_{\mathcal{M}}/2} (Theorem E.9). The bound is tight without a smoothness hypothesis, since two networks can share an identical training trajectory yet disagree on a held-out point (Section E.3).

The reservoir variance 1n​𝑮​𝑷res​𝜺\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{G}\bm{P}_{\mathrm{res}}\bm{\varepsilon} is identically zero: whatever portion of the label noise the optimizer placed in ker⁡𝑾\ker\bm{W} during training never reaches the test predictions, because 𝑮\bm{G} kills that subspace.

The signal-channel variance 𝒗sig=1n​𝑮​𝑷sig​𝜺\bm{v}_{\mathrm{sig}}=\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{G}\bm{P}_{\mathrm{sig}}\bm{\varepsilon} is the only failure mode that survives. Two effects bound it. First, the drift-diffusion separation (Theorem 4.1): on a parameter with population gradient μ\mu and per-example variance σ2\sigma^{2}, SGD’s mean update grows like η​T​μ\eta T\mu while its diffusion grows like σ​η​T/b\sigma\sqrt{\eta T/b}, so signal dominates noise as T→∞T\to\infty at fixed batch and step size. Second, the population-risk gate (Section F.2): the per-parameter cutoff μk2>σk2/(b−1)\mu_{k}^{2}>\sigma_{k}^{2}/(b-1) is the unique binary mask that prevents adversarial first-order loss along a parameter whose batch signal cannot beat its noise.

The three pieces together.

Bias is small when 𝑨∘\bm{A}_{\circ} is the right interpolation operator, exact under squared loss and approximate under network smoothness. Reservoir variance is zero by construction. Signal-channel variance shrinks under SGD and shrinks faster under the population-risk gate. Each mechanism handles one term; (138) is small only when all three are.

E.6 On-Trajectory and Off-Trajectory Error

Intuition.

A fixed predictor’s error should be measured along the directions the gradient trajectory actually visits. Measuring it across the full time interval introduces slack from directions never excited by the run. The next theorem isolates the on-trajectory part and quantifies the off-trajectory excess.

Throughout this subsection, fix 0≤s≤T0\leq s\leq T and a test set QQ, and use the notation of Theorem E.2 with

𝑫\displaystyle\bm{D} ≜𝖣S​(T,s),\displaystyle\triangleq\mathsf{D}_{S}(T,s), 𝑮\displaystyle\bm{G} ≜𝖦Q​(T,s),\displaystyle\triangleq\mathsf{G}_{Q}(T,s), 𝑾\displaystyle\bm{W} ≜𝒲S​(s,T),\displaystyle\triangleq\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,T), (139)

and let 𝑨∘,𝑹⟂\bm{A}_{\circ},\bm{R}_{\perp} be the canonical predictor and irreducible remainder from Theorem E.2. For any linear predictor 𝑨:ℝn​p→ℝ|Q|​p\bm{A}:\mathbb{R}^{np}\to\mathbb{R}^{|Q|p}, define the path error

𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)≜(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)​𝑾†​(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)⊤.\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)\triangleq(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger}(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})^{\top}. (140)

The first theorem records the orthogonal split of the on-trajectory error.

Theorem E.14 (On-trajectory error split).

The on-trajectory path error decomposes as

𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)=𝑹⟂​𝑹⟂⊤+(𝑨−𝑨∘)​𝑫​𝑾†​𝑫⊤​(𝑨−𝑨∘)⊤,\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)=\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{R}_{\perp}^{\top}+(\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ})\bm{D}\bm{W}^{\dagger}\bm{D}^{\top}(\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ})^{\top}, (141)

which gives, in the positive-semidefinite order,

𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T) ⪰𝑹⟂​𝑹⟂⊤,\displaystyle\succeq\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{R}_{\perp}^{\top}, (142)
inf𝑨𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)\displaystyle\inf_{\bm{A}}\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T) =𝑹⟂​𝑹⟂⊤,\displaystyle=\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{R}_{\perp}^{\top}, (143)

with equality in the first line iff 𝐀​𝐃=𝐀∘​𝐃\bm{A}\bm{D}=\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D}.

The next theorem promotes the cumulative error operator to a positive-semidefinite split: the on-trajectory part plus an off-trajectory slack.

Theorem E.15 (On-/off-trajectory split of the cumulative error).

The cumulative error operator

𝒟𝑨​(s,T)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}(s,T) ≜∫sTΔ𝑨​(τ)​𝑲S​S​(τ)†​Δ𝑨​(τ)⊤​𝑑τ,\displaystyle\triangleq\int_{s}^{T}\Delta_{\bm{A}}(\tau)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{\dagger}\Delta_{\bm{A}}(\tau)^{\top}d\tau, Δ𝑨​(τ)\displaystyle\Delta_{\bm{A}}(\tau) ≜𝑲Q​S​(τ)−𝑨​𝑲S​S​(τ),\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)-\bm{A}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau), (144)
admits the split
𝒟𝑨​(s,T)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}(s,T) =𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)+𝒩𝑨​(s,T),\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)+\mathcal{N}_{\bm{A}}(s,T), 𝒩𝑨​(s,T)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\bm{A}}(s,T) ⪰0.\displaystyle\succeq 0. (145)

The final theorem of this trio converts the operator-level statement into a deterministic bound on test displacement along the realized trajectory.

Theorem E.16 (Trajectory bound from the on-trajectory error).

On the true trajectory,

‖𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)−𝑨⁡(𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s))‖22≤‖𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)‖op​(ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T))).\displaystyle\|\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)-\bm{A}(\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s))\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}\bigl(\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T))\bigr). (146)

If the predictor is preserved along the trajectory, train motion fully determines test motion.

Corollary E.17 (Exact fixed transfer under perfect predictor invariance).

If Δ𝐀​(τ)=0\Delta_{\bm{A}}(\tau)=0 for a.e. τ∈[s,T]\tau\in[s,T], equivalently 𝒟𝐀​(s,T)=0\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}(s,T)=0, then

𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T) =0,\displaystyle=0, (147)
𝑮\displaystyle\bm{G} =𝑨​𝑫,\displaystyle=\bm{A}\bm{D}, (148)
𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s) =𝑨⁡(𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s)).\displaystyle=\bm{A}\bigl(\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s)\bigr). (149)

The off-trajectory version overestimates by the off-path slack 𝒩𝑨\mathcal{N}_{\bm{A}}.

Corollary E.18 (Sharp on-trajectory bound and coarse off-trajectory bound).

For every linear predictor 𝐀\bm{A}, the visible infimum is sharp and bounds the lifted infimum:

‖𝑹⟂‖op2\displaystyle\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{2} ≤‖𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)‖op≤‖𝒟𝑨​(s,T)‖op,\displaystyle\leq\|\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}\leq\|\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}, (150)
inf𝑨‖𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)‖op\displaystyle\inf_{\bm{A}}\|\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}} =‖𝑹⟂‖op2≤inf𝑨‖𝒟𝑨​(s,T)‖op.\displaystyle=\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{2}\leq\inf_{\bm{A}}\|\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}. (151)
Remark E.19 (Anchored transfer as a computable coarse bound).

The anchor 𝑨s≜𝑲Q​S​(s)​𝑲S​S​(s)†\bm{A}_{s}\triangleq\bm{K}_{\!QS}(s)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(s)^{\dagger} gives the anchored off-trajectory bound

‖𝑹⟂‖op2≤‖∫sT(𝑲Q​S​(τ)−𝑨s​𝑲S​S​(τ))​𝑲S​S​(τ)†​(𝑲Q​S​(τ)−𝑨s​𝑲S​S​(τ))⊤​𝑑τ‖op.\displaystyle\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{2}\leq\left\|\int_{s}^{T}\bigl(\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)-\bm{A}_{s}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\bigr)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{\dagger}\bigl(\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)-\bm{A}_{s}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\bigr)^{\top}d\tau\right\|_{\operatorname{op}}. (152)

By Theorem E.15, this bound exceeds the visible error by a positive-semidefinite off-trajectory slack and therefore vanishes under 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) raw kernel drift when the transfer operator is preserved, leaving the on-path remainder 𝑹⟂\bm{R}_{\perp} as the limit of fixed transfer.

Proof of Theorem E.14, Theorem E.15, and Theorem E.16.

Set ℋs,T≜L2​([s,T],ℝn​p)\mathcal{H}_{s,T}\triangleq L^{2}([s,T];\mathbb{R}^{np}) and define the lift sending 𝒉∈ℝn​p\bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{np} to its time-indexed path,

(𝒯s,T​𝒉)​(τ)\displaystyle(\mathcal{T}_{s,T}\bm{h})(\tau) ≜𝑲S​S​(τ)1/2​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒉,\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{1/2}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{h}, (153)
𝒯s,T∗​𝝃\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{s,T}^{\ast}\bm{\xi} =∫sT𝒫g​(τ,s)⊤​𝑲S​S​(τ)1/2​𝝃​(τ)​𝑑τ,\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{T}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)^{\top}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{1/2}\bm{\xi}(\tau)d\tau, (154)
𝒯s,T∗​𝒯s,T\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{s,T}^{\ast}\mathcal{T}_{s,T} =𝑾.\displaystyle=\bm{W}. (155)

Since the domain of 𝒯s,T\mathcal{T}_{s,T} is finite-dimensional, range⁡(𝒯s,T)\operatorname{range}(\mathcal{T}_{s,T}) is closed, so

Pvis​(s,T)≜𝒯s,T​𝑾†​𝒯s,T∗\displaystyle P_{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)\triangleq\mathcal{T}_{s,T}\bm{W}^{\dagger}\mathcal{T}_{s,T}^{\ast} (156)

is the orthogonal projector onto range⁡(𝒯s,T)⊂ℋs,T\operatorname{range}(\mathcal{T}_{s,T})\subset\mathcal{H}_{s,T}.

Now define the extended train/test maps

ℒS​𝝃\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{S}\bm{\xi} ≜∫sT𝑲S​S​(τ)1/2​𝝃​(τ)​𝑑τ,\displaystyle\triangleq\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{1/2}\bm{\xi}(\tau)d\tau, (157)
ℒQ​𝝃\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{Q}\bm{\xi} ≜∫sT𝑲Q​S(τ)𝑲S​S(τ)†/2𝝃(τ)dτ.\displaystyle\triangleq\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{\dagger/2}\bm{\xi}(\tau)d\tau. (158)

Since 𝑲Q​S​(τ)\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau) annihilates ker⁡𝑲S​S​(τ)\ker\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau), both maps are well-defined and bounded, and

ℒS​𝒯s,T​𝒉\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{S}\mathcal{T}_{s,T}\bm{h} =∫sT𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒉​𝑑τ=𝑫​𝒉,\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{h}d\tau=\bm{D}\bm{h}, (159)
ℒQ​𝒯s,T​𝒉\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{Q}\mathcal{T}_{s,T}\bm{h} =∫sT𝑲Q​S(τ)𝑲S​S(τ)†/2𝑲S​S(τ)1/2𝒫g(τ,s)𝒉dτ\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{\dagger/2}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{1/2}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{h}d\tau (160)
=∫sT𝑲Q​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒉​𝑑τ=𝑮​𝒉.\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{h}d\tau=\bm{G}\bm{h}. (161)

Hence 𝑮−𝑨​𝑫=(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)​𝒯s,T\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D}=(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})\mathcal{T}_{s,T}, and

𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T) =(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)​𝑾†​(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)⊤\displaystyle=(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger}(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})^{\top} (162)
=(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)​𝒯s,T​𝑾†​𝒯s,T∗​(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)⊤\displaystyle=(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})\mathcal{T}_{s,T}\bm{W}^{\dagger}\mathcal{T}_{s,T}^{\ast}(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})^{\top} (163)
=(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)​Pvis​(s,T)​(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)⊤.\displaystyle=(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})P_{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})^{\top}. (164)

Next, (80) from Theorem E.2 gives

(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)​𝑾†​(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)⊤=𝑹⟂​𝑹⟂⊤+(𝑨−𝑨∘)​𝑫​𝑾†​𝑫⊤​(𝑨−𝑨∘)⊤,\displaystyle(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger}(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})^{\top}=\bm{R}_{\perp}\bm{R}_{\perp}^{\top}+(\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ})\bm{D}\bm{W}^{\dagger}\bm{D}^{\top}(\bm{A}-\bm{A}_{\circ})^{\top}, (165)

which is (141). The positive-semidefinite lower bound (142) and the infimum (143) follow immediately, with equality iff the misspecification term vanishes, i.e. 𝑨​𝑫=𝑨∘​𝑫\bm{A}\bm{D}=\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D}.

It remains to identify the slack term in the off-trajectory error. For any 𝒚∈ℝ|Q|​p\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{|Q|p},

(ℒQ−𝑨ℒS)⊤𝒚(τ)=𝑲S​S(τ)†/2Δ𝑨(τ)⊤𝒚,\displaystyle(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})^{\top}\bm{y}(\tau)=\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{\dagger/2}\Delta_{\bm{A}}(\tau)^{\top}\bm{y}, (166)

using 𝑨𝑲S​S(τ)1/2=𝑨𝑲S​S(τ)𝑲S​S(τ)†/2\bm{A}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{1/2}=\bm{A}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{\dagger/2}. Therefore

(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)​(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)⊤=∫sTΔ𝑨​(τ)​𝑲S​S​(τ)†​Δ𝑨​(τ)⊤​𝑑τ=𝒟𝑨​(s,T).\displaystyle(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})^{\top}=\int_{s}^{T}\Delta_{\bm{A}}(\tau)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)^{\dagger}\Delta_{\bm{A}}(\tau)^{\top}d\tau=\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}(s,T). (167)

Splitting I=Pvis​(s,T)+(I−Pvis​(s,T))I=P_{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)+(I-P_{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)) gives

𝒟𝑨​(s,T)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}(s,T) =(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)​Pvis​(s,T)​(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)⊤\displaystyle=(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})P_{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})^{\top} (168)
+(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)​(I−Pvis​(s,T))​(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)⊤\displaystyle{}+(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})(I-P_{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T))(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})^{\top} (169)
=𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)+𝒩𝑨​(s,T),\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)+\mathcal{N}_{\bm{A}}(s,T), (170)

where

𝒩𝑨​(s,T)≜(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)​(I−Pvis​(s,T))​(ℒQ−𝑨​ℒS)⊤⪰0.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\bm{A}}(s,T)\triangleq(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})(I-P_{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T))(\mathcal{L}_{Q}-\bm{A}\mathcal{L}_{S})^{\top}\succeq 0. (171)

This proves (145).

Finally, 𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)−𝑨⁡(𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s))=−(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)​𝒈​(s)\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)-\bm{A}(\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s))=-(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{g}(s), so by Section 3 and Section 3,

‖𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)−𝑨⁡(𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s))‖22\displaystyle\|\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)-\bm{A}(\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s))\|_{2}^{2} ≤∥(𝑮−𝑨𝑫)𝑾†/2∥op2𝒈(s)⊤𝑾𝒈(s)\displaystyle\leq\|(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{2}\bm{g}(s)^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{g}(s) (172)
=‖𝒟𝑨vis​(s,T)‖op​(ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T))),\displaystyle=\|\mathcal{D}_{\bm{A}}^{\mathrm{vis}}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}\bigl(\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T))\bigr), (173)

which is (146). ∎

E.7 Test Prediction Bounds from Network Smoothness

Intuition.

Two scalars, the visibility Gramian ΓQ\Gamma_{Q} and the irreducible remainder 𝑹⟂\bm{R}_{\perp}, give the path-error bounds along the realized trajectory. Both are computable from forward and backward ODE solves on the observed window through the Dual Transfer Theorem (Section E.8), so the bounds are practical to evaluate from a single training run.

Corollary E.20 (Path-error bounds).

Under the notation of Theorem 5.1, ‖ΓQ​(s,T)‖op\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}} and ‖𝐑⟂‖op\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}} satisfy

‖ΓQ​(s,T)‖op\displaystyle\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}} =sup𝒉∉ker⁡𝑾‖𝑮​𝒉‖22𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉,\displaystyle=\sup_{\bm{h}\notin\ker\bm{W}}\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}\|_{2}^{2}}{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}, (174)
‖𝑹⟂‖op2\displaystyle\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{2} =inf𝑨∥(𝑮−𝑨𝑫)𝑾†/2∥op2=sup𝒉∉ker⁡𝑾𝑫​𝒉=0‖𝑮​𝒉‖22𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉.\displaystyle=\inf_{\bm{A}}\|(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{2}=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{h}\notin\ker\bm{W}\\ \bm{D}\bm{h}=0\end{subarray}}\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}\|_{2}^{2}}{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}. (175)

Along the true trajectory,

‖𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)\|_{2} ≤‖ΓQ​(s,T)‖op1/2​ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T)),\displaystyle\leq\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{1/2}\sqrt{\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T))}, (176)
‖𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)−𝑨∘​(𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s))‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s)-\bm{A}_{\circ}\bigl(\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s)\bigr)\|_{2} ≤‖𝑹⟂‖op​ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T)).\displaystyle\leq\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}\sqrt{\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T))}. (177)

The proof is given in Section E.1; the remainder characterization follows from Section E.2, the visibility characterization from Section 3, and the path-error inequalities from the path-error decomposition (Theorem E.14).

Remark E.21 (Transfer characterization).

Prediction from the observed training displacement (‖𝑹⟂‖op=0\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}=0) holds if and only if ker⁡𝑫⊆ker⁡𝑮\ker\bm{D}\subseteq\ker\bm{G}. In the frozen-kernel limit [17], ‖ΓQ‖op1/2\|\Gamma_{Q}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{1/2} recovers the classical NTK test-invisibility constant ΠQ\Pi_{Q} and ‖𝑹⟂‖op\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}} recovers the kernel-regression residual.

Proof of Section E.7.

Operator norm of ΓQ​(s,T)\Gamma_{Q}(s,T). By Section 3,

𝑮⊤𝑮=𝑾1/2ΓQ(s,T)𝑾1/2,ΓQ(s,T)=𝑾†/2𝑮⊤𝑮𝑾†/2⪰0.\displaystyle\bm{G}^{\top}\bm{G}=\bm{W}^{1/2}\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\bm{W}^{1/2},\hskip 9.24994pt\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)=\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\bm{G}^{\top}\bm{G}\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\succeq 0. (178)

The substitution 𝒛=𝑾1/2​𝒉\bm{z}=\bm{W}^{1/2}\bm{h} gives

‖ΓQ​(s,T)‖op=sup𝒉∉ker⁡𝑾‖𝑮​𝒉‖22𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉.\displaystyle\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}=\sup_{\bm{h}\notin\ker\bm{W}}\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}\|_{2}^{2}}{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}. (179)

Variational characterization of ‖𝑹⟂‖op\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}. By (81),

inf𝑨∥(𝑮−𝑨𝑫)𝑾†/2∥op=∥𝑹⟂∥op=sup𝒉∉ker⁡𝑾𝑫​𝒉=0‖𝑮​𝒉‖2𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉.\displaystyle\inf_{\bm{A}}\|(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\|_{\operatorname{op}}=\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{h}\notin\ker\bm{W}\\ \bm{D}\bm{h}=0\end{subarray}}\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}\|_{2}}{\sqrt{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}}. (180)

Squaring gives the stated expression. The infimum characterization is equivalent, since the same substitution gives

inf{c≥0:(𝑮−𝑨𝑫)⊤(𝑮−𝑨𝑫)⪯c𝑾}=∥(𝑮−𝑨𝑫)𝑾†/2∥op2.\displaystyle\inf\{c\geq 0:(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})^{\top}(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\preceq c\bm{W}\}=\|(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{W}^{\dagger/2}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{2}. (181)

Equations (176)–(177). By Section 3,

𝑼Q​(T)−𝑼Q​(s)\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}(s) =−𝑮​𝒈​(s),\displaystyle=-\bm{G}\bm{g}(s), 𝒖⁡(T)−𝒖⁡(s)\displaystyle\bm{u}(T)-\bm{u}(s) =−𝑫​𝒈​(s),\displaystyle=-\bm{D}\bm{g}(s), (182)
𝒈​(s)⊤​𝑾​𝒈​(s)\displaystyle\bm{g}(s)^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{g}(s) =ΦS​(𝒖⁡(s))−ΦS​(𝒖⁡(T)).\displaystyle=\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(s))-\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}(T)). (183)

Setting 𝒉=𝒈⁡(s)\bm{h}=\bm{g}(s) in the two variational formulas gives

‖(𝑮−𝑨∘​𝑫)​𝒈​(s)‖22\displaystyle\|(\bm{G}-\bm{A}_{\circ}\bm{D})\bm{g}(s)\|_{2}^{2} ≤‖𝑹⟂‖op2​𝒈​(s)⊤​𝑾​𝒈​(s),\displaystyle\leq\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{2}\bm{g}(s)^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{g}(s), (185)

which are (176)–(177) after square roots. ∎

E.8 Computing Transfer Operators by Forward-Backward ODE Solves

Intuition.

The pathwise operators 𝑾=𝒲S​(s,t)\bm{W}=\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,t), 𝑫=𝖣S​(t,s)\bm{D}=\mathsf{D}_{S}(t,s), and 𝑮=𝖦Q​(t,s)\bm{G}=\mathsf{G}_{Q}(t,s) are computable. On any observed window [s,t][s,t], applying any one of them amounts to forward and backward linear ODE solves along the realized feature-learning trajectory. The visibility Gramian ΓQ\Gamma_{Q} and remainder 𝑹⟂\bm{R}_{\perp} thus become matrix-free quantities computable from a single run, in the spirit of adjoint-based influence computation [18]. Throughout this subsection, fix an observed window 0≤s<t0\leq s<t along the training run and write 𝑨⁡(τ)≜𝑩⁡(τ)​𝑲S​S​(τ)\bm{A}(\tau)\triangleq\bm{B}(\tau)\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau).

Proposition E.22 (Dual Transfer).

Forward solves. For 𝐡∈ℝn​p\bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{np}, the forward solution 𝐳h:[s,t]→ℝn​p\bm{z}_{h}:[s,t]\to\mathbb{R}^{np} to ∂τ𝐳h​(τ)=−𝐀⁡(τ)​𝐳h​(τ)\partial_{\tau}\bm{z}_{h}(\tau)=-\bm{A}(\tau)\bm{z}_{h}(\tau), 𝐳h​(s)=𝐡\bm{z}_{h}(s)=\bm{h}, satisfies

𝑫​𝒉\displaystyle\bm{D}\bm{h} =∫st𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒛h​(τ)​𝑑τ,\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\bm{z}_{h}(\tau)d\tau, (186)
𝑮​𝒉\displaystyle\bm{G}\bm{h} =∫st𝑲Q​S​(τ)​𝒛h​(τ)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\bm{K}_{\!QS}(\tau)\bm{z}_{h}(\tau)d\tau. (187)

Backward solves. For 𝐡∈ℝn​p\bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{np}, 𝛏∈ℝ|Q|​p\bm{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{|Q|p}, 𝛈∈ℝn​p\bm{\eta}\in\mathbb{R}^{np}, the backward solutions 𝐦h,𝐪ξ,𝐝η:[s,t]→ℝn​p\bm{m}_{h},\bm{q}_{\xi},\bm{d}_{\eta}:[s,t]\to\mathbb{R}^{np} with terminal value zero at τ=t\tau=t to

−∂τ𝒎h(τ)\displaystyle-\partial_{\tau}\bm{m}_{h}(\tau) =−𝑨​(τ)⊤​𝒎h​(τ)+𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒛h​(τ),\displaystyle=-\bm{A}(\tau)^{\top}\bm{m}_{h}(\tau)+\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\bm{z}_{h}(\tau), (188)
−∂τ𝒒ξ(τ)\displaystyle-\partial_{\tau}\bm{q}_{\xi}(\tau) =−𝑨​(τ)⊤​𝒒ξ​(τ)+𝑲S​Q​(τ)​𝝃,\displaystyle=-\bm{A}(\tau)^{\top}\bm{q}_{\xi}(\tau)+\bm{K}_{\!SQ}(\tau)\bm{\xi}, (189)
−∂τ𝒅η(τ)\displaystyle-\partial_{\tau}\bm{d}_{\eta}(\tau) =−𝑨​(τ)⊤​𝒅η​(τ)+𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝜼,\displaystyle=-\bm{A}(\tau)^{\top}\bm{d}_{\eta}(\tau)+\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\bm{\eta}, (190)
recover the operator actions at τ=s\tau=s,
𝒎h​(s)\displaystyle\bm{m}_{h}(s) =𝑾​𝒉,\displaystyle=\bm{W}\bm{h}, (191)
𝒒ξ​(s)\displaystyle\bm{q}_{\xi}(s) =𝑮⊤​𝝃,\displaystyle=\bm{G}^{\top}\bm{\xi}, (192)
𝒅η​(s)\displaystyle\bm{d}_{\eta}(s) =𝑫⊤​𝜼.\displaystyle=\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{\eta}. (193)
Corollary E.23 (Matrix-Free Pathwise Quantities).

On the observed window, the pathwise quantities ‖ΓQ​(s,t)‖op\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,t)\|_{\operatorname{op}} and ‖𝐑⟂‖op\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}} satisfy

‖ΓQ​(s,t)‖op\displaystyle\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,t)\|_{\operatorname{op}} =sup𝒉∉ker⁡𝑾‖𝑮​𝒉‖22𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉,\displaystyle=\sup_{\bm{h}\notin\ker\bm{W}}\frac{\|\bm{G}\bm{h}\|_{2}^{2}}{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}, (194)
‖𝑹⟂‖op2\displaystyle\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{2} =inf𝑨sup𝒉∉ker⁡𝑾‖(𝑮−𝑨​𝑫)​𝒉‖22𝒉⊤​𝑾​𝒉,\displaystyle=\inf_{\bm{A}}\sup_{\bm{h}\notin\ker\bm{W}}\frac{\|(\bm{G}-\bm{A}\bm{D})\bm{h}\|_{2}^{2}}{\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{W}\bm{h}}, (195)

and are one-run matrix-free quantities: every application of 𝐖\bm{W}, 𝐃\bm{D}, 𝐃⊤\bm{D}^{\top}, 𝐆\bm{G}, and 𝐆⊤\bm{G}^{\top} reduces to forward/backward linear ODE solves on the realized feature-learning path via Section E.8, valid for arbitrary kernel drift.

Proof.

Since 𝒛h​(τ)=𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒉\bm{z}_{h}(\tau)=\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{h}, Equation 186 and Equation 187 are the definitions of 𝑫\bm{D} and 𝑮\bm{G}. Variation of constants on the three backward equations gives

𝒎h​(s)\displaystyle\bm{m}_{h}(s) =∫st𝒫g​(τ,s)⊤​𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒛h​(τ)​𝑑τ\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)^{\top}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\bm{z}_{h}(\tau)d\tau (196)
=∫st𝒫g​(τ,s)⊤​𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝒉​𝑑τ=𝑾​𝒉,\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)^{\top}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)\bm{h}d\tau=\bm{W}\bm{h}, (197)
𝒒ξ​(s)\displaystyle\bm{q}_{\xi}(s) =∫st𝒫g​(τ,s)⊤​𝑲S​Q​(τ)​𝝃​𝑑τ=𝑮⊤​𝝃,\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)^{\top}\bm{K}_{\!SQ}(\tau)\bm{\xi}d\tau=\bm{G}^{\top}\bm{\xi}, (198)
𝒅η​(s)\displaystyle\bm{d}_{\eta}(s) =∫st𝒫g​(τ,s)⊤​𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝜼​𝑑τ=𝑫⊤​𝜼.\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)^{\top}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\bm{\eta}d\tau=\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{\eta}. (199)

The remaining claim follows because ‖ΓQ‖op\|\Gamma_{Q}\|_{\operatorname{op}} and ‖𝑹⟂‖op\|\bm{R}_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}} depend only on applications of 𝑾\bm{W}, 𝑫\bm{D}, 𝑫⊤\bm{D}^{\top}, 𝑮\bm{G}, and 𝑮⊤\bm{G}^{\top}. ∎

Appendix F Population Risk Training: Proofs and Algorithm

F.1 Exchangeability

Intuition.

Each leave-one-out evaluation places a held-out training point against a model that did not see it, which is distributionally indistinguishable from a fresh draw against a model trained on n−1n-1 independent samples. Averaging over ii converts the empirical average of leave-one-out losses to a population risk.

Proof of Section 6.

For any fixed ii, the i.i.d. assumption gives

(S−i,Zi)=d(Sn−1,Z),Sn−1∼𝒟n−1,Z∼𝒟​ independent of ​Sn−1.\displaystyle(S_{-i},Z_{i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(S_{n-1},Z),\hskip 18.49988ptS_{n-1}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n-1},\hskip 9.24994ptZ\sim\mathcal{D}\text{ independent of }S_{n-1}. (200)

Averaging 𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(𝒘T​(S−i),Zi)]=𝔼⁡[ℒ𝒟​(𝒘T​(Sn−1))]\mathbb{E}[\ell(\bm{w}_{T}(S_{-i}),Z_{i})]=\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}(\bm{w}_{T}(S_{n-1}))] over ii yields the claim. ∎

F.2 Population Risk from Kernel-Block Agreement

Per-example triple, kernel block, and leave-one-out expansion.

Specializing Theorem 6.2 to a one-step window from the current iterate, fix the optimizer history ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, let 𝒘t\bm{w}_{t} and a base preconditioner 𝑷t⪰0\bm{P}_{t}\succeq 0 be ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable, and let B=(z1,…,zb)B=(z_{1},\dots,z_{b}) be an exchangeable batch independent of ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}. For each example record the output residual, the per-example Jacobian, and the parameter-space gradient,

𝒓a=∇𝒖ℓ​(F⁡(𝒘t,za),za),𝑱a=D𝒘​F​(𝒘t,za),𝒈a=𝑱a⊤​𝒓a.\displaystyle\bm{r}_{a}=\nabla_{\bm{u}}\ell\bigl(F(\bm{w}_{t},z_{a}),z_{a}\bigr),\hskip 18.49988pt\bm{J}_{a}=D_{\bm{w}}F(\bm{w}_{t},z_{a}),\hskip 18.49988pt\bm{g}_{a}=\bm{J}_{a}^{\top}\bm{r}_{a}. (201)

A preconditioner M⪰0M\succeq 0 induces the pairwise kernel block Ka​cM=𝑱a​M​𝑱c⊤K_{ac}^{M}=\bm{J}_{a}M\bm{J}_{c}^{\top}, which is the (a,c)(a,c) block of 𝑲S​SM\bm{K}_{\!SS}^{M}. If example aa is evaluated on a step trained without it, the update is 𝒘−a+=𝒘t−η​M​𝒈¯−a\bm{w}_{-a}^{+}=\bm{w}_{t}-\eta M\bar{\bm{g}}_{-a} with 𝒈¯−a=(b−1)−1​∑c≠a𝒈c\bar{\bm{g}}_{-a}=(b-1)^{-1}\sum_{c\neq a}\bm{g}_{c}, and a first-order expansion lifts the parameter inner product to a kernel block:

ℓa​(𝒘−a+)=ℓa​(𝒘t)−ηb−1​∑c≠a𝒓a⊤​Ka​cM​𝒓c+O⁡(η2).\displaystyle\ell_{a}(\bm{w}_{-a}^{+})=\ell_{a}(\bm{w}_{t})-\frac{\eta}{b-1}\sum_{c\neq a}\bm{r}_{a}^{\top}K_{ac}^{M}\bm{r}_{c}+O(\eta^{2}). (202)

Averaging over aa, the first-order population-safe improvement of the kernel increment induced by MM is the off-diagonal agreement

ΩB​(M)=1b⁡(b−1)​∑a≠c𝒓a⊤​Ka​cM​𝒓c.\displaystyle\Omega_{B}(M)=\frac{1}{b(b-1)}\sum_{a\neq c}\bm{r}_{a}^{\top}K_{ac}^{M}\bm{r}_{c}. (203)

The diagonal terms a=ca=c are absent: those are the self-use terms removed by leave-one-out. A kernel increment improves population risk to the extent that distinct examples agree through it.

Collapse to parameter space.

Substituting 𝒈a=𝑱a⊤​𝒓a\bm{g}_{a}=\bm{J}_{a}^{\top}\bm{r}_{a} rewrites the kernel-block agreement as an inner product on parameter gradients,

ΩB​(M)=1b⁡(b−1)​∑a≠c𝒈a⊤​M​𝒈c=𝒈¯B⊤​M​𝒈¯B−1b−1​tr⁡(M​𝚺B)=tr⁡(M​𝑨B),\displaystyle\Omega_{B}(M)=\frac{1}{b(b-1)}\sum_{a\neq c}\bm{g}_{a}^{\top}M\bm{g}_{c}=\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}^{\top}M\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}-\frac{1}{b-1}\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{\Sigma}_{B})=\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{A}_{B}), (204)

with 𝒈¯B=b−1​∑a𝒈a\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}=b^{-1}\sum_{a}\bm{g}_{a}, centered residuals 𝒄a=𝒈a−𝒈¯B\bm{c}_{a}=\bm{g}_{a}-\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}, minibatch covariance 𝚺B=b−1​∑a𝒄a​𝒄a⊤\bm{\Sigma}_{B}=b^{-1}\sum_{a}\bm{c}_{a}\bm{c}_{a}^{\top}, and the off-diagonal rate matrix

𝑨B≜𝒈¯B​𝒈¯B⊤−1b−1​𝚺B.\displaystyle\bm{A}_{B}\triangleq\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}^{\top}-\frac{1}{b-1}\bm{\Sigma}_{B}. (205)
Theorem F.1 (Kernel-increment population risk).

Let ℛ1​e​x,Bη=b−1​∑aℓa​(𝐰−a+)\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{1ex},B}^{\eta}=b^{-1}\sum_{a}\ell_{a}(\bm{w}_{-a}^{+}) be the average leave-one-out risk on the current batch. Conditional on ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, exchangeability gives (B−a,Za)=d(Sb−1,Z)(B_{-a},Z_{a})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(S_{b-1},Z), so 𝔼⁡[ℛ1​e​x,Bη∣ℱt]\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{1ex},B}^{\eta}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}] is the population risk of the one-step learner trained on an independent (b−1)(b-1)-sample. To first order in η\eta,

ℛ1​e​x,Bη=L^B​(𝒘t)−η​tr⁡(M​𝑨B)+O⁡(η2),\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{1ex},B}^{\eta}=\widehat{L}_{B}(\bm{w}_{t})-\eta\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{A}_{B})+O(\eta^{2}), (206)

so maximizing tr⁡(M​𝐀B)\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{A}_{B}) over M⪰0M\succeq 0 is the first-order population-risk rule for selecting the next kernel increment 𝐉S​M​𝐉S⊤\bm{J}_{S}M\bm{J}_{S}^{\top} added to 𝒲SM\mathcal{W}_{S}^{M}. Given a base preconditioner 𝐏t⪰0\bm{P}_{t}\succeq 0, the unique MM with 0⪯M⪯𝐏t0\preceq M\preceq\bm{P}_{t} attaining this maximum is the spectral projector through the optimizer’s metric,

M⋆=𝑷t1/2​𝟏(0,∞)​(𝑷t1/2​𝑨B​𝑷t1/2)​𝑷t1/2,\displaystyle M^{\star}=\bm{P}_{t}^{1/2}\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}\!\bigl(\bm{P}_{t}^{1/2}\bm{A}_{B}\bm{P}_{t}^{1/2}\bigr)\bm{P}_{t}^{1/2}, (207)

which keeps the positive eigenspace of 𝐀B\bm{A}_{B} as seen through 𝐏t\bm{P}_{t} and discards the rest.

Corollary F.2 (Diagonal gate).

For diagonal 𝐏t=diag⁡(pk)\bm{P}_{t}=\operatorname{diag}(p_{k}), M⋆M^{\star} in (207) updates parameter kk exactly when

μk2>σk2/(b−1),μk=g¯B,k,σk2=(𝚺B)k​k.\displaystyle\mu_{k}^{2}>\sigma_{k}^{2}/(b-1),\hskip 18.49988pt\mu_{k}=\bar{g}_{B,k},\hskip 9.24994pt\sigma_{k}^{2}=(\bm{\Sigma}_{B})_{kk}. (208)

The reverse direction is immediate: if the gate updates a parameter with μk2<σk2/(b−1)\mu_{k}^{2}<\sigma_{k}^{2}/(b-1), the worst-case loss curvature on that parameter forces a strict first-order increase in population risk.

=ηb−1​∑c≠a𝒓a⊤​Ka​cM​𝒓c+O⁡(η2).\displaystyle=\frac{\eta}{b-1}\sum_{c\neq a}\bm{r}_{a}^{\top}K_{ac}^{M}\bm{r}_{c}+O(\eta^{2}). (214)

Averaging over aa yields (25). Proof of Theorem F.1.

Set the centered residual, the batch step, and the leave-one-out step,

𝒄a\displaystyle\bm{c}_{a} ≜𝒈a−𝒈¯B,\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{g}_{a}-\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}, 𝒘+\displaystyle\bm{w}^{+} ≜𝒘t−η​M​𝒈¯B,\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{w}_{t}-\eta M\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}, 𝒘−a+\displaystyle\bm{w}_{-a}^{+} =𝒘++ηb−1​M​𝒄a,\displaystyle=\bm{w}^{+}+\frac{\eta}{b-1}M\bm{c}_{a}, (215)

𝔼[ℓa(𝒘−a+)∣ℱt]=𝔼Sb−1,Z[ℓ(𝒘t−ηM∇LSb−1(𝒘t),Z)∣ℱt],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\ell_{a}(\bm{w}_{-a}^{+})\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=\mathbb{E}_{S_{b-1},Z}\!\left[\ell\bigl(\bm{w}_{t}-\eta M\nabla L_{S_{b-1}}(\bm{w}_{t}),Z\bigr)\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}\right], (222)

which is the population risk of the one-step learner on b−1b-1 independent samples; averaging over aa closes the proof. ∎

Proof of Section F.2, full-matrix and diagonal forms.

The objective tr⁡(M​𝑨B)\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{A}_{B}) is linear in MM. Writing M=𝑷t1/2​N​𝑷t1/2M=\bm{P}_{t}^{1/2}N\bm{P}_{t}^{1/2} with 0⪯N⪯I0\preceq N\preceq I and C=𝑷t1/2​𝑨B​𝑷t1/2C=\bm{P}_{t}^{1/2}\bm{A}_{B}\bm{P}_{t}^{1/2}, the change of variable yields

tr⁡(M​𝑨B)\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{A}_{B}) =tr⁡(N​C),\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}(NC), (223)
N⋆\displaystyle N^{\star} =𝟏(0,∞)​(C),\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}(C), (224)

where N⋆N^{\star} is the unique maximizer over {0⪯N⪯I}\{0\preceq N\preceq I\}, placing weight 11 on every positive eigenspace of CC and zero on every nonpositive one; conjugating back gives M⋆M^{\star} in (207).

For the diagonal form, take M=diag⁡(qk​pk)M=\operatorname{diag}(q_{k}p_{k}) to obtain

tr⁡(M​𝑨B)\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{A}_{B}) =∑kqk​pk​[μk2−σk2b−1].\displaystyle=\sum_{k}q_{k}p_{k}\!\left[\mu_{k}^{2}-\frac{\sigma_{k}^{2}}{b-1}\right]. (225)

With pk≥0p_{k}\geq 0, every summand is nonnegative iff μk2>σk2/(b−1)\mu_{k}^{2}>\sigma_{k}^{2}/(b-1), which matches the diagonal of M⋆M^{\star} when 𝑷t\bm{P}_{t} is diagonal. Any parameter with μk2<σk2/(b−1)\mu_{k}^{2}<\sigma_{k}^{2}/(b-1) admits an adversarial loss curvature that produces a strict first-order increase in population risk, so the threshold is tight. ∎

For multi-epoch training, replayed batches carry information about 𝒘t\bm{w}_{t} and the independence used above is replaced by a total-variation bound; see Appendix D.

Per-example parameter gradients factor as 𝒈a=𝑱a⊤​𝒓a\bm{g}_{a}=\bm{J}_{a}^{\top}\bm{r}_{a}. Writing 𝒓B=b−1​∑a(𝒆a⊗𝒓a)\bm{r}_{B}=b^{-1}\sum_{a}(\bm{e}_{a}\otimes\bm{r}_{a}) and using 𝒄a𝒘=𝑱S⊤​𝒄a𝒖\bm{c}_{a}^{\bm{w}}=\bm{J}_{S}^{\top}\bm{c}_{a}^{\bm{u}} for the output-space centering,
