(226)

Any output direction in ker⁡𝑲S​S=ker⁡𝑱S⊤\ker\bm{K}_{\!SS}=\ker\bm{J}_{S}^{\top} contributes zero to tr⁡(M​𝑨B)\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{A}_{B}) for every MM, so the inclusion ker⁡𝒲S⊆ker⁡𝖦\ker\mathcal{W}_{S}\subseteq\ker\mathsf{G} from Section 3 makes the reservoir silent for the population-safe rate and for every test prediction through the same factorization.

From a single step to the trajectory.

Each step adds the increment η​𝑲S​SMt​(t)\eta\bm{K}_{\!SS}^{M_{t}}(t) to the cumulative dissipation 𝒲SM\mathcal{W}_{S}^{M}, whose range is the signal channel of the run. The gate (207) chooses MtM_{t} to maximize the 𝖦\mathsf{G}-rate of that increment, and 𝒲SM\mathcal{W}_{S}^{M} at trajectory scale is the integral of these one-step maximizers. Population-risk training stands to the averaged test transfer 𝖦Qa,S−a\mathsf{G}_{Q_{a},S_{-a}} as plain SGD stands to the training transfer 𝑫\bm{D}.

F.3 Cross-Validation Risks as Population Risk

Intuition.

Cross-validation estimates test loss without a held-out set. We show that every kk-fold cross-validation risk equals, in expectation, the population risk of a learner trained on n−kn-k samples, and that the first-order correction around uniform sample weights is the same for every kk. A single centered trace therefore debiases the entire family.

For I⊂[n]I\subset[n] with |I|=k|I|=k, let 𝒘(−I)​(T)\bm{w}^{(-I)}(T) be the terminal model after training on the dataset S−IS_{-I} with the kk points in II removed and the remaining weights renormalized to 1n−k\tfrac{1}{n-k}. Define the kk-fold cross-validation risk

ℒkΨ​(T,Sn)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\Psi}(T,S_{n}) ≜(nk)−1​∑|I|=k1k​∑i∈IΨZi​(F⁡(𝒘(−I)​(T),Zi)−𝒚i).\displaystyle\triangleq\binom{n}{k}^{-1}\sum_{|I|=k}\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in I}\Psi_{Z_{i}}\!\big(F(\bm{w}^{(-I)}(T),Z_{i})-\bm{y}_{i}\big). (227)

Setting k=1k=1 recovers leave-one-out cross-validation; setting k=n/Kk=n/K recovers standard KK-fold cross-validation.

Theorem F.3 (Cross-validation as population risk).

For every k=1,…,n−1k=1,\dots,n-1,

𝔼Sn∼𝒟n​[ℒkΨ​(T,Sn)]=𝔼Sn−k∼𝒟n−k​[ℒ𝒟Ψ​(𝒘T​(Sn−k))].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{S_{n}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}\!\left[\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\Psi}(T,S_{n})\right]=\mathbb{E}_{S_{n-k}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n-k}}\!\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\Psi}(\bm{w}_{T}(S_{n-k}))\right]. (228)

Thus every kk-fold cross-validation risk is an exact sample-only population risk for the (n−k)(n{-}k)-sample learner: any architecture, any loss, any optimizer.

Proof.

By exchangeability, for any fixed II with |I|=k|I|=k,

(S−I,(Zi)i∈I)=d(Sn−k,Z1′,…,Zk′),\displaystyle(S_{-I},(Z_{i})_{i\in I})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(S_{n-k},Z_{1}^{\prime},\dots,Z_{k}^{\prime}), (229)

where Sn−k∼𝒟n−kS_{n-k}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n-k} and Zj′∼𝒟Z_{j}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D} are independent. Averaging over i∈Ii\in I gives the single-subset version; averaging over all (nk)\binom{n}{k} subsets yields the result. ∎

The next proposition shows that the first-order term is the same for every kk, so a single trace debiases the entire family.

Proposition F.4 (Common First Variation).

Let α(−I)∈Δ~n\alpha^{(-I)}\in\widetilde{\Delta}_{n} be the weight vector that places mass nn−k\frac{n}{n-k} on each point j∉Ij\notin I and 00 on each j∈Ij\in I. The average direction from a holdout weight vector back to the uniform weights α¯=𝟏\bar{\alpha}=\bm{1}, over all holdouts containing point ii, is

1(n−1k−1)​∑I∋i|I|=k(α¯−α(−I))=nn−1​𝑪n​𝒆i=𝝂(i),\displaystyle\frac{1}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\ni i\\ |I|=k\end{subarray}}\bigl(\bar{\alpha}-\alpha^{(-I)}\bigr)=\frac{n}{n-1}\bm{C}_{n}\bm{e}_{i}=\bm{\nu}^{(i)}, (230)

the mass-preserving delete-one direction, independent of kk.

Proof.

Fix j≠ij\neq i. Among the (n−1k−1)\binom{n-1}{k-1} holdouts I∋iI\ni i, the (n−2k−2)\binom{n-2}{k-2} that contain jj contribute 11, and the (n−2k−1)\binom{n-2}{k-1} that do not contribute 1−nn−k=−kn−k1-\tfrac{n}{n-k}=-\tfrac{k}{n-k}. The binomial ratios (n−2k−2)/(n−1k−1)=(k−1)/(n−1)\binom{n-2}{k-2}/\binom{n-1}{k-1}=(k-1)/(n-1) and (n−2k−1)/(n−1k−1)=(n−k)/(n−1)\binom{n-2}{k-1}/\binom{n-1}{k-1}=(n-k)/(n-1) then give

1(n−1k−1)​∑I∋i|I|=k(α¯−α(−I))j\displaystyle\frac{1}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\ni i\\ |I|=k\end{subarray}}\bigl(\bar{\alpha}-\alpha^{(-I)}\bigr)_{j} =k−1n−1+n−kn−1​(−kn−k)=−1n−1.\displaystyle=\frac{k-1}{n-1}+\frac{n-k}{n-1}\!\left(-\frac{k}{n-k}\right)=-\frac{1}{n-1}. (231)

The ii-th component equals 11 for every I∋iI\ni i, so the averaged vector has entry 11 at position ii and −1n−1-\tfrac{1}{n-1} elsewhere,

1(n−1k−1)​∑I∋i|I|=k(α¯−α(−I))\displaystyle\frac{1}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\ni i\\ |I|=k\end{subarray}}\bigl(\bar{\alpha}-\alpha^{(-I)}\bigr) =nn−1​(𝒆i−1n​𝟏)=nn−1​𝑪n​𝒆i=𝝂(i),\displaystyle=\frac{n}{n-1}\!\left(\bm{e}_{i}-\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{1}\right)=\frac{n}{n-1}\bm{C}_{n}\bm{e}_{i}=\bm{\nu}^{(i)}, (232)

which is independent of kk. ∎

Every kk-fold cross-validation population risk is expanded around the same uniform weights α¯\bar{\alpha}, and the averaged holdout direction matches for all kk. The first-order Taylor expansion therefore produces a kk-independent leading term and a remainder RkR_{k},

ℒkΨ​(T,S)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\Psi}(T,S) =ℒpopΨ​(T,S)+Rk​(T,S),\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pop}}^{\Psi}(T,S)+R_{k}(T,S), (233)
ℒpopΨ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pop}}^{\Psi} =ℒ^SΨ+1n−1​tr⁡(𝖩Ψ​𝑪n).\displaystyle=\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{S}^{\Psi}+\frac{1}{n-1}\operatorname{tr}(\mathsf{J}_{\Psi}\bm{C}_{n}). (234)

The centered influence trace tr⁡(𝖩Ψ​𝑪n)\operatorname{tr}(\mathsf{J}_{\Psi}\bm{C}_{n}) is the common first variation across leave-one-out, KK-fold, and any exchangeable holdout mask; only the second-order remainder RkR_{k} varies with kk.

F.4 Variance Estimator and Algorithm Details

Intuition.

The kernel-block one-step rule of Section F.2,

ΩB​(M)=𝒈¯B⊤​M​𝒈¯B−1b−1​tr⁡(M​𝚺B),\displaystyle\Omega_{B}(M)=\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}^{\top}M\bar{\bm{g}}_{B}-\tfrac{1}{b-1}\operatorname{tr}(M\bm{\Sigma}_{B}), (235)

yields a practical algorithm once we supply a streaming estimate of the per-parameter variance, a conversion between fresh-batch and finite-dataset regimes, and a soft relaxation of the gate.

Fresh-batch and finite-dataset regimes.

The streaming variance estimator 𝒔^t\hat{\bm{s}}_{t} tracks the per-batch variance (𝚺B)k​k/(b−1)(\bm{\Sigma}_{B})_{kk}/(b-1). The translation to the full-dataset variance is the finite-population correction below.

Theorem F.5 (Minibatch covariance).

Let B⊂[n]B\subset[n] be a size-bb subset sampled uniformly without replacement, 𝐠B=b−1​∑i∈B𝐠i\bm{g}_{B}=b^{-1}\sum_{i\in B}\bm{g}_{i}, and

𝚺g=1n​∑i(𝒈i−𝒈¯)​(𝒈i−𝒈¯)⊤.\displaystyle\bm{\Sigma}_{g}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}(\bm{g}_{i}-\bar{\bm{g}})(\bm{g}_{i}-\bar{\bm{g}})^{\top}. (236)

For any 𝐏⪰0\bm{P}\succeq 0,

CovB⁡(𝒈B)\displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}_{B}(\bm{g}_{B}) =n−bb⁡(n−1)​𝚺g,\displaystyle=\frac{n-b}{b(n-1)}\bm{\Sigma}_{g}, (237)
1n−1​tr⁡(𝑷​𝚺g)\displaystyle\frac{1}{n-1}\operatorname{tr}(\bm{P}\bm{\Sigma}_{g}) =bn−b​tr⁡(𝑷​Cov⁡(𝒈B)).\displaystyle=\frac{b}{n-b}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\bm{P}\operatorname{Cov}(\bm{g}_{B})\bigr). (238)

The streaming LOO coefficient is therefore α=1\alpha=1 in the fresh-batch (online) regime and α=b/(n−b)\alpha=b/(n-b) in the finite-dataset regime.

Proof.

Write 𝒈B−𝒈¯=b−1​∑i∈B𝒄i\bm{g}_{B}-\bar{\bm{g}}=b^{-1}\sum_{i\in B}\bm{c}_{i} with 𝒄i=𝒈i−𝒈¯\bm{c}_{i}=\bm{g}_{i}-\bar{\bm{g}}. Using Pr⁡(i∈B)=b/n\Pr(i\in B)=b/n and Pr⁡(i,j∈B)=b⁡(b−1)/(n⁡(n−1))\Pr(i,j\in B)=b(b-1)/(n(n-1)) for i≠ji\neq j, together with ∑i≠j𝒄i𝒄j⊤=−∑i𝒄i𝒄i⊤\sum_{i\neq j}\bm{c}_{i}\bm{c}_{j}^{\top}=-\sum_{i}\bm{c}_{i}\bm{c}_{i}^{\top},

Cov⁡(𝒈B)=1b2​[bn−b⁡(b−1)n⁡(n−1)]​∑i𝒄i​𝒄i⊤=n−bb⁡(n−1)​𝚺g.\displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}(\bm{g}_{B})=\frac{1}{b^{2}}\!\left[\frac{b}{n}-\frac{b(b-1)}{n(n-1)}\right]\sum_{i}\bm{c}_{i}\bm{c}_{i}^{\top}=\frac{n-b}{b(n-1)}\bm{\Sigma}_{g}. (239)

∎

Streaming variance estimator.

The exponential moving estimate

𝒔t=ρ​𝒔t−1+(1−ρ)​(𝒈t−𝒎t−1)⊙2\displaystyle\bm{s}_{t}=\rho\bm{s}_{t-1}+(1-\rho)(\bm{g}_{t}-\bm{m}_{t-1})^{\odot 2} (240)

tracks the diagonal of Var⁡(𝒈¯B,k)=(𝚺B)k​k/(b−1)\operatorname{Var}(\bar{\bm{g}}_{B,k})=(\bm{\Sigma}_{B})_{kk}/(b-1) when consecutive minibatches are approximately i.i.d. and parameter drift between steps is small. In highly non-stationary settings, 𝒔t\bm{s}_{t} can be replaced by the exact per-batch variance computed from per-example gradients via vmap, at the cost of one extra backward pass per step. This style of estimator follows the stochastic trace tradition of 16.

Hard, soft, and SNR gates.

Three forms of the per-parameter gate, paired with the parameter update on top of an Adam preconditioner, are

qkhard\displaystyle q_{k}^{\mathrm{hard}} =𝟏{m^k2>αs^k},\displaystyle=\bm{1}\{\hat{m}_{k}^{2}>\alpha\hat{s}_{k}\}, (241)
qksoft\displaystyle q_{k}^{\mathrm{soft}} =(m^k2−α​s^k)+(m^k2−α​s^k)++λpop​s^k+ε,\displaystyle=\frac{(\hat{m}_{k}^{2}-\alpha\hat{s}_{k})_{+}}{(\hat{m}_{k}^{2}-\alpha\hat{s}_{k})_{+}+\lambda_{\mathrm{pop}}\hat{s}_{k}+\varepsilon}, (242)
qkSNR\displaystyle q_{k}^{\mathrm{SNR}} =m^k2m^k2+λ​s^k+ε,\displaystyle=\frac{\hat{m}_{k}^{2}}{\hat{m}_{k}^{2}+\lambda\hat{s}_{k}+\varepsilon}, (243)
𝒘t+1\displaystyle\bm{w}_{t+1} =𝒘t−ηt​𝒒t⊙𝒎^t𝒗^t+ϵ−ηt​λwd​𝒘t.\displaystyle=\bm{w}_{t}-\eta_{t}\bm{q}_{t}\odot\frac{\hat{\bm{m}}_{t}}{\sqrt{\hat{\bm{v}}_{t}}+\epsilon}-\eta_{t}\lambda_{\mathrm{wd}}\bm{w}_{t}. (244)

The hard gate is the unique binary rule keeping the first-order improvement nonnegative on every parameter (Section F.2). The soft gate preserves that first-order safety while smoothing the cutoff: its numerator vanishes when m^k2≤α​s^k\hat{m}_{k}^{2}\leq\alpha\hat{s}_{k}, and its denominator is bounded below by λpop​s^k+ε\lambda_{\mathrm{pop}}\hat{s}_{k}+\varepsilon. The SNR shrinker used in prior work assigns positive weight even when m^k2<α​s^k\hat{m}_{k}^{2}<\alpha\hat{s}_{k}.

The hyperparameter λpop\lambda_{\mathrm{pop}} plays the role of a dimensionless regularization scale. At the finite-dataset boundary,

λpop​𝒔^t≈1n−1​𝚺^g,t=bn−b​Cov⁡(𝒈B),\displaystyle\lambda_{\mathrm{pop}}\hat{\bm{s}}_{t}\approx\tfrac{1}{n-1}\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{g,t}=\tfrac{b}{n-b}\operatorname{Cov}(\bm{g}_{B}), (245)

which is typically unnecessary at scale.

F.5 Leave-One-Out Risk

Intuition.

Leave-one-out treats each training point as a one-element held-out set: point ii is evaluated against the model trained without it. The same transfer operators 𝖦Qi\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i}} that govern training also describe the delete-one prediction displacement, so the expected generalization gap reduces to a one-step loss difference between the original dataset and the one-point-replaced dataset.

Define the training residual, the delete-one displacement, and the leave-one-out exclusion risk,

𝒆i​(T)\displaystyle\bm{e}_{i}(T) ≜𝑼QiS​(T)−𝒚i,\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{U}_{Q_{i}}^{S}(T)-\bm{y}_{i}, (246)
𝚫iex​(T)\displaystyle\bm{\Delta}_{i}^{\mathrm{ex}}(T) ≜𝑼QiS−i​(T)−𝑼QiS​(T)=𝖦Qi,S​(T)​𝒈S​(0)−𝖦Qi,S−i​(T)​𝒈S−i​(0),\displaystyle\triangleq\bm{U}_{Q_{i}}^{S_{-i}}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q_{i}}^{S}(T)=\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i},S}(T)\bm{g}_{S}(0)-\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i},S_{-i}}(T)\bm{g}_{S_{-i}}(0), (247)
ℒexΨ​(T,S)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ex}}^{\Psi}(T,S) =1n​∑i=1nΨZi​(𝒆i​(T)+𝚫iex​(T)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Psi_{Z_{i}}\!\big(\bm{e}_{i}(T)+\bm{\Delta}_{i}^{\mathrm{ex}}(T)\big), (248)

where the second line specializes the dataset-level transfer to Q=QiQ=Q_{i} on the two datasets SS and S−iS_{-i}.

Theorem F.6 (Self-influence).

Let S(i)S^{(i)} denote the dataset with ZiZ_{i} replaced by an independent draw Zi′Z_{i}^{\prime}, and define the generalization gap

γΨ​(T,S)\displaystyle\gamma_{\Psi}(T,S) ≜ℒ𝒟Ψ​(𝒘T​(S))−ℒ^SΨ​(𝒘T​(S)).\displaystyle\triangleq\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\Psi}(\bm{w}_{T}(S))-\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{S}^{\Psi}(\bm{w}_{T}(S)). (249)

Then

𝔼​[γΨ​(T,S)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\gamma_{\Psi}(T,S)] =1n​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[ΨZi​(𝑼QiS(i)​(T)−𝒚i)−ΨZi​(𝑼QiS​(T)−𝒚i)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Psi_{Z_{i}}\!\big(\bm{U}_{Q_{i}}^{S^{(i)}}(T)-\bm{y}_{i}\big)-\Psi_{Z_{i}}\!\big(\bm{U}_{Q_{i}}^{S}(T)-\bm{y}_{i}\big)\right], (250)
𝚫i​(T)\displaystyle\bm{\Delta}_{i}(T) =𝖦Qi,S​(T)​𝒈S​(0)−𝖦Qi,S(i)​(T)​𝒈S(i)​(0).\displaystyle=\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i},S}(T)\bm{g}_{S}(0)-\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i},S^{(i)}}(T)\bm{g}_{S^{(i)}}(0). (251)

The full version is in subsubsection G.3.1.

F.6 Algorithm Pseudocode

Intuition.

The algorithm is Adam with one extra parameter-sized state vector tracking a running variance 𝒔\bm{s} of per-example gradients. The only deviation from a standard moment optimizer is a per-parameter gate that suppresses the update on parameter kk whenever the squared mean gradient m^k2\hat{m}_{k}^{2} is below the variance threshold α​s^k\alpha\hat{s}_{k}. This is the population-risk safe rule derived in the local one-step theory: parameters whose batch signal is dominated by leave-one-out noise contribute nothing positive to first-order population improvement, so they sit out the step.

Appendix G Complexity Measure and Self-Influence

G.1 Optimal Signal Directions for a Complexity Measure RR

Intuition.

Test-invisibility identifies the directions in which training motion has no effect on test predictions. The signal channel contains every direction in which training reduced loss, including those that reflect transferable structure together with those that reflect memorization. A complexity measure R≻0R\succ 0 on output space resolves this within the signal channel: the top eigenspace of R−1/2𝒲SR−1/2R^{-1/2}\mathcal{W}_{S}R^{-1/2} is the worst-case-optimal way to read out signal from a training run, and the split between signal and memorization is determined by the choice of RR together with the cumulative dissipation Gramian 𝒲S\mathcal{W}_{S}, with the test set entering only through a scalar visibility constant. The graph-Laplacian metric RS,γ=I+γ​L^SR_{\!S,\gamma}=I+\gamma\widehat{L}_{S} is one valid choice; the self-influence metric RS,γ,βa​(s,T)R_{S,\gamma,\beta}^{a}(s,T) defined below is another, and the theorem holds for any R≻0R\succ 0.

Theorem G.1 (Optimal signal directions: hard projectors).

Fix 0≤s≤T0\leq s\leq T, a test set QQ, and a complexity measure R≻0R\succ 0 on ℝn​p\mathbb{R}^{np}. Write 𝐖≜𝒲S​(s,T)\bm{W}\triangleq\mathcal{W}_{S}(s,T) and CR(s,T)≜R−1/2𝐖R−1/2⪰0C_{R}(s,T)\triangleq R^{-1/2}\bm{W}R^{-1/2}\succeq 0, with spectral decomposition CR​(s,T)=∑j=1ρλjR​ϕjR​(ϕjR)⊤C_{R}(s,T)=\sum_{j=1}^{\rho}\lambda_{j}^{R}\phi_{j}^{R}(\phi_{j}^{R})^{\top}, λ1R≥⋯≥λρR>0\lambda_{1}^{R}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{\rho}^{R}>0. Let 𝐐rR≜∑j≤rϕjR​(ϕjR)⊤\bm{Q}_{r}^{R}\triangleq\sum_{j\leq r}\phi_{j}^{R}(\phi_{j}^{R})^{\top} be the top-rr spectral projector, and recall the visibility Gramian ΓQ​(s,T)\Gamma_{Q}(s,T) from Equation 11.

For hard rank-rr subspaces, define the projector class

𝒫r≜{𝑸∈ℝn​p×n​p:𝑸2=𝑸,𝑸⊤=𝑸,rank(𝑸)=r}\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{r}\triangleq\{\bm{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{np\times np}:\ \bm{Q}^{2}=\bm{Q},\ \bm{Q}^{\top}=\bm{Q},\ \operatorname{rank}(\bm{Q})=r\} (252)

and, for 𝐐∈𝒫r\bm{Q}\in\mathcal{P}_{r}, the worst-case lost test motion

ℰr​(𝑸)≜sup0⪯𝖠⪯‖ΓQ​(s,T)‖op​CR​(s,T)‖(I−𝑸)​𝖠​(I−𝑸)‖op.\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{r}(\bm{Q})\triangleq\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\preceq\mathsf{A}\preceq\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}C_{R}(s,T)\end{subarray}}\|(I-\bm{Q})\mathsf{A}(I-\bm{Q})\|_{\operatorname{op}}. (253)

Then

inf𝑸∈𝒫rℰr​(𝑸)=‖ΓQ​(s,T)‖op​λr+1R,\displaystyle\inf_{\bm{Q}\in\mathcal{P}_{r}}\mathcal{E}_{r}(\bm{Q})=\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}\lambda_{r+1}^{R}, (254)

and the infimum is attained by the hard spectral projector 𝐐=𝐐rR\bm{Q}=\bm{Q}_{r}^{R}. If λrR>λr+1R\lambda_{r}^{R}>\lambda_{r+1}^{R}, the minimizer is unique among orthogonal projectors.

Remark (Contractions admit multiple optima). For the relaxed class ℳr={𝐌:0⪯𝐌⪯I,rank(𝐌)≤r}\mathcal{M}_{r}=\{\bm{M}:0\preceq\bm{M}\preceq I,\ \operatorname{rank}(\bm{M})\leq r\}, several minimizers can attain the optimal value. For example, with CR=diag⁡(100,1)C_{R}=\operatorname{diag}(100,1) and r=1r=1, both diag⁡(1,0)\operatorname{diag}(1,0) and diag⁡(0.9,0)\operatorname{diag}(0.9,0) achieve the same tail bound λ2=1\lambda_{2}=1. The corresponding statement for contractions is the spectral relaxation in subsubsection G.2.1.

Here signal denotes directions where training dissipated the most loss per unit of complexity. The realized test-visible operator satisfies the spectral bound

R−1/2𝑮⊤𝑮R−1/2⪯∥ΓQ(s,T)∥opCR(s,T),\displaystyle R^{-1/2}\bm{G}^{\top}\bm{G}R^{-1/2}\preceq\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}C_{R}(s,T), (255)

so that choosing R=RS,γR=R_{\!S,\gamma} recovers the graph-Laplacian case and the later choice R=RS,γ,βa​(s,T)R=R_{S,\gamma,\beta}^{a}(s,T) incorporates self-influence within the same theorem. The signal basis is fixed before observing the test predictor, and the realized test operator refines that basis.

The hard projector restricts the controller class to idempotent operators. Allowing spectral contractions with a trace budget yields a spectral filter of CR​(s,T)C_{R}(s,T) that attenuates small eigenvalues more strongly than large ones (subsubsection G.2.1 in subsubsection G.2.1).

Three successive filters identify the directions that drive test error. The reservoir of low-dissipation directions is test-invisible. Among the remaining test-visible directions, leakage is captured by ‖R⟂‖op\|R_{\perp}\|_{\operatorname{op}}, the deviation of test motion from what training motion predicts. Among directions that are mobile and test-visible, those of high complexity rank low in CR​(s,T)C_{R}(s,T) and are deprioritized by the signal theorem. Transferable signal remains after all three. The signal-channel partition records what training moved, and the complexity filter separates structure from nuisance within the signal channel.

G.2 Proofs for the Optimal Signal Directions Theorem

Intuition.

Among rank-rr summaries of a training run, the one that retains the most test-relevant motion per unit of training cost is identified by an Eckart–Young-style argument: the optimal projector is given by the leading eigenvectors of CR​(s,T)C_{R}(s,T), with the metric RR replacing the Euclidean inner product used in the classical statement. This appendix proves the optimal-signal-direction theorem of Appendix G.

G.2.1 Deferred Parts of the Signal Principle

Intuition.

The optimal-signal-direction theorem combines two ingredients: a ceiling on how strongly the test predictor reacts along any direction (admissibility), and a tail bound that controls the test motion lost when only the top-rr directions are retained. We state both pieces here and then combine them in the proof. With the notation of Theorem G.1, let 𝑮≜𝖦Q​(T,s)\bm{G}\triangleq\mathsf{G}_{Q}(T,s) and define the RR-orthogonal projector 𝚷rR≜R−1/2𝑸rRR1/2\bm{\Pi}_{r}^{R}\triangleq R^{-1/2}\bm{Q}_{r}^{R}R^{1/2}.

Admissible class.

The realized test predictor satisfies

R−1/2𝑮⊤𝑮R−1/2⪯∥ΓQ(s,T)∥opCR(s,T).\displaystyle R^{-1/2}\bm{G}^{\top}\bm{G}R^{-1/2}\preceq\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}C_{R}(s,T). (256)
Tail bound.

For every 𝒉∈ℝn​p\bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{np} and every r≥0r\geq 0,

‖𝑮⁡(I−𝚷rR)​𝒉‖22≤‖ΓQ​(s,T)‖op​λr+1R​𝒉⊤​R​(I−𝚷rR)​𝒉,\displaystyle\|\bm{G}(I-\bm{\Pi}_{r}^{R})\bm{h}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|\Gamma_{Q}(s,T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}\lambda_{r+1}^{R}\bm{h}^{\top}R(I-\bm{\Pi}_{r}^{R})\bm{h}, (257)

with the convention λr+1R=0\lambda_{r+1}^{R}=0 if r≥ρr\geq\rho. Projecting into the tail eigenspace of CR​(s,T)C_{R}(s,T) and applying the admissibility bound yields (257) as a corollary of the admissible class.

Remark G.2 (Continuous relaxation).

Relaxing from rank-rr projectors to trace-bounded contractions {V:0⪯V⪯I,tr(V)≤τ}\{V:0\preceq V\preceq I,\ \operatorname{tr}(V)\leq\tau\} yields a spectral filter of CR​(s,T)C_{R}(s,T) that attenuates each eigendirection in proportion to its eigenvalue, diagonal in the eigenbasis of CRC_{R}, and fully suppressing small eigenvalues while preserving large ones. The hard rank-rr result above is the idempotent special case.

G.3 Self-Influence and Adjoint Reweighting

Intuition.

The population-risk gap can be read off from a single training run by examining how each training point would have responded to its own removal: each example carries a self-influence whose average over the dataset equals the generalization gap. This appendix proves Theorem G.3 and the reweighting sensitivity formula, extending classical influence functions [8, 18] to feature-learning trajectories and connecting with the leave-one-out stability tradition of 7, 13. The full statement contains three pieces: the population-risk gap equals an average over training points of a one-shot loss difference; when the loss is differentiable, that loss difference becomes an integral over a prediction-displacement vector; and when the training objective is separable per example, the displacement vector decomposes into a content-change part and an observation-channel-change part. We state these as a base theorem and two corollaries so that each piece can be cited on its own.

G.3.1 Full Statement of the Self-Influence Theorem

Theorem G.3 (Self-Influence, base form).

Under the notation of Section 6,

𝔼⁡[γΨ​(T,S)]=1n​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[ΨZi​(𝑼QiS(i)​(T)−𝒚i)−ΨZi​(𝑼QiS​(T)−𝒚i)].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\gamma_{\Psi}(T,S)]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Psi_{Z_{i}}\!\big(\bm{U}_{Q_{i}}^{S^{(i)}}(T)-\bm{y}_{i}\big)-\Psi_{Z_{i}}\!\big(\bm{U}_{Q_{i}}^{S}(T)-\bm{y}_{i}\big)\right]. (280)
Corollary G.4 (Integral representation of the gap).

If each Ψz\Psi_{z} is differentiable, define the prediction displacement

𝚫i​(T)\displaystyle\bm{\Delta}_{i}(T) =𝖦Qi,S​(T)​𝒈S​(0)−𝖦Qi,S(i)​(T)​𝒈S(i)​(0).\displaystyle=\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i},S}(T)\bm{g}_{S}(0)-\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i},S^{(i)}}(T)\bm{g}_{S^{(i)}}(0). (281)

Then the gap admits the integral representation

𝔼​[γΨ​(T,S)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\gamma_{\Psi}(T,S)] =1n​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[∫01⟨∇ΨZi​(𝒆i​(T)+θ​𝚫i​(T)),𝚫i​(T)⟩​𝑑θ].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{1}\left\langle\nabla\Psi_{Z_{i}}\!\big(\bm{e}_{i}(T)+\theta\bm{\Delta}_{i}(T)\big),\bm{\Delta}_{i}(T)\right\rangle d\theta\right]. (282)
Corollary G.5 (Displacement under a separable objective).

Under the separable training objective of subsubsection G.3.3,

𝚫i​(T)\displaystyle\bm{\Delta}_{i}(T) =𝖦Qi,S(i)​(T)​𝜹i+(𝖦Qi,S​(T)−𝖦Qi,S(i)​(T))​𝒈S(i)​(0),\displaystyle=\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i},S}^{(i)}(T)\bm{\delta}_{i}+\bigl(\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i},S}(T)-\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i},S^{(i)}}(T)\bigr)\bm{g}_{S^{(i)}}(0), (283)

where 𝛅i\bm{\delta}_{i} is the initial gradient difference of the replaced example.

Remark G.6 (Content vs. channel split).

Each dataset induces its own train-test decomposition, so the displacement splits into a content-change term and a channel-change term. Writing

𝒛S\displaystyle\bm{z}_{S} =𝑾S1/2​𝒈S​(0),\displaystyle=\bm{W}_{S}^{1/2}\bm{g}_{S}(0), 𝑪i,S\displaystyle\bm{C}_{i,S} =𝖦Qi,S(T)𝑾S†/2,\displaystyle=\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i},S}(T)\bm{W}_{S}^{\dagger/2}, (284)
with the same definitions for S(i)S^{(i)},
𝚫i​(T)\displaystyle\bm{\Delta}_{i}(T) =𝑪i,S​(𝒛S−𝒛S(i))+(𝑪i,S−𝑪i,S(i))​𝒛S(i).\displaystyle=\bm{C}_{i,S}(\bm{z}_{S}-\bm{z}_{S^{(i)}})+(\bm{C}_{i,S}-\bm{C}_{i,S^{(i)}})\bm{z}_{S^{(i)}}. (285)

The first term measures how much the learned content changed; the second measures how much the observation channel for point ii changed. The generalization gap is the average loss response to both.

Proof of Theorem F.6.

By the law of the unconscious statistician and exchangeability (S(i),Zi)=d(S,Zi′)(S^{(i)},Z_{i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(S,Z_{i}^{\prime}),

𝔼⁡[ℒ𝒟Ψ​(𝒘T​(S))]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\Psi}(\bm{w}_{T}(S))\big] =1n​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[ΨZi​(F⁡(𝒘T​(S(i)),Zi)−𝒚i)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Psi_{Z_{i}}\!\big(F(\bm{w}_{T}(S^{(i)}),Z_{i})-\bm{y}_{i}\big)\right], (286)
𝔼⁡[ℒ^SΨ​(𝒘T​(S))]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{S}^{\Psi}(\bm{w}_{T}(S))\right] =1n​∑i=1n𝔼⁡[ΨZi​(F⁡(𝒘T​(S),Zi)−𝒚i)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Psi_{Z_{i}}\!\big(F(\bm{w}_{T}(S),Z_{i})-\bm{y}_{i}\big)\right], (287)

and subtracting gives (250). For (282), apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to θ↦ΨZi​(𝒆i​(T)+θ​𝚫i​(T))\theta\mapsto\Psi_{Z_{i}}\!\big(\bm{e}_{i}(T)+\theta\bm{\Delta}_{i}(T)\big). Finally, (251) follows from 𝑼QS​(T)=𝑼Q​(𝒘0,Q)−𝖦Q,S​(T)​𝒈S​(0)\bm{U}_{Q}^{S}(T)=\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}_{0};Q)-\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}(T)\bm{g}_{S}(0) applied to Q=QiQ=Q_{i} and the two datasets SS and S(i)S^{(i)}; (283) is subsubsection G.3.3 with Q=QiQ=Q_{i}. ∎

G.3.2 Self-Influence from the Training Displacement

Intuition.

Self-influence (Theorem F.6) tracks how each training point’s loss responds to its own removal, while the signal spectrum (Appendix G) tracks how training motion translates to test-visible displacement per unit data roughness. Both quantities arise from the same train-displacement operator, so a single forward pass and a single backward pass produce both at once.

Proposition G.7 (Self-influence decomposition).

Fix an observed window 0≤s≤T0\leq s\leq T and write

𝑫≜𝖣S​(T,s)=∫sT𝑲S​S​(τ)​𝒫g​(τ,s)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle\bm{D}\triangleq\mathsf{D}_{S}(T,s)=\int_{s}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!SS}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g}(\tau,s)d\tau. (288)

For covectors 𝐚=(𝐚1,…,𝐚n)\bm{a}=(\bm{a}_{1},\dots,\bm{a}_{n}) with 𝐚i∈ℝp\bm{a}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, define the block contraction

𝑨𝒂:ℝn​p→ℝn,\displaystyle\bm{A}_{\bm{a}}:\mathbb{R}^{np}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, (289)
𝑨𝒂​(𝒙1,…,𝒙n)≜(⟨𝒂1,𝒙1⟩,…,⟨𝒂n,𝒙n⟩).\displaystyle\bm{A}_{\bm{a}}(\bm{x}_{1};\dots;\bm{x}_{n})\triangleq(\langle\bm{a}_{1},\bm{x}_{1}\rangle,\dots,\langle\bm{a}_{n},\bm{x}_{n}\rangle). (290)

Let Qi={zi}Q_{i}=\{z_{i}\} denote the singleton containing the ii-th training point. Then for every 𝐡∈ℝn​p\bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{np},

(𝑨𝒂𝑫𝒉)i=⟨𝒂i,𝖦Qi(T,s)𝒉⟩,i=1,…,n.\displaystyle(\bm{A}_{\bm{a}}\bm{D}\bm{h})_{i}=\langle\bm{a}_{i},\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i}}(T,s)\bm{h}\rangle,\hskip 18.49988pti=1,\dots,n. (291)

If 𝐚i=∇Ψzi​(𝐞i​(s))\bm{a}_{i}=\nabla\Psi_{z_{i}}(\bm{e}_{i}(s)) with 𝐞i​(s)=𝐔Qi​(s)−𝐲i\bm{e}_{i}(s)=\bm{U}_{Q_{i}}(s)-\bm{y}_{i}, then 𝐃⊤​𝐀𝐚⊤​𝐀𝐚​𝐃\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{A}_{\bm{a}}^{\top}\bm{A}_{\bm{a}}\bm{D} is the exact quadratic expression for self-influence through 𝐃\bm{D} on the observed window.

subsubsection G.3.2shows that the quadratic 𝑫⊤​𝑨𝒂⊤​𝑨𝒂​𝑫\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{A}_{\bm{a}}^{\top}\bm{A}_{\bm{a}}\bm{D} shares its forward and backward solves with the transfer operators of Section E.8, so the same ODE solves suffice. The covectors 𝒂i=∇Ψzi​(𝒆i​(s))\bm{a}_{i}=\nabla\Psi_{z_{i}}(\bm{e}_{i}(s)) are available at the window start ss, so the construction uses only quantities observed before the terminal state.

Definition G.8 (Self-influence transfer).

For β≥0\beta\geq 0, define the centered self-influence metric and the associated self-influence-weighted signal operator,

RS,γ,βa​(s,T)\displaystyle R_{S,\gamma,\beta}^{a}(s,T) ≜RS,γ+β​𝑫⊤​𝑨𝒂⊤​𝑪n​𝑨𝒂​𝑫,\displaystyle\triangleq R_{\!S,\gamma}+\beta\bm{D}^{\top}\bm{A}_{\bm{a}}^{\top}\bm{C}_{n}\bm{A}_{\bm{a}}\bm{D}, (292)
TQ,γ,βa​(s,T)\displaystyle T_{Q,\gamma,\beta}^{a}(s,T) ≜RS,γ,βa(s,T)−1/2𝖦Q(T,s)⊤𝖦Q(T,s)RS,γ,βa(s,T)−1/2,\displaystyle\triangleq R_{S,\gamma,\beta}^{a}(s,T)^{-1/2}\mathsf{G}_{Q}(T,s)^{\top}\mathsf{G}_{Q}(T,s)R_{S,\gamma,\beta}^{a}(s,T)^{-1/2}, (293)

where 𝑪n=𝑰−1n​𝟏𝟏⊤\bm{C}_{n}=\bm{I}-\frac{1}{n}\bm{1}\bm{1}^{\top} is the centering projector. The centering penalizes per-example deviations from the batch mean (the centered directions 𝑪n​𝒆i\bm{C}_{n}\bm{e}_{i}) and preserves the common mode of uniform shifts across all examples. Since RS,γ,βa≻0R_{S,\gamma,\beta}^{a}\succ 0, Theorem G.1 applies with R=RS,γ,βaR=R_{S,\gamma,\beta}^{a}: the top-rr eigenspaces of CRS,γ,βa​(s,T)C_{R_{S,\gamma,\beta}^{a}}(s,T) are the unique rank-rr subspaces minimizing worst-case lost test motion, and the Eckart–Young–Mirsky and Courant–Fischer bounds carry over with RS,γR_{\!S,\gamma} replaced by RS,γ,βaR_{S,\gamma,\beta}^{a}. The case β=0\beta=0 recovers the graph-Laplacian setup of Appendix G.

Together these objects describe the training process at four levels: the dynamics determine which directions training moves; the transfer operator determines what reaches test outputs; the signal spectrum determines which fast directions carry transferable structure; and self-influence supplies the observable scores that make all three measurable. The same centering projector 𝑪n\bm{C}_{n} appears in both the self-influence metric and the population-risk objective

ℒpopΨ=ℒ^SΨ+1n−1​tr⁡(𝖩Ψ​𝑪n)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pop}}^{\Psi}=\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{S}^{\Psi}+\frac{1}{n-1}\operatorname{tr}(\mathsf{J}_{\Psi}\bm{C}_{n}) (294)

of Section 6, so the signal spectrum and the population-risk correction share a common data-weight centering.

Proof of subsubsection G.3.2.

Since 𝑫=𝖦S​(T,s)\bm{D}=\mathsf{G}_{S}(T,s) is the transfer operator with test set equal to the full training set, the ii-th pp-block of 𝑫​𝒉\bm{D}\bm{h} is 𝖦Qi​(T,s)​𝒉\mathsf{G}_{Q_{i}}(T,s)\bm{h}. Contracting that block against 𝒂i\bm{a}_{i} gives the first display. The quadratic expression follows from the chain rule. ∎

G.3.3 Stability Under Example Replacement

Intuition.

Resampling one training point and rerunning training from the same initialization shifts the test prediction by the sum of two transparent quantities: the initial-gradient effect of the replaced example, and a drift in the transfer operator between the two neighboring datasets. This decomposition matches the algorithmic stability framework of 7, 13 and turns those uniform stability bounds into computable, run-specific quantities.

For a dataset SS and test set QQ, define the transfer operator

𝖦Q,S​(T)≜∫0T𝑲Q​SS​(τ)​𝒫g,S​(τ,0)​𝑑τ,\displaystyle\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}(T)\triangleq\int_{0}^{T}\bm{K}_{\!QS}^{S}(\tau)\mathcal{P}_{g,S}(\tau,0)d\tau, (295)

so that Section 3 gives

𝑼QS​(T)=𝑼Q​(𝒘0,Q)−𝖦Q,S​(T)​𝒈S​(0).\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}^{S}(T)=\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}_{0};Q)-\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}(T)\bm{g}_{S}(0). (296)

Write 𝖦Q,S(i)​(T):ℝp→ℝ|Q|​p\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}^{(i)}(T):\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R}^{|Q|p} for the ii-th pp-column block of 𝖦Q,S​(T)\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}(T).

Lemma G.9 (Stability Under Example Replacement).

Fix T≥0T\geq 0 and a test set QQ. Let S′=S(i←z′)S^{\prime}=S^{(i\leftarrow z^{\prime})} and train both datasets from the same initialization 𝐰0\bm{w}_{0}.

For a general training objective ΦS\Phi_{S},

𝑼QS​(T)−𝑼QS′​(T)=−𝖦Q,S​(T)​(𝒈S​(0)−𝒈S′​(0))−(𝖦Q,S​(T)−𝖦Q,S′​(T))​𝒈S′​(0).\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}^{S}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}^{S^{\prime}}(T)=-\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}(T)\bigl(\bm{g}_{S}(0)-\bm{g}_{S^{\prime}}(0)\bigr)-\bigl(\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}(T)-\mathsf{G}_{Q,S^{\prime}}(T)\bigr)\bm{g}_{S^{\prime}}(0). (297)

If, in addition, the training objective is the empirical average of a per-example loss with ϕ⁡(⋅,z)\phi(\cdot;z) convex and C2C^{2} for every zz, then

ΦS​(𝒖)\displaystyle\Phi_{S}(\bm{u}) =1n​∑j=1nϕ⁡(uj,zj),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\phi(u_{j};z_{j}), (298)
𝒈S​(0)−𝒈S′​(0)\displaystyle\bm{g}_{S}(0)-\bm{g}_{S^{\prime}}(0) =𝒆i⊗𝜹i,\displaystyle=\bm{e}_{i}\otimes\bm{\delta}_{i}, (299)
𝜹i\displaystyle\bm{\delta}_{i} ≜1n​(∇𝒖ϕ​(F⁡(𝒘0,zi),zi)−∇𝒖ϕ​(F⁡(𝒘0,z′),z′)),\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{1}{n}\Bigl(\nabla_{\bm{u}}\phi(F(\bm{w}_{0},z_{i});z_{i})-\nabla_{\bm{u}}\phi(F(\bm{w}_{0},z^{\prime});z^{\prime})\Bigr), (300)
and so
𝑼QS​(T)−𝑼QS′​(T)\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}^{S}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}^{S^{\prime}}(T) =−𝖦Q,S(i)​(T)​𝜹i−(𝖦Q,S​(T)−𝖦Q,S′​(T))​𝒈S′​(0),\displaystyle=-\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}^{(i)}(T)\bm{\delta}_{i}-\bigl(\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}(T)-\mathsf{G}_{Q,S^{\prime}}(T)\bigr)\bm{g}_{S^{\prime}}(0), (301)
‖𝑼QS​(T)−𝑼QS′​(T)‖2\displaystyle\|\bm{U}_{Q}^{S}(T)-\bm{U}_{Q}^{S^{\prime}}(T)\|_{2} ≤‖𝖦Q,S(i)​(T)‖op​‖𝜹i‖2+‖𝖦Q,S​(T)−𝖦Q,S′​(T)‖op​‖𝒈S′​(0)‖2.\displaystyle\leq\|\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}^{(i)}(T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}\|\bm{\delta}_{i}\|_{2}+\|\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}(T)-\mathsf{G}_{Q,S^{\prime}}(T)\|_{\operatorname{op}}\|\bm{g}_{S^{\prime}}(0)\|_{2}. (302)
Proof.

By Section 3,

𝑼QS​(T)\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}^{S}(T) =𝑼Q​(𝒘0,Q)−𝖦Q,S​(T)​𝒈S​(0),\displaystyle=\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}_{0};Q)-\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}(T)\bm{g}_{S}(0), (303)
𝑼QS′​(T)\displaystyle\bm{U}_{Q}^{S^{\prime}}(T) =𝑼Q​(𝒘0,Q)−𝖦Q,S′​(T)​𝒈S′​(0),\displaystyle=\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}_{0};Q)-\mathsf{G}_{Q,S^{\prime}}(T)\bm{g}_{S^{\prime}}(0), (304)
and subtracting yields (297). Under the separable empirical loss only the replaced block changes at time 00, so
𝒈S​(0)−𝒈S′​(0)\displaystyle\bm{g}_{S}(0)-\bm{g}_{S^{\prime}}(0) =𝒆i⊗𝜹i.\displaystyle=\bm{e}_{i}\otimes\bm{\delta}_{i}. (305)

Substituting into (297) gives (301), and (302) follows from the triangle inequality. ∎

The two terms in (302) read off directly. The first measures the effect of the replaced example’s initial gradient, and the second measures the transfer-operator drift between the two neighboring datasets. For any test loss with Lipschitz constant LQL_{Q} in prediction space, multiplying the right-hand side of (302) by LQL_{Q} yields a replace-one stability bound [7]. The quantity ‖𝖦Q,S(i)​(T)‖op\|\mathsf{G}_{Q,S}^{(i)}(T)\|_{\operatorname{op}} is an example-specific, test-specific influence score controlled by test-invisibility (Section 5): directions in ker⁡𝑲Q​S\ker\bm{K}_{\!QS} leave 𝖦Q,S\mathsf{G}_{Q,S} unchanged, so noise-trapped gradient stays clear of test predictions.

G.3.4 Reweighting Sensitivity and Generalization Estimation

Intuition.

The integral expression for the gap involves the transfer-operator difference 𝚫i​(T)\bm{\Delta}_{i}(T), which would require retraining for every ii. The first variation of the test functional under an infinitesimal reweighting of a training point, captured by a single backward sensitivity solve along the realized run, gives the same information without retraining, extending classical influence functions [8, 18] to the full feature-learning trajectory. From that one solve the entire self-influence matrix is read off, and its centered trace is an unbiased estimate of the population-risk gap.

Theorem G.10 (One-Run Reweighting Sensitivity Formula).

Assume the training objective is separable:

LS​(𝒘)=1n​∑j=1nℓj​(𝒘),\displaystyle L_{S}(\bm{w})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\ell_{j}(\bm{w}), (306)
ℓj​(𝒘)≜ϕ⁡(F⁡(𝒘,zj),zj),\displaystyle\ell_{j}(\bm{w})\triangleq\phi(F(\bm{w},z_{j});z_{j}), (307)

with each ℓj∈C2\ell_{j}\in C^{2}. Fix a test set QQ and a C1C^{1} test functional ψ:ℝ|Q|​p→ℝ\psi:\mathbb{R}^{|Q|p}\to\mathbb{R}. For a reweighting direction 𝛎∈ℝn\bm{\nu}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, let 𝐰λ\bm{w}^{\lambda} solve gradient flow for

LSλ​(𝒘)≜1n​∑j=1n(1−λ​νj)​ℓj​(𝒘),\displaystyle L_{S}^{\lambda}(\bm{w})\triangleq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1-\lambda\nu_{j})\ell_{j}(\bm{w}), (308)
𝒘λ​(0)=𝒘0.\displaystyle\bm{w}^{\lambda}(0)=\bm{w}_{0}. (309)

Assume λ↦𝐰λ​(T)\lambda\mapsto\bm{w}^{\lambda}(T) is differentiable at λ=0\lambda=0, and write 𝐰​(t)≜𝐰0​(t)\bm{w}(t)\triangleq\bm{w}^{0}(t). Then

dd​λ|λ=0​ψ​(𝑼Q​(𝒘λ​(T)))=1n​∫0T⟨𝒑ψ,Q​(τ),∑j=1nνj​∇𝒘ℓj​(𝒘⁡(τ))⟩​𝑑τ,\displaystyle\left.\frac{d}{d\lambda}\right|_{\lambda=0}\psi(\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}^{\lambda}(T)))=\frac{1}{n}\int_{0}^{T}\left\langle\bm{p}_{\psi,Q}(\tau),\sum_{j=1}^{n}\nu_{j}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell_{j}(\bm{w}(\tau))\right\rangle d\tau, (310)

where 𝐩ψ,Q\bm{p}_{\psi,Q} is the backward sensitivity along the realized run:

∂τ𝒑ψ,Q​(τ)=∇𝒘2LS​(𝒘⁡(τ))​𝒑ψ,Q​(τ),\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}\bm{p}_{\psi,Q}(\tau)=\nabla_{\bm{w}}^{2}L_{S}(\bm{w}(\tau))\bm{p}_{\psi,Q}(\tau), (311)
𝒑ψ,Q(T)=𝑱Q(𝒘(T))⊤∇ψ(𝑼Q(𝒘(T))).\displaystyle\bm{p}_{\psi,Q}(T)=\bm{J}_{Q}(\bm{w}(T))^{\top}\nabla\psi(\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}(T))). (312)

Equivalently, if 𝐯𝛎\bm{v}_{\bm{\nu}} solves the forward sensitivity equation

∂τ𝒗𝝂​(τ)=−∇𝒘2LS​(𝒘⁡(τ))​𝒗𝝂​(τ)+1n​∑j=1nνj​∇𝒘ℓj​(𝒘⁡(τ)),\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}\bm{v}_{\bm{\nu}}(\tau)=-\nabla_{\bm{w}}^{2}L_{S}(\bm{w}(\tau))\bm{v}_{\bm{\nu}}(\tau)+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\nu_{j}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell_{j}(\bm{w}(\tau)), (313)
𝒗𝝂​(0)=0,\displaystyle\bm{v}_{\bm{\nu}}(0)=0, (314)

then

dd​λ|λ=0​ψ​(𝑼Q​(𝒘λ​(T)))=⟨∇ψ​(𝑼Q​(𝒘⁡(T))),𝑱Q​(𝒘⁡(T))​𝒗𝝂​(T)⟩.\displaystyle\left.\frac{d}{d\lambda}\right|_{\lambda=0}\psi(\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}^{\lambda}(T)))=\bigl\langle\nabla\psi(\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}(T))),\bm{J}_{Q}(\bm{w}(T))\bm{v}_{\bm{\nu}}(T)\bigr\rangle. (315)
Proof.

Differentiating the weighted flow at λ=0\lambda=0 gives the forward sensitivity equation, and the chain rule yields the terminal formula

dd​λ|λ=0​ψ​(𝑼Q​(𝒘λ​(T)))=⟨∇ψ​(𝑼Q​(𝒘⁡(T))),𝑱Q​(𝒘⁡(T))​𝒗𝝂​(T)⟩.\displaystyle\left.\frac{d}{d\lambda}\right|_{\lambda=0}\psi(\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}^{\lambda}(T)))=\bigl\langle\nabla\psi(\bm{U}_{Q}(\bm{w}(T))),\bm{J}_{Q}(\bm{w}(T))\bm{v}_{\bm{\nu}}(T)\bigr\rangle. (316)

Set 𝑯⁡(τ)≜∇𝒘2​LS​(𝒘⁡(τ))\bm{H}(\tau)\triangleq\nabla_{\bm{w}}^{2}L_{S}(\bm{w}(\tau)). Combining

∂τ𝒗𝝂​(τ)\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}\bm{v}_{\bm{\nu}}(\tau) =−𝑯⁡(τ)​𝒗𝝂​(τ)+1n​∑j=1nνj​∇𝒘ℓj​(𝒘⁡(τ)),\displaystyle=-\bm{H}(\tau)\bm{v}_{\bm{\nu}}(\tau)+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\nu_{j}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell_{j}(\bm{w}(\tau)), (317)
∂τ𝒑ψ,Q​(τ)\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}\bm{p}_{\psi,Q}(\tau) =𝑯⁡(τ)​𝒑ψ,Q​(τ),\displaystyle=\bm{H}(\tau)\bm{p}_{\psi,Q}(\tau), (318)
the cross-term cancels and
dd​τ​⟨𝒑ψ,Q​(τ),𝒗𝝂​(τ)⟩\displaystyle\frac{d}{d\tau}\langle\bm{p}_{\psi,Q}(\tau),\bm{v}_{\bm{\nu}}(\tau)\rangle =1n​⟨𝒑ψ,Q​(τ),∑j=1nνj​∇𝒘ℓj​(𝒘⁡(τ))⟩.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\left\langle\bm{p}_{\psi,Q}(\tau),\sum_{j=1}^{n}\nu_{j}\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell_{j}(\bm{w}(\tau))\right\rangle. (319)

Integrating over [0,T][0,T], using 𝒗𝝂​(0)=0\bm{v}_{\bm{\nu}}(0)=0, and inserting the terminal condition for 𝒑ψ,Q\bm{p}_{\psi,Q} gives the sensitivity formula. ∎

Entry 𝖩i​j\mathsf{J}_{ij} measures how much the test loss at point ii would move under a small downweighting of training point jj. The centered trace tr⁡(𝖩​𝑪n)\operatorname{tr}(\mathsf{J}\bm{C}_{n}) keeps only relative changes among examples.

Definition G.11 (Self-Influence Matrix).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem G.10, fix i,j∈{1,…,n}i,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}, write Qi={zi}Q_{i}=\{z_{i}\}, and let 𝒘(j,λ)\bm{w}^{(j,\lambda)} denote the weighted flow corresponding to 𝝂=𝒆j\bm{\nu}=\bm{e}_{j}. Set

ψi​(𝒖)\displaystyle\psi_{i}(\bm{u}) =ΨZi​(𝒖−𝒚i),\displaystyle=\Psi_{Z_{i}}(\bm{u}-\bm{y}_{i}), (320)
𝒆i​(T)\displaystyle\bm{e}_{i}(T) =𝑼Qi​(𝒘⁡(T))−𝒚i.\displaystyle=\bm{U}_{Q_{i}}(\bm{w}(T))-\bm{y}_{i}. (321)
The self-influence matrix is
𝖩Ψ​(T,S)\displaystyle\mathsf{J}_{\Psi}(T,S) =[𝖩i​j​(T,S)]i,j=1n,\displaystyle=\bigl[\mathsf{J}_{ij}(T,S)\bigr]_{i,j=1}^{n}, (322)
𝖩i​j​(T,S)\displaystyle\mathsf{J}_{ij}(T,S) ≜dd​λ|λ=0​ψi​(𝑼Qi​(𝒘(j,λ)​(T))).\displaystyle\triangleq\left.\frac{d}{d\lambda}\right|_{\lambda=0}\psi_{i}\!\bigl(\bm{U}_{Q_{i}}(\bm{w}^{(j,\lambda)}(T))\bigr). (323)

A single backward sensitivity solve produces every entry 𝖩i​j\mathsf{J}_{ij} along the realized run, and its centered trace estimates population risk from one training pass.

Theorem G.12 (Self-influence matrix from a backward solve).

Under the notation of subsubsection G.3.4, with 𝐉i​(𝐰⁡(T))≜Dw​F​(𝐰⁡(T),zi)\bm{J}_{i}(\bm{w}(T))\triangleq D_{w}F(\bm{w}(T),z_{i}) and 𝐩i\bm{p}_{i} solving the backward sensitivity equation

∂τ𝒑i​(τ)\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}\bm{p}_{i}(\tau) =∇𝒘2​LS​(𝒘⁡(τ))​𝒑i​(τ),\displaystyle=\nabla_{\bm{w}}^{2}L_{S}(\bm{w}(\tau))\bm{p}_{i}(\tau), (324)
𝒑i​(T)\displaystyle\bm{p}_{i}(T) =𝑱i(𝒘(T))⊤∇ΨZi(𝒆i(T)),\displaystyle=\bm{J}_{i}(\bm{w}(T))^{\top}\nabla\Psi_{Z_{i}}(\bm{e}_{i}(T)), (325)
the self-influence matrix entry is
𝖩i​j​(T,S)\displaystyle\mathsf{J}_{ij}(T,S) =1n​∫0T⟨𝒑i​(τ),∇𝒘ℓj​(𝒘⁡(τ))⟩​𝑑τ.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\int_{0}^{T}\langle\bm{p}_{i}(\tau),\nabla_{\bm{w}}\ell_{j}(\bm{w}(\tau))\rangle d\tau. (326)
Corollary G.13 (Generalization estimator from the diagonal).

Under the same hypotheses, the centered trace estimator

Γ^adj​(T,S)\displaystyle\widehat{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{adj}}(T,S) ≜1n​∑i=1n𝖩i​i​(T,S)=1n​tr⁡𝖩Ψ​(T,S)\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathsf{J}_{ii}(T,S)=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{tr}\mathsf{J}_{\Psi}(T,S) (327)

collects the diagonal entries of the self-influence matrix. Set

qi​(λ)≜ψi​(𝑼Qi​(𝒘(i,λ)​(T))).\displaystyle q_{i}(\lambda)\triangleq\psi_{i}\!\bigl(\bm{U}_{Q_{i}}(\bm{w}^{(i,\lambda)}(T))\bigr). (328)

If qiq_{i} is twice differentiable on [0,1][0,1], Taylor with integral remainder gives

qi​(1)−qi​(0)=𝖩i​i​(T,S)+∫01(1−λ)​qi′′​(λ)​𝑑λ.\displaystyle q_{i}(1)-q_{i}(0)=\mathsf{J}_{ii}(T,S)+\int_{0}^{1}(1-\lambda)q_{i}^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)d\lambda. (329)

Appendix H Frozen-Kernel Limit and Classical Phenomena

Intuition.

Classical generalization phenomena (benign overfitting, double descent, implicit bias, grokking, ridge shrinkage) are usually told as separate stories. We show here that, in the frozen-kernel limit, each is a different choice of the spectral filter 𝑴\bm{M} in Theorem H.1. Picking 𝑴\bm{M} selects the phenomenon; the underlying decomposition is unchanged.

In the frozen-kernel limit [17], the signal-channel-and-reservoir picture recovers the classical bias-variance split. Benign overfitting, double descent, implicit bias, and grokking then appear as four choices of the spectral filter 𝑴\bm{M} in Theorem H.1. This appendix collects those instances and shows how each classical phenomenon falls out of a single decomposition.

H.1 Unified Bias–Variance Decomposition

Intuition.

Theorem H.1 below states an exact bias–variance split for any self-adjoint contraction 𝑴\bm{M}: the bias is a quadratic form in the unfit signal direction and the variance is a trace against the noise covariance. Specializing 𝑴\bm{M} to a gradient-flow filter recovers implicit bias and grokking; to a ridge filter, ridge regression; to a hard threshold, the bias–variance trade-off; to a rank truncation, benign overfitting and double descent.

In the frozen-kernel, squared-loss regime, every choice of spectral filter 𝑴\bm{M} produces a single bias-variance decomposition. The bias is a quadratic form in the unfit signal direction, and the variance is a trace against the noise covariance. Picking 𝑴\bm{M} to be a gradient-flow filter, a ridge filter, a hard threshold, or a rank truncation reproduces, respectively, implicit bias and grokking, ridge regression, the bias-variance trade-off, and benign overfitting plus double descent.

A single bias–variance decomposition governs every 𝑴\bm{M}.

Along the predictive-rank path of Section H.1, adding mode r+1r+1 lowers risk iff its signal exceeds its noise and raises risk iff the reverse inequality holds, so the U-shape is the sequence of sign changes of ℛr+1−ℛr\mathcal{R}_{r+1}-\mathcal{R}_{r}.

Remark H.6 (Implicit bias and grokking are the same decomposition in two regimes).

Implicit bias [26, 12] is the 𝑴=𝑴t\bm{M}=\bm{M}_{t} branch of Theorem H.1: gradient flow activates high-mobility modes first because 𝑴t=𝑰−e−t𝚺2/n\bm{M}_{t}=\bm{I}-e^{-t\bm{\Sigma}^{2}/n} is monotone in σj2\sigma_{j}^{2}, and the full interpolating limit is the minimum-norm solution. Grokking [25] is the nonstationary continuation of the same selection principle: in the frozen-kernel, no-manifold limit (γ=0)(\gamma=0) the test transfer mass on the mobile singular space is exactly the spectrum of 𝑴t​𝚪0​𝑴t\bm{M}_{t}\bm{\Gamma}_{0}\bm{M}_{t},

The optimal signal directions theorem (Theorem G.1) is the dynamic extension of the same spectral decomposition: delayed generalization occurs when the leading filtered predictive modes of 𝑴t​𝚪0​𝑴t\bm{M}_{t}\bm{\Gamma}_{0}\bm{M}_{t} (or, in the full theory, CR​(s,T)C_{R}(s,T)) finally dominate the tail.

H.2 Linear Models: from Gradient Flow to Ridge Regression

Intuition.

As a sanity check, we specialize the general theory to a linear model: every operator becomes a closed-form expression in the SVD of the data matrix, and weight-decayed gradient flow interpolates smoothly between two classical limits. Sending the weight decay λ→0\lambda\to 0 recovers minimum-norm interpolation; keeping λ>0\lambda>0 recovers kernel ridge regression. The same spectral filter calculus survives, with the saturation filter replaced by a shrinkage filter.

In the linear-model setting every object in the general theory is available in closed form. Weight-decayed gradient flow then recovers two classical estimators as limits of a single trajectory: minimum-norm interpolation at λ=0\lambda=0, kernel ridge regression at λ>0\lambda>0. We use the linear case to give explicit expressions for the propagator, the cumulative dissipation Gramian, the training displacement, and the transfer operator, and to show that the spectral filter calculus survives the addition of weight decay.

Let F⁡(𝒘,z)=𝒘⊤​𝒙F(\bm{w},z)=\bm{w}^{\top}\bm{x} with p=1p=1 and squared loss ΦS​(𝒖)=12​n​‖𝒖−𝒚‖22\Phi_{S}(\bm{u})=\tfrac{1}{2n}\|\bm{u}-\bm{y}\|_{2}^{2}, and write the data matrix 𝑿=[𝒙1⋯𝒙n]⊤∈ℝn×d\bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1}\ \cdots\ \bm{x}_{n}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} with compact SVD 𝑿=𝑼​𝚺​𝑽⊤\bm{X}=\bm{U}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{V}^{\top}, 𝚺=diag⁡(σ1,…,σr)\bm{\Sigma}=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{r}), r=rank⁡(𝑿)r=\operatorname{rank}(\bm{X}). The Jacobian 𝑱S=𝑿\bm{J}_{S}=\bm{X}, the kernel 𝑲S​S=𝑿​𝑿⊤=𝑼​𝚺2​𝑼⊤\bm{K}_{\!SS}=\bm{X}\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{U}\bm{\Sigma}^{2}\bm{U}^{\top}, and the loss Hessian 𝑩=1n​𝑰\bm{B}=\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{I} are constant; write 𝒂≜𝑼⊤​(𝒚−𝑿​𝒘0)\bm{a}\triangleq\bm{U}^{\top}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\bm{w}_{0}) and 𝑷mob≜𝑼​𝑼⊤\bm{P}_{\mathrm{mob}}\triangleq\bm{U}\bm{U}^{\top}.

Proposition H.7 (Explicit operators for the linear model).

The propagator, cumulative dissipation, training displacement, and test transfer operator on [0,T][0,T] are

𝒫g​(t,0)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{g}(t,0) =e−t𝑲S​S/n,\displaystyle=e^{-t\bm{K}_{\!SS}/n}, 𝒲S​(0,T)\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{S}(0,T) =n2(𝑰−e−2T𝑲S​S/n)𝑷mob,\displaystyle=\tfrac{n}{2}\bigl(\bm{I}-e^{-2T\bm{K}_{\!SS}/n}\bigr)\bm{P}_{\mathrm{mob}}, (358)

where 𝐊S​S−1\bm{K}_{\!SS}^{-1} acts on range⁡(𝐊S​S)\operatorname{range}(\bm{K}_{\!SS}). The optimal predictor is the frozen-kernel map 𝐀∘=𝐊Q​S​𝐊S​S†\bm{A}_{\circ}=\bm{K}_{\!QS}\bm{K}_{\!SS}^{\dagger} and the irreducible remainder vanishes, 𝐑⟂=𝟎\bm{R}_{\perp}=\bm{0}, by Theorem 5.1.

Proof.

Constant 𝑱S\bm{J}_{S} reduces the propagator ODE ∂t𝒫g=−1n​𝑲S​S​𝒫g\partial_{t}\mathcal{P}_{g}=-\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{K}_{\!SS}\mathcal{P}_{g} to a linear matrix equation with solution 𝒫g(t,0)=e−t𝑲S​S/n\mathcal{P}_{g}(t,0)=e^{-t\bm{K}_{\!SS}/n}. Substituting into the definitions and integrating on each eigenspace of 𝑲S​S\bm{K}_{\!SS} via

∫0Tσj2e−2τσj2/ndτ=n2(1−e−2Tσj2/n),\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\sigma_{j}^{2}e^{-2\tau\sigma_{j}^{2}/n}d\tau=\tfrac{n}{2}(1-e^{-2T\sigma_{j}^{2}/n}), (360)

and likewise for 𝑫\bm{D} and 𝑮\bm{G}, yields the displayed formulas. Since 1−e−Tσj2/n>01-e^{-T\sigma_{j}^{2}/n}>0 for every σj>0\sigma_{j}>0, ker⁡𝑫=ker⁡𝑲S​S=ker⁡𝒲S\ker\bm{D}=\ker\bm{K}_{\!SS}=\ker\mathcal{W}_{S}, so 𝑹⟂=𝟎\bm{R}_{\perp}=\bm{0}. Under pure gradient flow from 𝒘0\bm{w}_{0}, the output-space filter is 𝑴t=𝑰−e−t𝚺2/n\bm{M}_{t}=\bm{I}-e^{-t\bm{\Sigma}^{2}/n} and the output evolves as 𝒖⁡(t)=𝒖⁡(0)+𝑼​𝑴t​𝒂\bm{u}(t)=\bm{u}(0)+\bm{U}\bm{M}_{t}\bm{a}. As t→∞t\to\infty the filter saturates (𝑴t→𝑰r\bm{M}_{t}\to\bm{I}_{r}) and the parameters converge to 𝒘0+𝑿†​(𝒚−𝑿​𝒘0)\bm{w}_{0}+\bm{X}^{\dagger}(\bm{y}-\bm{X}\bm{w}_{0}), the minimum-Euclidean-norm interpolant; this is the 𝑴=𝑴t\bm{M}=\bm{M}_{t} instance of the unified bias–variance decomposition (Theorem H.1).

The output-space framework of Section 3 starts from the unpenalized flow ∂t𝒘=−𝑱S⊤​𝒈\partial_{t}\bm{w}=-\bm{J}_{S}^{\top}\bm{g}; weight decay extends the dynamics by adding a −λ​𝒘-\lambda\bm{w} term, and in the linear-model setting the extended dynamics remain explicitly solvable.

Theorem H.8 (Weight-decayed gradient flow converges to ridge regression).

Proposition H.9 (Bias–variance trade-off along the ridge path).

Both the gradient-flow filter 𝐌t=𝐈−e−t𝚺2/n\bm{M}_{t}=\bm{I}-e^{-t\bm{\Sigma}^{2}/n} and the ridge filter 𝐌λ=𝚺2​(𝚺2+n​λ​𝐈)−1\bm{M}_{\lambda}=\bm{\Sigma}^{2}(\bm{\Sigma}^{2}+n\lambda\bm{I})^{-1} are self-adjoint contractions 0⪯𝐌⪯𝐈r0\preceq\bm{M}\preceq\bm{I}_{r}, so the unified bias–variance decomposition (Theorem H.1) applies to each. Gradient flow (𝐌=𝐌t\bm{M}=\bm{M}_{t}) drives the bias to zero as t→∞t\to\infty at the cost of full interpolation variance tr⁡(𝚪0​𝚺𝛇)\operatorname{tr}(\bm{\Gamma}_{0}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{\zeta}}). Ridge regression (𝐌=𝐌λ\bm{M}=\bm{M}_{\lambda}) trades nonzero bias for reduced variance, and the optimal λ\lambda minimizes

𝒂¯⊤​(𝑰−𝑴λ)​𝚪0​(𝑰−𝑴λ)​𝒂¯+tr⁡(𝑴λ​𝚪0​𝑴λ​𝚺𝜻).\displaystyle\bar{\bm{a}}^{\top}(\bm{I}-\bm{M}_{\lambda})\bm{\Gamma}_{0}(\bm{I}-\bm{M}_{\lambda})\bar{\bm{a}}+\operatorname{tr}(\bm{M}_{\lambda}\bm{\Gamma}_{0}\bm{M}_{\lambda}\bm{\Sigma}_{\bm{\zeta}}). (373)
Remark H.10 (Two limits of one dynamics).

The filters in Theorem H.1 and Theorem H.8 are the λ=0\lambda=0 and λ>0\lambda>0 limits of the same weight-decayed flow, whose output-space filter has jj-th diagonal entry

Mjλ(t)=σj2σj2+n​λ(1−e−(σj2+nλ)t/n).\displaystyle M_{j}^{\lambda}(t)=\frac{\sigma_{j}^{2}}{\sigma_{j}^{2}+n\lambda}\bigl(1-e^{-(\sigma_{j}^{2}+n\lambda)t/n}\bigr). (374)

Setting λ=0\lambda=0 and t→∞t\to\infty recovers minimum-norm interpolation; setting λ>0\lambda>0 and t→∞t\to\infty recovers kernel ridge regression. Weight decay preserves the spectral filter calculus and replaces the saturation filter with a shrinkage filter.

Appendix I Additional Experiments

This section reports three additional experiments where empirical-risk training has a documented failure mode (chaotic-dynamics rollout from noisy observations, INR denoising, noisy-preference DPO) and the population-risk update prevents it.

Chaotic dynamics from noisy state observations.

A neural one-step predictor for Lorenz ’63 is trained from sensor-noisy state observations and evaluated against clean held-out dynamics over 33 seeds. The smooth vector field has a coherent gradient mean across minibatches; point-specific sensor noise produces zero-mean, high-variance fluctuations and is suppressed by the population-risk update.

Physics-informed networks with noisy initial conditions.

A PINN solves the linear advection equation ut+β​ux=0u_{t}+\beta u_{x}=0 with periodic boundary at β=5\beta=5, trained from initial-condition observations corrupted by Gaussian sensor noise and evaluated against the clean analytical solution. Empirical-risk fitting drives the network to interpolate the noisy IC and damages the physical prediction; population-risk training suppresses the noise-fitting channel and reaches the target test error substantially faster than any learning-rate-tuned AdamW baseline. The main-text Figure 3 reports relative ℓ2\ell_{2} trajectories, iterations-to-target, and pointwise error fields.

Implicit neural representation denoising.

A coordinate MLP is trained on noisy RGB pixel observations and evaluated against the clean image. The smooth image structure is the coherent signal across coordinate minibatches; pixel-level sensor noise is incoherent.

Noisy preference alignment.

We fine-tune Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with DPO on UltraFeedback preferences where 30%30\% of training pairs have chosen and rejected responses swapped (annotator disagreement). The clean held-out eval set has no label noise; all hyperparameters are shared between AdamW and population-risk training; results are over 3 seeds. The main-text Figure 5 reports sustained accuracy, reward drift from the reference policy, and the accuracy–drift phase plot.
